passages.title: Disavowal of the treaties with the polytheists
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are a single legal document read aloud to Arabia: a formal notice that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are withdrawing from the treaties that bound the Muslims to the idolaters, with a graded timetable of respite for each group affected — and a standing offer of safe conduct to any one of them who wants to come and hear the Qur'an for himself.

One proclamation holds them together. Ayah 1 announces the disavowal; ayah 2 sets the general four-month grace period; ayah 3 makes it public at the year's largest gathering; ayah 4 protects those who had kept faith; ayah 5 states what follows when the grace period runs out; ayah 6 leaves a door deliberately open.

## A surah that opens without the Bismillah

This is the one surah not headed by *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm*, and why sets the tone for what follows. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Jibrīl would indicate where each revealed ayah belonged, and at the seam between surahs the Bismillah would come down to mark the join. With Sūrah At-Tawbah — among the very last surahs revealed — none came, and the Prophet ﷺ did not instruct the scribes to write one. Ibn Kathir notes the same: the Companions did not write it in the muṣḥaf they collected under ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him.

The reason comes from ʿUthmān himself, in a narration found in Abū Dāwūd, An-Nasāʾī, the Musnad of Aḥmad and Tirmidhī. Ibn ʿAbbās asked why this surah follows Al-Anfāl when the ordering principle — longer surahs first — would have put it before. ʿUthmān replied that the Qurʼān was a serious matter and precaution was required: At-Tawbah might not be an independent surah at all but part of Al-Anfāl. (ʿUthmān also reported that in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime the two were called *qarīnatayn*, "the two connected ones" — via Mazharī.) Al-Anfāl's verses came earlier, and no revelation authorised putting later material first, so the order stood; and if At-Tawbah were a continuation, a Bismillah there would be like writing one mid-surah. A space was left instead.

ʿAlī, reported through Ibn ʿAbbās, added another angle: the Bismillah is an assurance of protection, and this surah is precisely where the assurance of protection and the pledge of peace given to the disbelievers is terminated. Maʿārif treats this as "a refinement of approach" that does not displace the documented cause.

**A practical ruling follows.** One reciting straight through from Al-Anfāl should not say the Bismillah; one *beginning* at this surah, or in its middle, should. Maʿārif corrects two common errors: thinking it is never permitted here, and substituting *aʿūdhu billāhi min an-nār* ("I seek Allah's protection from the Fire"), for which there is no proof from the Prophet ﷺ or his Companions.

The two names summarise the surah: **Barāʾah**, disengagement from any responsibility for what the disbelievers do; and **At-Tawbah**, the announcement that the repentance of the believers has been accepted (Mazharī).

## How Arabia arrived at this moment

In year 6 of the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ set out for ʿUmrah; the Quraysh blocked him, and the treaty of Ḥudaybiyah followed — a ten-year moratorium on war (its term as reported in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*). A clause let the other tribes attach themselves to whichever side they chose: Khuzāʿah allied with the Prophet ﷺ, Banū Bakr with the Quraysh. Crucially, an ally counted as the party itself — attacking an allied tribe, or arming an aggressor against it, breached the treaty. In year 7 the Muslims performed the missed ʿUmrah and left after three days exactly as stipulated. Neither side had violated anything.

Then, within five or six months, Banū Bakr launched a night ambush on Banū Khuzāʿah — and the Quraysh supplied them weapons and men, calculating that the Prophet ﷺ was far away and darkness would hide it. Khuzāʿah brought him the news. He began quiet preparations for war and said nothing publicly at all.

That silence terrified Makkah. After Badr, Uḥud and the Aḥzāb the Quraysh no longer trusted their own strength; they had come to accept that some unseen power was working for the Muslims. They sent Abū Sufyān to Madinah to apologise and renew the treaty; he saw the war preparations, asked one senior Companion after another to intercede, and every one refused. On the tenth of Ramaḍān, year 8, the Prophet ﷺ marched out, and Makkah was conquered.

**And then he forgave them.** Those who had privately believed came forward openly. Those who clung to disbelief were, with a few exceptions, granted amnesty. He said to them what Yūsuf عليه السلام said to his brothers in Egypt: *"This day, there is no blame on you."* Revenge, punishment, even reproach for the past — none of it entered his thinking. Maʿārif calls it a demonstration of morals others could not have dreamed of.

That amnesty is the backdrop to ayat 1–6. This is not a victor settling scores; the scores had already been dropped.

## Four groups, four different rulings

Treaties had been openly flouted and secretly conspired against, and this led the Prophet ﷺ, by long experience and divinely inspired indication, to decide that no further treaties would be made and the Arabian Peninsula would be a Muslim heartland. But turning people out without giving them time was, says Maʿārif, not appropriate under Islam's principle of justice and equity, nor under the Prophet's ﷺ own universal mercy. So the surah opens with four rulings for four situations:

**1. Those who broke the treaty themselves — the Quraysh of Makkah.** They had forfeited their rights, so no extra respite was owed; but the sacred months were in force and their sanctity had to be honoured. Their ruling is **ayah 5**: when the sacred months expire, they must leave, accept Islam, or face war.

**2. Those with a fixed-term treaty who had honoured it** — Banū Ḍamurah and Banū Mudlaj of Banū Kinānah, who (as Khazin reports) still had nine months to run. Their ruling is **ayah 4**: *"they have abated nothing of your rights and backed no one against you, so fulfil the treaty with them up to their term."* Ibn Kathir stresses that anyone holding a covenant with Allah's Messenger ﷺ kept it to its own expiry date, however distant — provided they neither broke its terms nor helped others against the Muslims. The ayah closes, *"Surely Allah loves those who have taqwā"* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as those who keep their promises.

**3 and 4. Those with an open-ended treaty, and those with no treaty at all.** One ruling covers both: **ayat 1–2**, four months to move freely through the land. Ibn Kathir adds that this absorbed anyone whose treaty had less than four months left — their term was extended up to four.

Notice the shape: the group that betrayed the treaty got the *least*, the group that kept it got the *most*. Fidelity was rewarded even amid a general disengagement.

## The proclamation at Mina

The rulings took effect from the moment they were publicly promulgated across Arabia — and ayah 3 is that promulgation: *"a declaration from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the greatest day of Hajj."*

Ibn Kathir records that this part of the surah came down after the Prophet's ﷺ return from Tabūk, during the Hajj season. He considered attending, then remembered that the idolaters would be there as always, circling the House naked, and he disliked to be among them at that. So he sent Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the Hajj of year 9 and teach the people their rites, and to tell the idolaters this was their last Hajj.

After Abū Bakr had departed, he sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib to deliver this news to the idolaters on the Messenger's ﷺ behalf; Ibn Kathir gives the reason that ʿAlī was the Messenger's cousin. Ibn Kathir also relays a narration that Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, who said that when Barāʾah was revealed and Abū Bakr had already been sent to oversee the Hajj rites, the Prophet ﷺ was asked, "O Messenger of Allah, why not send this message to Abū Bakr?" He answered: *"It will not be accepted to have been from me if it is not from a man from my family."* He then called ʿAlī and gave him the opening section of Barāʾah to proclaim at Minā on the Day of Sacrifice: that no disbeliever would enter Paradise, no idolater would perform Hajj after that year, there would be no naked ṭawāf, and whoever held a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have it honoured until its term expired.

ʿAlī rode the Prophet's ﷺ camel Al-ʿAḍbāʾ and caught Abū Bakr on the road. Abū Bakr asked, "Are you here as a commander or a follower?" ʿAlī answered, "A follower." They went on together — Abū Bakr leading the Hajj, ʿAlī proclaiming among the tribes camped in their old familiar places. Abū Hurayrah, in a report in Al-Bukhārī, says he was among those sent through Minā on the Day of Sacrifice to announce that no idolater would perform Hajj after that year and no naked person would circle the Kaʿbah — and by the year of the Farewell Hajj, not one idolater performed Hajj.

Abū Maʿshar Al-Madanī reports from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb Al-Quraẓī and others that ʿAlī carried thirty or forty ayat of Barāʾah, recited them on the day of ʿArafah, and that the four months were counted out concretely: the remaining twenty days of Dhūl-Ḥijjah, then Muḥarram, Ṣafar, Rabīʿ al-Awwal, and ten days of Rabīʿ ath-Thānī.

Maʿārif, commenting on this same ayah, adds that as a further precaution the proclamation was carried by ʿAlī to distant Yemen as well, and works out what the four rulings meant as dates on a calendar: the Makkans who had broken the treaty had until the end of Muḥarram of year 10; Banū Ḍamurah and Banū Mudlaj until Ramaḍān of year 10; and the third and fourth groups until the tenth of Rabīʿ ath-Thānī of year 10. Anyone who defied the order after his date made himself liable to armed confrontation — and by the following year's Hajj, no disbeliever was to remain within the state's limits.

## "The greatest day of Hajj"

The scholars differed over *yawm al-ḥajj al-akbar* in ayah 3. Ibn Kathir takes it as the Day of Sacrifice — the most visible day of the rites, when the largest crowd gathers. Maʿārif reports that Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn az-Zubayr held it to mean the day of ʿArafah, on the strength of the Prophet's ﷺ words *"ʿArafah is the Hajj"* (Abū Dāwūd, Tirmidhī); others said the tenth of Dhūl-Ḥijjah, the Day of Sacrifice. Sufyān ath-Thawrī and others reconciled the views by holding that all five days of Hajj are its substantiation, ʿArafah and the Day of Sacrifice included — the singular "day" for a stretch of days being ordinary Arabic, as the Qurʼān calls the several days of Badr *yawm al-furqān*. It is the *greater* hajj because ʿUmrah is the lesser.

## Ayah 5 — "the ayah of the sword," read in its place

Ayah 5 is famous, and famously lifted out of its setting. Read where it sits, it is the enforcement clause of a notice publicly served months in advance.

*"So when the sacred months have passed…"* — Mujāhid, ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, Qatādah, As-Suddī and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam all understood the months here to be the four-month grace period of ayah 2. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: upon the end of the four months during which fighting was withheld — the grace period We gave them — then fight them. *"Wherever you find them"* means the earth in general, excluding the Sacred Precinct, since Allah said, *"And fight them not at Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām unless they fight you there"* (2:191). *"Capture them"* — some executed, some taken prisoner. *"Besiege them and lie in wait for them in every ambush"* — not waiting passively, Ibn Kathir explains, but seeking them in their strongholds and watching the roads, so that the wide land closes in around them.

Then the clause that ends the whole matter in a breath: *"But if they repent and establish the prayer and give zakāh, then leave their way free. Verily Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* Ibn Kathir observes that Allah names the highest elements of Islam after the two testimonies — the prayer, which is Allah's right, and zakāh, which benefits the poor and needy — which is why the two are so often paired. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh."*

Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq argued from this ayah, among others, when he fought those who withheld zakāh after the Prophet ﷺ died; Maʿārif notes that by pointing to this verse he satisfied the Companions, and draws the principle: the credibility of a professed entry into Islam rests on three things together — repentance from past disbelief, establishing the prayer, and paying zakāh.

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said this ayah abrogated every peace agreement, treaty and term between the Prophet ﷺ and any idolater — hence its name, the ayah of the sword. Al-ʿAwfī reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said the same historically: after Barāʾah was revealed and announced, no idolater retained a treaty or promise of safety, and the four months together with every earlier peace treaty had ended by the tenth of Rabīʿ al-Ākhir.

## Ayah 6 — the door left open

And yet the passage does not end on the sword. Ayah 6 addresses the Prophet ﷺ about the very people he has just been commanded to fight: *"And if anyone of the idolaters seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the Word of Allah; then escort him to where he can be secure — that is because they are a people who do not know."*

Ibn Kathir reads it exactly so: one of those whose blood and property had been made lawful asks for safe conduct — grant it, recite the Qurʼān to him, present the religion so that Allah's proof is established, then see him safely back to his own land. Mujāhid (via Ibn Abī Najīḥ) says the ayah concerns whoever comes to hear what was revealed: safe on the way, safe while he listens, safe on the way home. The reason is in the ayah's closing words — they simply do not know; this is how the call of Allah spreads among His servants.

This was already the Prophet's ﷺ practice. Ibn Kathir recalls the Quraysh envoys at Ḥudaybiyah — ʿUrwah ibn Masʿūd, Mikraz ibn Ḥafṣ, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr — who came to mediate and were so astonished by the reverence the Muslims showed the Prophet ﷺ, unlike anything they had seen for kings, that they carried the report home; this was among the reasons many later accepted Islam. Even the emissary of Musaylimah the Liar was spared, the Prophet ﷺ telling him that only the rule that emissaries are not killed stood between him and execution. Ibn Kathir sums up: those who come from hostile territory bearing a message, for trade or to negotiate peace, and who ask a Muslim authority for safe conduct, are granted it until they go home.

From this ayah Maʿārif, drawing on Imām Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ, derives four points: if a non-Muslim asks Muslims to demonstrate the truth of Islam with sound proofs, it is a duty to answer him; it is obligatory to admit and protect anyone coming to learn about Islam, and impermissible to harm him — though Al-Qurṭubī restricts this to one whose purpose is to hear the Word of Allah, other purposes being left to the authorities' discretion; the stay is bounded by that purpose; and the ruler must arrange the visitor's safe return.

## Living it

- **Victory is not a licence for revenge.** The amnesty at Makkah is the model: an enemy standing helpless before you is not to be paid back. The relief of revenge is momentary; Allah's pleasure and the ranks of Paradise are lasting. Restraint in triumph also proves the fight was never for the self — the line, says Maʿārif, between jihād and a king's war.
- **Forgiveness is not naïveté.** Pardoning does not mean leaving yourself open to the next betrayal; you take the lesson of experience and close the gaps. The Prophet ﷺ said that a person is not bitten twice from the same hole. The staged withdrawal in these ayat *is* that wisdom in action.
- **No one is moved without notice.** Driving weak people out, or attacking them, without reasonable warning is cowardly and ignoble. A public announcement comes first, with real time to leave — which is what year 9's proclamation and graded deadlines gave.
- **Honour an agreement to its last day.** Even where annulling a treaty is permitted, it is far better to let it expire on its own, as with Banū Ḍamurah and Banū Mudlaj. The closing words of ayah 4 — that Allah loves those of taqwā — hint, says Maʿārif, that Muslims should never hunt for lame excuses to escape a pledge, as nations at large habitually do.
- **The enmity is to disbelief, not to persons.** Muslims oppose disbelief because it is what ruins a person here and hereafter, so even their opposition is at root a wish for that person's good — which is why the chance to offer sincere counsel is never let go, in war or peace. Read ayat 1–6 again with that in mind and you can hear it: alongside the withdrawal runs a strain of sympathetic insistence — *"if you repent, it is better for you"* in ayah 3, *"if they repent… leave their way free"* in ayah 5, and in ayah 6 an armed escort for a man whose only request was to listen.

passages.title: Why treaty-breakers forfeit their covenant
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat answer the question any reader of the opening of Sūrat al-Tawbah is bound to ask: on what grounds does Allah dissolve the treaties with the idolaters? The answer is not simply "because they are idolaters." It is because they had already torn the agreement up themselves — and the passage proves it, diagnoses why, and then, remarkably, leaves the door open for them to walk back in.

The unit moves in a single arc: a challenging question (ayah 7), an exception carved out for the party that kept faith (also 7), the evidence and the root cause of the treachery (8–10), the way back into the community (11), and finally the ruling if the treachery is repeated (12).

## The history that unlocks the passage

Ibn Kathir explains that here Allah "mentions the wisdom in dissolving all obligations to the idolators" after giving them a four-month period of safety. That wisdom is a story, and it is worth having in front of you as you read.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that a cease-fire agreement with the Quraysh of Makkah had been concluded at Ḥudaybiyah in the sixth year after the Hijrah — the very occasion the Qur'an refers to elsewhere when it describes the Makkans as "the ones who disbelieved and hindered you from Al-Masjid Al-Haram" (48:25). Ibn Kathir records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims preserved the terms of that treaty — which included a peace of ten years — from the month of Dhul-Qaʿdah of that sixth year onward. The breach did not come from the Muslim side.

It came when the Quraysh broke the treaty and helped their allies, Banū Bakr, against Khuzāʿah, who were the allies of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Aided by the Quraysh, Banū Bakr killed some of Banū Khuzāʿah — and did it inside the Sacred Area. The treaty was dead, and it was the Quraysh who had killed it.

What followed is worth reading slowly. In the month of Ramadan of the eighth year the Messenger of Allah ﷺ led an army to Makkah, and Allah opened the Sacred Area for him. Ibn Kathir's account of the aftermath is striking: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ freed those of the Quraysh who embraced Islam after they were overpowered and defeated — they numbered around two thousand, and they were referred to afterwards by the name *Tulaqāʾ*. And those among them who remained in disbelief and ran away from Allah's Messenger ﷺ were sent promises of safe refuge for four months, during which they were allowed to move about freely. They included Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl and many others. Ibn Kathir closes the account by noting that Allah later guided them to Islam, and they became excellent believers.

So when ayah 7 asks **"How can such polytheists have a treaty with Allah and His Messenger?"** — the question is not cruelty. It is put to people who had already answered it by their own actions.

## The exception, and the discipline it teaches

The question in ayah 7 is rhetorical, but Allah does not let it become a blanket verdict. He immediately excepts "those with whom you made a covenant near Al-Masjid Al-Haram" — that is, Ibn Kathir says, on the day of Ḥudaybiyah — and commands: *fa-mā istaqāmū lakum fa-staqīmū lahum*, "So long as they are true to you, stand you true to them," which Ibn Kathir glosses as: if they keep the terms of the treaties you conducted with them, you keep them too.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this exception is doing, and it is one of the most important lessons in the passage. The fact was that most of the Makkans had broken their pledge. Naturally, when something like this happens, people tend to make a sweeping allegation against everyone. The Qur'an refuses. By saying "except those with whom you made a treaty near al-Masjid al-Ḥarām," it exempts those who had *not* broken their pledge, and then orders that the Muslims stay firm on their commitment as long as the others remain committed and faithful to theirs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: the breach of trust committed by other people should in no case influence their stance, so that they themselves are led to become breakers of the pledge given to them.

That is why the ayah ends not with a threat but with **"Verily, Allah loves those who have Taqwa."** Whatever else taqwā includes, this ayah places within it the keeping of your word to a hostile party for as long as they keep theirs — and it says that Allah loves those who do it.

## "Ill" and "dhimmah": the two bonds they would not honour

Ayah 8 presses the question again — *kayfa*, "how?" — and then supplies the reason: **"How? When if you are overpowered by them, they regard not the ties, either of kinship (*ill*) or of covenant (*dhimmah*)?"** Two words carry the weight here, and both are technical.

Ibn Kathir reports that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, ʿIkrimah and al-ʿAwfī narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said: **"*Ill* means kinship, while *dhimmah* means covenant."** Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk and As-Suddī said similarly.

Ibn Kathir's own summary of the ayah is that if these disbelievers have a chance to defeat the Muslims, they will cause great mischief, leave nothing unharmed, and disregard the ties of kinship and the sanctity of their vows. That is what makes such a treaty worthless — not the paper, but the character of the party signing it. Ibn Kathir adds that in this ayah Allah encourages the believers to show enmity to the idolaters and to dissociate from them, affirming that they do not deserve to enjoy a covenant of peace, because of their Shirk in Allah and disbelief in Allah's Messenger ﷺ.

The second half of ayah 8 turns from behaviour to interior: **"With their mouths they please you, but their hearts are averse to you, and most of them are rebellious."** Notice *most*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the precision: when the text says *aktharuhum fāsiqūn* ("most of them are sinners"), it hints that all of them were not like that. There were some nice people among them too, who wanted to stand by their commitment, but they were not heard before others. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this to the same subject the Qur'an takes up elsewhere in very clear terms: *"and malice against a people should not bid you to not doing justice"* (5:8). Even in a passage declaring the end of a treaty, the Qur'an will not let hatred round the numbers up.

## The diagnosis: what a soul sells, and for how much

Ayah 9 gives the root cause: **"They have purchased with the Ayat of Allah a little gain, and they hindered men from His way; evil indeed is that which they used to do."**

Ibn Kathir explains the transaction: the idolaters exchanged following the Ayat of Allah for "the lower affairs of life that they indulged in," and then went further — trying to prevent the believers from following the truth. Betrayal was not their first sin; it was a symptom.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on why these Mushriks were so chronically treacherous and what it was that ailed them, and answers: their relentless love of the material. The desire to acquire, possess and expend the limitless range of things of this world had blinded them to the limit that they would not hesitate to sell off the very Words of Allah and their own faith in exchange for paltry gains. And it makes a point easily missed: this diagnosis was given to them as a prescription of hope to ponder about, so that they could still correct themselves if they chose to — not only an indictment. At the same time, Muslims at large were served with a warning that they should take their guard against the pitfall of treachery and disobedience which had sucked these people in, and make total abstention from this behaviour model their distinct life style.

Notice the pricing in the words *thaman qalīl*, "a little gain." Allah does not say they got nothing. They got something — it was simply not worth what they paid for it.

Ayah 10 then repeats the phrase from ayah 8 with one change: **"With regard to a believer, they respect not the ties, either of kinship or of covenant! It is they who are the transgressors."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the shift: this was no isolated case of disbelieving people acting treacherously against Muslims to whom they were bound by ties of kinship and treaty obligations. It describes a settled pattern — a people who would never consider kinship or pledge as valid grounds when dealing with Muslims.

## Ayah 11: the door that stays open

Given that behaviour pattern, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, it could have been but natural for Muslims to have become disillusioned with them forever and to refuse any brotherly relationship with them under any condition. **"Therefore, as the Qur'anic justice and equity would have it,"** the eleventh verse gives this instruction: **"But if they repent, perform the Salah and give the Zakah, then they are your brethren in religion."**

Not "then leave them alone." Not "then tolerate them." *Brothers.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the demand this places on the offended party: once an enemy — no matter how deadly and no matter how hurtful he has been — becomes a Muslim, things change dramatically. Allah forgives his past sins, all of them. So it becomes obligatory on Muslims too that they should forget the past, start afresh, take them as their brothers in faith, and do whatever it takes to fulfil the rights enjoined under such a relationship.

**Why these three conditions?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as the three conditions of entry into the Islamic brotherhood: (1) *tawbah*, repentance from Kufr and Shirk; (2) establishment of Salah; (3) payment of Zakah. And it explains the wisdom: *īmān* (faith) and *tawbah* (repentance) are concealed matters, and common Muslims cannot find out their reality — no one can see into a heart. Therefore two of their outward signs were mentioned, Salah and Zakah, as the visible evidence the community can actually act on.

Two consequences follow, both reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:

**Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās** said that this verse has made the blood of Muslims who qualify as "the people of the Qiblah" unlawful (*ḥarām*). In other words, people who establish Salah, pay Zakah, and have said or done nothing against Islam as proved against them shall be taken as Muslims in the matter of all religious injunctions — even though they may not have true *īmān* in their hearts, or have hypocrisy (*nifāq*). The community judges by what is visible; hearts belong to Allah.

**Sayyidnā Abū Bakr** quoted this verse in support of his declaration of jihād against those who had refused to pay Zakah after the passing away of the Holy Prophet ﷺ — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes (citing Ibn Kathir) that the noble Companions before whom he made this assertion were satisfied with his approach. The logic is the ayah's own: brotherhood was granted on three stated conditions, so a group that publicly discards one of them has stepped outside the terms it was granted on.

The ayah closes: **"And We elaborate the verses for people who understand."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as a stress upon the need to abide by the given injunctions — both those regarding people covered under a treaty and those who have repented. The detail is given so that it will be followed.

## Ayah 12: if they break it again

**"But if they violate their oaths after their covenant, and attack your religion with disapproval and criticism, then fight (you) against the leaders of disbelief — for surely, their oaths are nothing to them — so that they may stop."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a striking choice of words. The situation in the text demanded *fa-qātilūhum*, "then fight **them**." Instead the Qur'an says *fa-qātilū aʾimmata l-kufr*, "then fight **the leaders of infidelity**," bypassing the shorter pronoun — *aʾimmah* being the plural of *imām*. The sense, it explains, is that these people, by breaking their word of honour, turned into leaders of infidelity and thus became deserving of a war against them. The statement also carries the wisdom and the justification of the command to fight. Some commentators, it adds, say that "leaders of infidelity" here refers to the chiefs of the tribe of Quraysh in Makkah who kept on instigating people against Muslims and remained busy making war preparations — mentioned particularly because these people were the real source of the power the Makkans were credited with, and because they were the ones with whom the Muslims had bonds of close kinship, so there was the possible apprehension that some concession could be granted in their case.

Ibn Kathir reports that **Qatādah and others** said the leaders of disbelief were Abū Jahl, ʿUtbah and Shaybah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and he went on to mention several others. Ibn Kathir also relates that **al-Aʿmash narrated from Zayd ibn Wahb from Ḥudhayfah**: "The people of this Ayah were never fought again," and that a similar statement was reported from **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn Kathir's own judgement, however, is that this ayah is general, even though the specific reason behind revealing it was the idolaters of Quraysh — so it generally applies to them and others as well, "Allah knows best."

Ibn Kathir then relates that **al-Walīd ibn Muslim said that Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr narrated that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr said** that when **Abū Bakr** sent an army to Ash-Shām, he advised them: "You will find some people with shaved heads. Therefore, strike the swords upon the parts that contain the devil, for by Allah, it is better to me to kill one of these people than to kill seventy other men. This is because Allah said, *(then fight (you) against the leaders of disbelief.)*" Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected it.

**"And attack your religion."** Ibn Kathir takes this second condition seriously: it is because of this, he says, that one who curses the Messenger, peace be upon him, or attacks the religion of Islam by way of criticism and disapproval, is to be fought.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important qualification, and it matters for how a Muslim society treats its non-Muslim citizens. Some commentators have interpreted "speak evil of your Faith" to mean that speaking evil of the Faith of Muslims is included under contravention of the pledge — a person who speaks evil of Islam and its Sharīʿah cannot continue to be a party to the treaty with Muslims. But, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states, **according to a consensus of Muslim jurists**, what is meant is vilification that is done to insult and belittle Islam and Muslims, openly and publicly. Honest intellectual criticism, while conducting research into problems and rulings, remains exempt from its purview — then it is not supposed to be vilification in its lexical sense. The conclusion it draws: for non-Muslim citizens of Dār al-Islām, any honest intellectual criticism can be allowed, but what cannot be allowed is vilification, contempt, insult or outrage against Islam.

**"Their oaths are nothing to them."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings, and both are instructive. First: these are the kind of people none of whose oaths are trustworthy, because they are addicted to breaking their oaths and committing breaches of trust. Second, taking the plural form seriously: when they broke their oath, they also absolved the Muslims of any responsibility for their own oath and pledge. A contract torn by one hand does not stay binding on the other.

## Why the passage ends the way it does

The last words of ayah 12 are *laʿallahum yantahūn* — **"so that they may stop."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: so that they may refrain from the disbelief, rebellion and the transgression they indulge in.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds the whole ethic of the passage on this closing clause. The objective of the jihād carried out by Muslims should never be the conquest of countries like common kings, or to hurt the enemy and take vengeance as belligerent people around the world would love to do. Instead, when it comes to fighting that they must, the driving objective should be **compassion for the enemy** — the empathy and the desire that they would stop doing what was not right.

That is a remarkable place for the passage to land, and it is consistent with everything before it: the treaty upheld with whoever kept it, the refusal to condemn all for the sin of most, the door left open in ayah 11, and now a war aim defined as *the enemy stopping*, not the enemy ending.

## Living it

- **Keep your word first, and keep it longest.** Ayah 7 ends by saying that Allah loves those who have taqwā, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the rule explicit: someone else's breach of trust is never a licence for yours.
- **Do not let "most of them" become "all of them."** Ayah 8 says *most*, and the Qur'an elsewhere forbids letting malice against a people push you into injustice (5:8).
- **Audit the price.** Ayah 9 describes people who sold the Words of Allah for a paltry gain. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as a warning served on Muslims too — not only a description of someone else.
- **Let repentance close the file.** Ayah 11 obliges you to receive a former enemy as a brother in faith once Allah has forgiven him. Holding the past over a new Muslim is not caution; it is a refusal of what this ayah commands.
- **Distinguish honest criticism from contempt.** The jurists' consensus reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws that line for a whole society; a believer can at least draw it in his own dealings.

passages.title: The command to fight and the believers' test
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat finish the case for fighting the treaty-breakers and then turn the question around onto the believers themselves. Ayat 13–15 lay out why this enemy had forfeited its treaty and what Allah intends to accomplish *through the hands of the believers*; ayah 16 asks the believers whether they imagined they would be left alone, untested. The thread holding all four together is that the fighting is never only about the enemy — it is also about what Allah is doing with the hearts of those He commands.

## A question that is really a summons (13)

Ayah 13 does not open with an order. It opens with a question: **أَلَا تُقَٰتِلُونَ قَوۡمٗا** — "Will you not fight a people…?" Ibn Kathir says these ayat "encourage, direct and recommend" fighting against the idolaters who broke the terms of their covenants. The form is persuasion rather than bare command: the listener is being brought to see the case for himself.

Then come three charges, each stated as settled fact:

- **نَّكَثُوٓاْ أَيۡمَٰنَهُمۡ** — they broke their oaths.
- They "intended to expel the Messenger" ﷺ — in Ibn Kathir's rendering of the second charge.
- **وَهُم بَدَءُوكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ** — and they were the ones who attacked first.

Ibn Kathir places three other ayat beside the second charge, showing it is a documented pattern rather than a rhetorical flourish: the plot "to imprison you, or to kill you, or to expel you" (8:30); "and have driven out the Messenger and yourselves… because you believe in Allah your Lord" (60:1); and "they were about to frighten you so much as to drive you out from the land" (17:76). The expulsion of the Prophet ﷺ is one of the recurring crimes the Qur'an records against his opponents.

## Who exactly is being described? Two readings

Here the commentators differ, and it is worth hearing both.

**Ibn Kathir** reads the passage as being about the Makkan idolaters — those "who tried to expel the Messenger ﷺ from Makkah."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads the phrase about conspiring to expel the Messenger ﷺ as referring to the Jews of Madinah, who had hatched a plan to drive him from the city and who had said, "the one having more honour and power will certainly expel the one being humble and weak from there" (63:8). In their own view, they were the people of honour and power while the Muslims were weak and lowly. Maʿārif observes that Allah answered them in His own way: He took their proud statement as it was and made it come true in a manner that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, by turning the Jews out of Madinah, proved that honour belonged to the Muslims and disgrace to those who had made the boast.

Both readings answer to the same description the ayah gives: a party that broke its oaths and wanted the Prophet ﷺ gone.

## "They started it" (13)

On **وَهُم بَدَءُوكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ**, Ibn Kathir reports two identifications. The first is Badr: the idolaters marched out to protect their caravan, and when they knew the caravan had escaped safely, they still went ahead with their intent to fight the Muslims, out of arrogance. The second — "it was also said" — is that these ayat refer to the idolaters breaking the peace agreement with the Muslims and aiding Banū Bakr, their allies, against Khuzāʿah, the ally of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ marched to Makkah in the year of the victory and conquered it.

Maʿārif draws the plain conclusion: they were the aggressors, and "what Muslims have to do now is simply to defend themselves, an action universally sane and normal." The passage is arguing, not merely commanding.

## "Do you fear them?" (13)

**أَتَخْشَوْنَهُمْ ۚ فَاللَّهُ أَحَقُّ أَن تَخْشَوْهُ** — "Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you should fear Him." Notice that the same verb of fearing is used both times. The ayah does not tell the believers to feel nothing; it tells them their fear is pointed at the wrong object.

Ibn Kathir renders the sense in Allah's own voice: 'Do not fear idolaters, but fear Me instead, for I am worthy of being feared by the servants due to My might and punishment. In My Hand lies the matter; whatever I will occurs, and whatever I do not will does not occur.' Maʿārif makes the practical point in a single line: fear Him, "for there is no power that can cause His punishment to disappear."

The clause **إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ**, "if you are believers," is the sharpest word in the ayah. Maʿārif takes it as a working definition: fearing anyone or anything other than Allah *in a manner that obstructs the fulfilment of the injunctions of the Sharīʿah of Islam* is not what a true believing, practising Muslim would do. That is a usable test. Fear as an emotion is not the problem. Fear that stops obedience is.

## One command, five outcomes (14–15)

Ayah 14 finally gives the order — **قَاتِلُوهُمْ**, "fight them" — and then attaches to it a chain of five consequences, each following from that single command:

1. **يُعَذِّبْهُمُ اللَّهُ بِأَيْدِيكُمْ** — Allah will punish them *by your hands*.
2. **وَيُخْزِهِمْ** — and disgrace them.
3. **وَيَنصُرْكُمْ عَلَيْهِمْ** — and give you victory over them.
4. **وَيَشْفِ صُدُورَ قَوْمٍ مُّؤْمِنِينَ** — and heal the breasts of a believing people.
5. **وَيُذْهِبْ غَيْظَ قُلُوبِهِمْ** — and remove the anger of their hearts.

Ibn Kathir introduces this as Allah "ordering the believers and explaining the wisdom of ordaining Jihād against them, all the while able to destroy their enemies with a command from Him." That last clause is the key to the whole passage: the outcome was never dependent on them. Maʿārif says the same thing from the other side: the enemy had already become deserving of divine punishment because of their evil deeds, but that punishment would not come down upon them from the heavens or up from beneath the earth — instead, "Allah shall punish them at their hands."

So the believer is the instrument, not the author. That single insight cancels two opposite errors at once: the arrogance of thinking the outcome is manufactured by our strength, and the passivity of thinking we may stand aside because Allah does not need us.

The fourth outcome uses the vocabulary of medicine — **يَشْفِ**, He heals — as if the long injury inflicted on the believers were a wound in the chest. Maʿārif spells it out: as a result of this fighting Allah will mollify the hearts of the Muslims after all those pains and sorrows continuously inflicted upon them by the disbelievers, and the anger which filled Muslim hearts because of their treachery and pledge-breaking was to be removed by Allah when He punishes them at their hands. Ibn Kathir notes that "a believing people" here **includes all believers**, even though Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and As-Suddī said it refers to Khuzāʿah.

## The intention test hidden inside the promise (14, read with 12)

Maʿārif makes the most searching observation in the whole passage, and it is easy to miss. In the previous ayah (12), the reason given was **لَعَلَّهُمْ يَنتَهُونَ**, "so that they may stop." Maʿārif reads that as an instruction to the Muslims themselves: they should not fight a people just to release their anger; rather they should make the correction and betterment of those people the main purpose of their action. And then — "when they cleanse their intention from all irrelevant shades, and let it be for Allah alone, and fight for none but Allah, then, Allah Taʿālā shall cause things to unfold in a manner that automatically removes the feelings of anger and sorrow raging in their hearts."

Read the two ayat together and something quietly profound emerges. The healing of the breast and the removal of rage promised in ayat 14 and 15 are a *gift*, not a goal. Make them the goal and, by Maʿārif's own standard, the intention has not been cleansed. Aim at Allah alone, and they are handed to you.

## "And Allah accepts the repentance of whom He wills" (15)

The last clause of ayah 15 — **وَيَتُوبُ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَاءُ** — is the most unexpected sentence in the passage. Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: from among His servants. Maʿārif draws out what that means here: this is an added gain as a result of this struggle — there would be many from among the enemies who would have the tawfīq of Islam (the divine enabling to accept it) and would become Muslims. And so it happened: at the Conquest of Makkah there were many arrogant ones who were put to disgrace, while there were many others who embraced Islam.

Sit with that. The people named at the head of the passage as oath-breakers and aggressors are, some of them, the community's own future. It fits with what Maʿārif drew from ayah 12: the purpose set before the Muslims was that the enemy should stop, and that their correction and betterment be the main aim — not the release of anger. A believer, then, is never entitled to write off the human being in front of him. The door Allah leaves open is not ours to close.

Maʿārif adds a further note: history proves that the circumstances and events predicted in these verses were witnessed one by one as pointed out by the Holy Qur'an, and therefore these verses contain many miracles. They were spoken before the outcome and verified by it.

## ʿAlīm and Ḥakīm (15)

Ayah 15 closes on two names. Ibn Kathir glosses **عَلِيمٌ** as All-Knowing "in what benefits His servants," and **حَكِيمٌ** as All-Wise "in His actions and statements, whether narrative or legislative." He then adds: "Allah does what He wills, decides what He wills, and He is the Just Who never wrongs any. Not even the weight of an atom of good or evil is ever neglected with Him, but rather, He compensates for it in this life and the Hereafter."

Placed at the end of a command to fight, this is a guarantee about the ledger. Nothing done by either side — an atom's weight of good, an atom's weight of evil — is mislaid.

## Ayah 16: the question turns around

**أَمۡ حَسِبۡتُمۡ أَن تُتۡرَكُواْ** — "Do you think that you shall be left alone?" Everything so far has been about them. Now it is about you.

Ibn Kathir unpacks it: do you think, O believers, that We will leave you untested "with matters that make apparent those who have pure, good intent from those who have false intent?" The wording of the ayah is *not yet* — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "while Allah has not yet tested those among you who have striven hard and fought."

The test has two markers, and the second is the more searching:

- **الَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا مِنكُمْ** — those among you who strove hard and fought.
- **وَلَمْ يَتَّخِذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ وَلَا رَسُولِهِ وَلَا الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلِيجَةً** — and who took no *walījah* besides Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the believers.

**Walījah** is the word to sit with. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "supporters and confidants" — the intimate you let inside, the one whose approval quietly steers you. The ayah does not merely ask whether a person turned up to the fight. It asks whether, while doing so, he kept a private line of loyalty running outside this circle. Ibn Kathir's contrast is exact: rather, "they are sincere for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ inwardly and outwardly." Outward participation with an inward second allegiance is precisely what the trial exposes.

Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels, and together they show this is a standing pattern rather than a one-off: "Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, 'We believe,' and will not be tested. And We indeed tested those who were before them…" (29:1–3); "Do you think that you will enter Paradise before Allah tests those of you who fought in His cause and also tests those who are patient?" (3:142); and "Allah will not leave the believers in the state in which you are now, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good" (3:179).

**On "while Allah has not yet tested…"** — Ibn Kathir gives his summary here. Since Allah legislated Jihād for His servants, He explained that the wisdom behind doing so includes testing His servants, distinguishing between those who obey Him and those who disobey Him. And in the same breath he affirms: "Allah, the Exalted, is the All-Knower of what occurred, what will occur, and the true essence of what might occur had He decided it. Therefore, Allah knows everything before it occurs and how it will occur." His knowledge encompasses even what would have happened had He decided otherwise. Ibn Kathir sets these two statements side by side without treating them as a difficulty — the testing is real, and Allah's knowledge is complete before anything occurs. He closes: "there is no deity worthy of worship except Him, nor a Lord except Him. Truly, there is none who can avert Allah's judgment and decision."

## Living it

- **Audit your fear.** The ayah does not ask you to feel nothing. Maʿārif's test is specific: fear becomes the problem when it obstructs the fulfilment of what the Sharīʿah requires of you.
- **Check for a walījah.** Is there someone outside the circle of Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers whose approval is quietly the thing you are actually steering by? Ayah 16 says a trial is how what is inward is made apparent.
- **Never act to vent.** Maʿārif's reading of ayah 12 together with ayah 14 is a rule for the heart: relief of your own anger may be granted to you, but it may not be your aim. Cleanse the intention and the relief comes as a gift.
- **Be an instrument, not an author.** "Allah will punish them by your hands" makes you responsible for the effort and leaves the outcome with Him, who was able to destroy them by a command from Him.
- **Keep the door open.** "Allah accepts the repentance of whom He wills" stands in the same passage as the command to fight, and Maʿārif reads it as the enemies themselves receiving the tawfīq of Islam — as many of them did at the Conquest of Makkah. If Allah has not written anyone off, neither may you.
- **Expect the test.** "Do you think that you shall be left alone?" is not a threat. Read with 29:1–3 and 3:179, it is Allah telling a community that He tests them so that what is true in them is distinguished from what is false.

passages.title: Who has the right to tend Allah's mosques
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath.** These six ayat settle a question of ownership: who actually has the right to tend Allah's houses of worship? Ayat 17–18 answer in principle — not those who associate partners with Allah, but those whose belief and practice match the purpose the building was raised for. Ayat 19–22 answer a rival claim: the services the Makkans boasted of — watering pilgrims, tending the Sacred Mosque — do not weigh against faith, migration and striving in Allah's way; then Allah names what awaits those who did strive. One principle holds the unit together: a deed is weighed by the faith behind it, not by the prestige of the place it is done in.

## The moment these ayat address

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the flow. The preceding ayat exposed how the Makkan mushrikūn broke their pledges, and ayah 16 told the Muslims that jihad is a test marking out the sincere believer from the hypocrite and the weak in faith. Ayat 17–18 now turn to a different purification: cleansing al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and the other mosques of false modes of worship and putting correct worship in their place.

After the conquest of Makkah the Prophet ﷺ cleared out of the Baytullah and the Sacred Mosque every idol the mushriks had worshipped. But he ﷺ had also granted his old enemies pardon and protection, and they carried on performing their worship and ṭawāf there in their own inherited manner. The site was clean of idols but not of idolatry.

The only way to finish the work was to bar the mushriks from the Sacred Mosque — yet that would have cut against the protection already promised, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that abiding by the terms of a treaty was far more important in Islam. So the order was not issued at once. It came the year after the conquest, when the Prophet ﷺ had Sayyidunā Abū Bakr and Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them) announce at Minā and ʿArafāt that no worship, Hajj or ṭawāf done in the mushrik way would be permitted there in future — and the jāhilī custom of circling the House naked ended in the same announcement. At Minā Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) proclaimed: *"After this year, no Mushrik will perform Hajj and no naked person will make Ṭawāf of Baytullah."*

## The word the passage turns on: ʿimārah

Everything hangs on the verb *yaʿmuru* and its noun *ʿimārah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it as a many-sided word covering three things:

1. **Building** — raising and finishing the mosque, inside and out.
2. **Maintaining** — security, sanitation, upkeep, supplies, administration.
3. **Populating** — believers actually present in the mosque for worship.

Of that third sense Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says there is no exact equivalent in English; the nearest is *to populate, to people, to fill up* — to make the mosque flourish in the number of those present and the quality of the worship they perform there. *ʿUmrah* takes its name from this same root, because one visits the Baytullah and makes the best of being there in worship.

## Ayah 17: why the claim fails

Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) reports the occasion. His father, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, still a mushrik then, was taken prisoner at Badr, and the Muslims reproached him for staying on the side of kufr. He answered: *"You only remember what is bad about us… Do you not know that we are the custodians of the Sacred Mosque? We take care of the building. We keep it filled with people. We manage it and we run a drinking water service for the pilgrims."* Thereupon ayah 17 was revealed.

The reply is not that these services were worthless in themselves, but that these men had no right to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason plainly: a masjid is a place built to worship Allah alone, and shirk and kufr are its antithesis. Their kind of worship would not let a mosque flourish; it would make it desolate. Ibn Kathir notes a reading of the ayah as *"Masjid Allah"* in the singular; on that reading it refers to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, the most honoured mosque on earth, built from the first day for the worship of Allah alone without partners, by Khalīl ar-Raḥmān, the Prophet Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him.

**"While they witness against themselves of disbelief."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir, gives two readings. It may mean that by what they did as mushriks they were virtually confessing their kufr. Or it refers to how they identified themselves socially — as As-Suddī put it, *"If you ask a Christian, 'What is your religion?', he will tell you he is a Christian. If you ask a Jew about his religion, he will say he is a Jew, and the same for a Ṣābi' and a Mushrik."* Either way, the testimony that disqualifies them is their own.

Then the verdict: their works are in vain — Ibn Kathir says *because of their shirk* — and in the Fire they will abide. He sets beside it 8:34, on those who hinder men from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām: *"And why should not Allah punish them while they hinder men from Al-Masjid Al-Haram, and they are not its guardians? None can be its guardians except those with Taqwa, but most of them know not."* (Taqwā: the mindfulness of one who keeps within Allah's limits.)

## Ayah 18: the positive side

Ayah 17 states the negative; ayah 18 takes up the positive. The word *innamā* ("only") restricts the role to a described type of person, and the description is fivefold. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: building mosques in the real sense can be done only by those bound by Allah's commandments in both their ʿaqīdah (belief) and their ʿamal (practice). Ibn Kathir draws out what this means from Allah's side: **Allah testifies to the faith of those who maintain the mosques.**

**Faith in Allah and the Last Day.** Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, glosses this as: he who singles out Allah in worship and has faith in the Last Day; he who believes in what Allah has revealed. Why is faith in the Messenger ﷺ not mentioned? Because, answers Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, there is no way one can have faith in Allah except by putting one's faith in His Messenger ﷺ and wholeheartedly accepting the commandments that come through him. Hence the Prophet ﷺ once asked his Companions, "Do you know what īmān in Allah is?" They said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: *"Īmān in Allah is that one bears witness that there is no one worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."* (Cited from Mazharī with reference to al-Bukhārī and Muslim.)

**Ṣalāh and zakāh.** Ibn Kathir reads the pair as two whole dimensions of life: ṣalāh is "one of the major acts of worship practised by the body," zakāh "the best act that benefits other people." Ibn ʿAbbās specifies ṣalāh here as the five daily prayers.

**"And fear none but Allah."** Ibn Kathir: they fear only Allah and none else; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as worshipping Allah alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a qualification: what is meant is that *in matters of religion* one should not abandon a command of Allah out of some fear. Ordinary fear of what causes pain or brings loss — beasts, snakes, thieves, robbers — is quite natural: when the magicians' ropes and staffs appeared as snakes, Sayyidunā Mūsā *"sensed fear within himself"* (20:67), and such normal fear is contrary neither to the injunction of the Qur'an nor to the station of a prophet, a walī or saint. What is forbidden is becoming so overcome by fear that one starts creating confusion about Allah's injunctions, or leaves them out altogether.

**"It may be that they are among the rightly guided."** Ibn ʿAbbās explains the force of the tentative-sounding *ʿasā*: Allah is saying, *"It is they who are the successful ones in truth."* He compares Allah's word to His Prophet ﷺ, *"It may be that your Lord will raise you to Maqām Maḥmūd"* (17:79) — and the report continues that Allah shall grant him a station of praise, that is, the intercession on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbās's rule: *"Every 'might' in the Qur'an means 'shall'."*

## From the Sunnah: the mosque and its people

- ʿAbd ar-Razzāq narrated that ʿAmr ibn Maymūn al-Awdī said: *"I met the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and they were saying, 'The Masjids are the Houses of Allah on the earth. It is a promise from Allah that He is generous to those who visit Him in the Masjids.'"* (These are the Companions' words, not the Prophet's ﷺ.)
- The Prophet ﷺ said: when you notice that a person is punctual with his presence in the mosque, bear witness to his īmān — because Allah has said, *"The mosques of Allah are built up only by those who believe in Allah…"* Imām Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah reported this on the authority of Sayyidunā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him).
- It appears in al-Bukhārī and Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ said: for a person who presents himself in the mosque morning and evening, Allah sets aside a rank of Paradise.
- Sayyidunā Salmān al-Fārisī (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said: one who comes into the mosque is a visiting guest of Allah — and it is incumbent on the host that He honour the guest. (Cited from Mazharī with reference to Ṭabarānī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Bayhaqī and others.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that whoever keeps coming to the mosque — to supervise its upkeep, or for dhikr, or to learn his religion, or to recite or teach the Qur'an — is a perfect believer. Qāḍī Thanā'ullāh of Pānīpat draws the other edge of the same word: tending the mosque also requires that it be **cleansed of things and practices it was not made for** — buying and selling, worldly conversation, searching for lost property, asking people for material help, idle poetry, disputation, fighting, and disturbing the peace with noise. (Mazharī)

**Two rulings** follow. Since "maintaining" here refers to the trusteeship and administrative responsibility of the mosque, a kāfir may not be appointed trustee or administrator of any Islamic waqf (endowment) — though for constructing the units of the structure, walls and doors, it does not matter if a non-Muslim is assigned the job (Tafsīr Marāghī). And when a non-Muslim makes a mosque as an act of thawāb (reward-earning merit), or contributes funds for its building, it is permissible to accept it — on condition that there is no danger of religious or worldly loss, or blame, or usurpation of the property later, or harping on the favour done (Al-Durr al-Mukhtār, Shāmī, Marāghī).

## Ayat 19–20: the comparison

Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained ayah 19 thus: the idolaters said, *"Maintaining Al-Masjid Al-Haram and providing water for pilgrims are better than embracing the faith and performing Jihad,"* and they used to boast and show off among the people on that basis. Ibn Kathir links this to 23:66–67, where Allah describes them turning back on their heels, *"in pride, talking evil about it by night"* — talking by night about their custodianship of the Sanctuary while shunning the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ.

**At Badr.** Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said the ayah was revealed about al-ʿAbbās when, captured at Badr, he said: *"If you rushed before us to embrace Islam, perform Hijrah and Jihad, we were maintaining Al-Masjid Al-Haram, providing water for the pilgrims and setting the indebted free."* Allah's answer, as Ibn ʿAbbās puts it: all these actions were performed while committing shirk, *"and I do not accept the good deeds that are performed while in a state of Shirk."* Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim describes the same scene.

**After al-ʿAbbās accepted Islam.** In narrations from the Musnad of ʿAbd ar-Razzāq, Sayyidunā Ṭalḥah ibn Shaybah, Sayyidunā al-ʿAbbās and Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them) were comparing merits: Ṭalḥah held the keys of the Baytullah, al-ʿAbbās administered the water service for pilgrims. ʿAlī said, "I do not understand that which makes you so proud. As for me, I have said my prayers facing the Baytullah six months before anyone of you, and I have participated in jihad with the Prophet ﷺ." Thereupon these ayat were revealed.

**By the Prophet's ﷺ pulpit.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, on the authority of Sayyidunā Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with him) — Ibn Kathir gives the same account as recorded by ʿAbd ar-Razzāq — that Companions sat near the Prophet's ﷺ pulpit on a Friday. One said he would care for no deed after Islam other than providing drinking water for pilgrims; another said the same of maintaining al-Masjid al-Ḥarām; a third said jihad in the cause of Allah is more righteous than what they had said. Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) admonished them — *"Do not raise your voices next to the Minbar of the Messenger of Allah"* — and said that as it was a Friday, they would pray the Friday prayer first and then go to the Prophet ﷺ and ask him. Then this ayah was revealed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles these: there is nothing far-fetched in the possibility that the ayat came down answering the pride of the mushriks, and that later, when unpleasant things took place among Muslims, the same ayat were used as the deciding argument — which may have given listeners the feeling they were revealed for that particular incident. Read contextually, faith and jihad are each superior to the two services: faith's superiority answers the mushriks, jihad's corrects the Muslims who ranked those services above it.

The close of ayah 19, *"And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people,"* is aimed at those very claimants: Ibn Kathir says Allah described them with injustice on account of their shirk, so their maintaining the mosque will not avail them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Allah does not bless the unjust and the wrongdoing with the gift of understanding, so they keep at their crooked hairsplitting into things that are otherwise open and obvious.

**A qualification about dhikr.** Qāḍī Thanā'ullāh says in Tafsīr Mazharī that jihad is given precedence over ʿimārah here *in terms of physical and outward maintenance* — building, repair, cleaning and allied arrangements. But ʿimārah is not restricted to that sense alone: it also means being present in the mosque for worship and the dhikr of Allah — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the genuine flowering of the whole purpose of making and manning a mosque comes out from this factor alone. Taken that way, the Prophet ﷺ himself placed it above jihad. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the report of Sayyidunā Abū ad-Dardā' (may Allah be pleased with him) appearing in the Musnad of Ahmad and in Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah: the Prophet ﷺ asked whether he should tell them of an act superior to all their acts, that would raise their ranks to the highest levels, superior to spending gold and silver in the way of Allah, and superior still to bravely fighting their enemies in jihad where they kill and are killed. The Companions said, "Do tell us about that act, yā Rasūlallāh." He said: *"That act is the dhikr of Allah."*

Why then does ayah 19 rank jihad above ʿimārah? Because, answers Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the pride shown by the mushriks was not based on dhikr and the worship performed in the mosque, but on its structural and administrative aspects. And the ranking shifts with attending conditions: when Islam and the Muslims must be defended at all costs, jihad is more meritorious than all other acts of worship — as at the battle of Khandaq, where the Prophet ﷺ had four of his daily prayers to make up. Conversely, when the need is not so acute, dhikr and worship are the more meritorious.

**Ayah 20** enlarges on *"they are not equal."* Those who believed, emigrated, and took up jihad in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives are *greater in rank in the sight of Allah*, and *"they are the successful ones."* The mushriks against them, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, simply had no measure of success whatsoever; and while Muslims in general share that success in essence, the success of those identified here had more to it.

## Ayat 21–22: what they are told

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān introduces these two ayat as telling us of the great reward and ranks these successful people shall have in the life to come: *"Their Lord gives them the happy news of Mercy from Him, and Pleasure, and of Gardens having an everlasting bliss for them, where they shall dwell forever. Surely, it is Allah with whom there is a great reward."*

**Mercy from Him** and **His pleasure** — riḍwān, that Allah is pleased with them — are named before the Gardens.

## Living it

- The real flourishing of a mosque shows in the number of those present and the quality of their worship — building and upkeep exist for the sake of that presence.
- Your steady presence there is a testimony Allah accepts about your faith.
- The boast at Badr warns anyone who does religious work: a service rendered to Allah's House does not sanctify the one who performs it. Deeds done in a state of shirk are not accepted; Allah weighs the faith behind the act.
- Never let fear of people move you to soften or abandon a command of Allah. Ordinary fear is natural; that particular surrender is not.

passages.title: When family becomes dearer than Allah
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Ayah 23 forbids the believer from taking even fathers and brothers as *awliyāʾ* — a word Ibn Kathir's translation renders "supporters" and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "friends" — when those relatives have chosen disbelief over faith. Ayah 24 turns the same principle into a question the reader cannot dodge: if eight of the dearest things in a person's life are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and *jihād* (striving hard and fighting in His cause), then wait and see what comes.

**Every bond has a limit, and that limit is where it collides with your bond to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ**. Ayah 23 states the rule; ayah 24 measures you against it.

## Where this passage sits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places these ayat among verses that mention the merits of *Hijrah* (migration) and *Jihād* — obligations that required a person to leave his country, relatives, friends, companions, wealth and property "all in one stroke." Surrendering all those attachments at once is most difficult and painful. So ayah 23 first disapproves of limitless attachment to those very things, and thereby prepares Muslim minds to welcome Hijrah and Jihād.

Ayah 24, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, was revealed essentially about people who did **not** migrate from Makkah at the time migration had been made obligatory for them. Their love for family and property had stopped them from carrying out their obligation to migrate.

## Ayah 23: "if they prefer disbelief to belief"

Ibn Kathir summarises the command: Allah commands shunning the disbelievers, even if they are one's parents or children, and prohibits taking them as supporters if they choose disbelief instead of faith.

**The condition.** The prohibition is not on fathers and brothers as such. It is tied to a clause: *in istaḥabbū al-kufra ʿalā al-īmān* — "if they prefer disbelief over faith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that as for the need to maintain strong bonds of kinship with parents, brothers and sisters and other kinsfolk, and to treat all of them generously, the Qurʼān remains full of relevant instructions. This ayah does not cancel any of that. What it makes clear is that **"each relationship has a limit"** — and that when kinship comes onto a collision course with one's relationship with Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, the relationship that has to be kept intact is the one with Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; all relationships competing against it are to be ignored.

The ayah ends by naming whoever befriends such people as one of *al-ẓālimūn* — rendered "the wrongdoers" in both commentaries before us.

## What Ibn Kathir brings alongside it

Ibn Kathir sets these ayat next to a verse of Sūrat al-Mujādilah (58:22): *You will not find any people who believe in Allah and the Last Day, making friendship with those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even though they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred. For such He has written faith in their hearts, and strengthened them with a Rūḥ from Himself. And He will admit them to Gardens under which rivers flow.*

That verse does not only prohibit — it **describes**: such friendship is simply not found among people who believe in Allah and the Last Day.

Ibn Kathir then reports that al-Ḥāfiẓ al-Bayhaqī recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin Shawdhab: the father of Abū ʿUbaydah bin al-Jarrāḥ was repeatedly praising the idols to his son on the day of Badr, and Abū ʿUbaydah kept avoiding him. When al-Jarrāḥ persisted, his son headed towards him and killed him — and this verse of Sūrat al-Mujādilah was revealed in his case. That is the sharpest edge of the principle, on a battlefield in open war. It stands here as Ibn Kathir places it: as the occasion of that verse — not as a description of how a Muslim ordinarily deals with a non-Muslim parent.

## Ayah 24: the eight things

The ayah counts:

1. **your fathers** — the people you came from
2. **your sons** — the people who came from you
3. **your brothers** — the ones beside you
4. **your wives** — the closest companionship
5. **your kindred** — the wider clan
6. **the wealth that you have gained** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as wealth "amassed and collected"
7. **the commerce in which you fear a decline** — not wealth in hand, but trade whose slump you dread
8. **the dwellings in which you delight** — Ibn Kathir: those you prefer and love because they are comfortable and good

Nothing on the list is shameful in itself. These are the very bonds the Qurʼān elsewhere commands us to honour, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses. The question is not whether they are loved but where they stand.

Against these eight the ayah sets three: **Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and striving hard and fighting in His cause**. And the word it uses is *aḥabb* — "dearer." It does not ask whether you love Allah. It asks whether these are dearer to you *than* He is.

## "Then wait until Allah brings about His command"

The response to failing this test is a single word of command: *fa-tarabbaṣū* — "then wait." Ibn Kathir reads it as: wait for what will befall you of Allah's punishment and torment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two named readings of what "His command" refers to:

- **Mujāhid** said the "command" here means the command to carry out Jihād and conquer Makkah: Makkah shall stand conquered, those who chose to discard their appointed duty shall face disgrace, and their bonds with the people and things they fancied shall be of no avail to them.
- **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** said the "command" here means the command of punishment: those who sacrificed their bonds relating to the Hereafter for the sake of what was merely material, and did not migrate as instructed, would be seized by it fairly soon — either here in this mortal world, or in the Hereafter, which is certain.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an observation. The warning is against abandoning the obligation of *migration* — yet what the ayah mentions is *Jihād*, the step after Hijrah. The hint embedded here, it says, is that the real thing has not happened yet. What had come so far was no more than the initial command to migrate, and there were people who did not have the courage to do even that. Ahead of them lay the command of Jihād, following which they would have to surrender all worldly attachments for the sake of love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and even stake their lives. (It also allows that migration may here have been made to stand for Jihād, since in reality Hijrah too is nothing but a department of Jihād.)

The closing clause — *And Allah does not lead the sinning people to the right path* — is read by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as a verdict on the whole calculation. Those who, despite the standing command of migration, opted for their temporal relationships and kept clinging to family, relatives, wealth and property shall soon find that this conduct of theirs was not going to serve their purpose **even in this mortal world**. Once the command of Jihād comes, these very attractions turn into burdens too cumbersome to go along with — because Allah does not allow the sinning and the disobedient to achieve their desired objective.

## From the Sunnah

**Imam Ahmad recorded** that Zuhrah bin Maʿbad said that his grandfather said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while he was holding the hand of ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb. ʿUmar said, 'By Allah! You, O Messenger of Allah, are dearer to me than everything, except for myself.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *'None among you will attain faith until I become dearer to him than even himself.'* ʿUmar said, 'Verily, now, you are dearer to me than myself, by Allah!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *'Now, O ʿUmar!'*" Ibn Kathir notes that **al-Bukhārī** also collected this hadith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith of Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) **in the two collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim**, that the Prophet ﷺ said: no one can be a true believer until he becomes to him dearer than his father, his children, and everyone else in this world.

It also cites a hadith of Abū Umāmah (may Allah be pleased with him) **appearing in Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī**, that the Prophet ﷺ said: anyone who takes a friend or makes an enemy for the sake of Allah, or spends his wealth or withholds it for the sake of Allah, has made his faith perfect. These narrations, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, prove that perfection of faith depends on the dominance of love for the Prophet ﷺ over every other love, friendship and enmity, concession and reservation — all of which must remain subservient to the will and command of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

And in a hadith **in al-Bukhārī and Muslim** cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the Prophet ﷺ named three traits which, if found in a person, would bless him with the **sweetness of faith**: that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are, in his sight, dearer than anything other than them; that he loves a servant of Allah for Allah's sake only; and that the very thought of *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) gives him the feeling of being thrown into the fire.

Ibn Kathir also records that **Imam Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd** (the wording being Abū Dāwūd's) reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *"If you transact in ʿīnah* — which the hadith itself identifies as a type of *ribā*, unlawful gain in a financial dealing — *follow the tails of cows (tilling the land), become content with agriculture and abandon Jihād, Allah will send on you disgrace that He will not remove until you return to your religion."* That is the seventh item of ayah 24 — the commerce whose decline is feared — followed to its end.

## Which love is being asked of you

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays something that rescues many readers from despair. Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī and other commentators said that there are very few people who could be considered exempt from the warning in this ayah, since even the greatest among those who practise and teach religion seem subdued by their love for family and belongings — with the exception of those Allah wills to be otherwise.

But al-Bayḍāwī explains further: **the "love" meant here is love that is within one's control.** It has nothing to do with the love that is natural — because Allah does not obligate anyone beyond his capacity and control. A person may have his heart full of natural love for worldly bonds; what is required is that he not let it overpower him to the point that he starts acting against the will and command of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. If he does not, this warning will not apply to him, and he will be taken as one who keeps his love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ above everything.

The illustration given is of a patient who gets nervous about an unpleasant medicine or an unexpected surgery. That nervousness is natural. But he agrees to the treatment rationally, since it is for his own good — and that is not blameworthy; nor does commonsense demand that he first rid himself of the nervousness. Likewise, if someone feels naturally uncomfortable in complying with some divine injunction because of his love for wealth and children, yet bears the discomfort and carries the injunction out, that is not blameworthy either. In fact, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is **praiseworthy**.

That said, the commentary does not lower the ceiling: love should come to prevail over one's nature as well, turning every discomfort welcome in doing what the Beloved would like. Think of the seekers of material comfort: day in and day out they embrace the hardest conceivable labour with a smile to get what they want; for a salary cheque at the end of the month, a man will sacrifice sleep, comfort and social relationships. The People of Allah, when they seek Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and the blessings of the life to come, reach a station of love which pales out any thought of pain and discomfort. The "sweetness of faith" in the hadith above names that very station — and, as the commentary puts it, love has its own chemistry of turning the sour into the sweet. Some Muslim scholars have pointed out that a heart enriched with the sweetness of faith starts passing it on to the other parts of the body, which begin to relish it during acts of worship and obedience; in some reports the same thing is called the ecstasy of faith. And in hadith — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes it without naming a collection — the Prophet ﷺ said: *the delight of my eyes is in Salāh.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two further voices. Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh of Pānīpat said in *Tafsīr Maẓharī* that this station of love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is a great blessing, but can be acquired only when one stays close to the People of Allah — which is why the Muslim mystics consider it necessary that it be sought with shaykhs (spiritual guides). And the author of *Rūḥ al-Bayān* said this station of friendship can be acquired by whoever is ready — like Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm *Khalīlullāh*, "the friend of Allah" (peace be upon him) — to sacrifice everything for the love of Allah: wealth, children, life, everything.

## The Companions as the proof

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this precedence as the way of the noble Companions, and the reason they rose to be the superior-most people of this Ummah: it was some trail they blazed, sacrificing all that was with them — life, wealth, property, relatives and bonds of all sorts — only for the sake of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

That the bond of Islam was supreme and universal stood proved when **Bilāl from Ethiopia, Ṣuhayb from Byzantium, Salmān from Persia**, the Quraysh from Makkah and the Anṣār from Madīnah became brothers to one another.
