Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the atmosphere: enemy foot soldiers and riders looking for them in hot pursuit; the hiding place no fortified fortress but just a cave, with the search party reaching close to its edges.

Inside, Abū Bakr was afraid — and both sources are careful about what he feared. Ibn Kathir: he "was afraid the pagans might discover them for fear that some harm might touch the Messenger ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: he "was worried, not for his own safety, but about his master," while the master himself "was sitting calm like a mountain at peace." Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet ﷺ kept reassuring him and strengthening his resolve. Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas that Abū Bakr said, "I said to the Prophet when we were in the cave, 'If any of them looks down at his feet, he will see us.'" He ﷺ replied: **"O Abū Bakr! What do you think about two, with Allah as their third?"** This is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

The Qur'an preserves his words to his companion as **"Be not sad; surely, Allah is with us."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the reader to put the conditions of that night before their eyes and ask whether someone dependent on mere material means could be that tranquil.

**"Then Allah sent down His sakīnah upon him."** *Sakīnah* is glossed in the translation itself as calmness, tranquillity, peace. Ibn Kathir gives one explanation and reports another without deciding between them: Allah "sent His aid and triumph to His Messenger ﷺ, or they say it refers to Abu Bakr."

**"And strengthened him with forces which you saw not."** Ibn Kathir: the angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows that "these troops could be troops of angels, and of the elemental forces of the entire universe too — for they are, so to say, a virtual army of Allah."

**"And made the word of those who disbelieved the lowermost, while the Word of Allah became the uppermost."** Ibn ʿAbbās commented: "The word of those who disbelieved" is *shirk* (idolatry — the creed of the idolaters who drove the Prophet ﷺ out), while "the Word of Allah" is *lā ilāha illa'llāh*, there is no god but Allah.

Ibn Kathir brings that same phrase forward as the measure of a fighter's intention. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a man who fights because of courage, or out of rage for his honour, or to show off — which of them is in the cause of Allah? He ﷺ said: **"He who fights so that Allah's Word is superior, then he fights in Allah's cause."**

The ayah closes on two of Allah's names. Ibn Kathir: **al-ʿAzīz**, the All-Mighty — "in His revenge and taking retribution, He is the Most Formidable," and those who seek refuge with Him and take shelter by adhering to what He instructs "are never made to suffer injustice"; and **al-Hakīm**, the All-Wise — wise "in His statements and actions."

## Ayah 41: light or heavy

**"March forth, whether you are light or heavy, and strive hard with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah."** Sufyān ath-Thawrī narrated from his father, from Abū ad-Duhā Muslim bin Subayh, that this ayah "was the first part to be revealed from Surah Bara'ah" — Sūrah Barā'ah being this sūrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in this fourth verse the command given earlier is repeated for emphasis: once the Prophet of Allah orders people to come out, they must come out as a matter of absolute obligation, "for on the compliance of this command hinges all that is good for them."

*Khifāfan wa thiqālan* — light and heavy — was filled in by the early authorities from several angles. Muʿtamir bin Sulaymān narrated that his father said Hadramī claimed he was told that some people used to declare they would gain no sin by lagging behind because they were ill or old, and that this ayah was revealed. As-Suddī glossed it: "whether you are rich, poor, strong, or weak." Ibn Kathir summarises the command as binding on the believers to march forth with the Messenger ﷺ "regardless whether they felt active, lazy, at ease or had difficult circumstances."

**Abū Talhah.** ʿAlī bin Zayd narrated that Anas said Abū Talhah commented on this ayah: "Whether you are old or young, Allah did not leave an excuse for anyone." Abū Talhah marched to Ash-Shām and fought until he was killed. In another narration, he was reciting Sūrah Barā'ah until he reached this ayah, and then said, "I see that Allah had called us to mobilize whether we are old or young. O my children! Prepare my supplies." His children said, "May Allah grant you His mercy! You conducted Jihad along with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until he died, then with Abu Bakr until he died, then with 'Umar until he died. Let us perform Jihad in your place." He refused, and went to the sea, where he died. They could not find an island to bury him on until nine days later, during which his body did not deteriorate or change; then they buried him on the island.

**The old man of Damascus.** Ibn Jarīr reported that Hibbān bin Zayd ash-Sharʿabī narrated: they had mobilised with Safwān bin ʿAmr, governor of Hims. Among the army was an old yet active man of Damascus, his eyebrows sunk over his eyes from age, riding on his animal. "O uncle! Allah has given you an excuse," Hibbān said to him. He replied: "O my nephew! Allah has mobilized us whether we are light or heavy. Verily, those whom Allah loves, He tests them. Then to Allah is their return and eternal dwelling. Allah tests from His servants whoever thanks Him and observes patience and remembrance of Him, all the while worshipping Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored, and worshipping none else."

**What of those genuinely unable?** Ibn Kathir records As-Suddī's account: a man came forward, and he was fat, and complained and asked permission to stay behind, and the Prophet ﷺ refused; then this ayah was revealed and it became hard on the people — so, in As-Suddī's words, Allah abrogated it with "There is no blame on those who are weak or ill or who find no resources to spend, if they are sincere and true in duty to Allah and His Messenger" (9:91).

**Wealth and lives.** Ibn Kathir reads **"and strive hard with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah"** as Allah encouraging spending in His cause and striving with one's life seeking His pleasure and the pleasure of His Messenger ﷺ. And **"this is better for you, if you but knew"**: better, he says, "in this life and the Hereafter. You might spend small amounts, but Allah will reward you the property of your enemy in this life, as well as, the honor that He will keep for you in the Hereafter." He then cites the Prophet ﷺ as saying that Allah has promised the one who strives in His cause that if He brings death to him He will enter him into Paradise, or He will return him to his house with whatever reward and war spoils he earns. (Ibn Kathir gives this without naming a collection.)

The "if you but knew" is answered by the ayah Ibn Kathir sets beside it: "Jihad is ordained for you though you dislike it, and it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you and that you like a thing which is bad for you. Allah knows but you do not know" (2:216). He closes with a report from Imam Ahmad: Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man, "Embrace Islam," and the man said, "I dislike doing so." The Messenger ﷺ said, "Embrace Islam even if you dislike it."

## What the passage asks of a reader

The disease this passage names is not confined to one campaign. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names one perfect treatment: concern for the Ākhirah, the Hereafter. It places that belief among the three principles on which the articles of faith rest: *Tawhīd* (the Oneness of Allah), *Risālah* (the true mission of the messenger and prophet sent by Allah), and *Ākhirah* (the Hereafter). Of these, it says, belief in the Hereafter "is, in all reality, the moving spirit for correction of deeds and serves as an iron wall before crimes and sins." It presses the point at the modern world: material progress has reached its zenith, laws proliferate, the machinery to implement them grows — and crime increases anyway, because the disease has not been properly diagnosed and the line of treatment is not sound. The only correction it knows for that frame of mind is to remember Allah and think about the life to come; and wherever that prescription was used, it says, whole societies became models of humanity at its best — as happened in the blessed period of the Prophet ﷺ and the age of his noble Companions.

So the four ayat, read together: ayah 38 names the heaviness and prescribes an accurate measure of what this world is actually worth. Ayah 39 warns that those who will not come out face a painful punishment and replacement by another people. Ayah 40 removes the thought that the religion depends on anyone's support, by pointing at two men in a cave with Allah as their third. And ayah 41 says: march, light or heavy, with your wealth and your lives. Abū Talhah, reading that last ayah aloud as an old man, drew from it the shortest summary of it — "Allah did not leave an excuse for anyone."

passages.title: The hypocrites who begged to stay behind
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are one sustained exposure of the men who came to the Prophet ﷺ with excuses so they would not have to march to Tabuk. A single question runs through all of them — *who asks to stay behind, and why?* — and the passage answers it by circling the same men from every side, tightening as it goes: an anonymous crowd whose loyalty has a price (42), the permission that let them hide (43), the line that separates two kinds of heart (44–45), the evidence that the excuse was empty and why their absence was a mercy (46–47), an old habit and not a sudden lapse (48), and at last a single speaker whose one sentence gives the whole game away (49).

Ibn Kathir sets the scene plainly: Allah is admonishing those who lagged behind and did not join the Prophet ﷺ for the battle of Tabuk — those who asked his permission to remain behind, falsely pretending to have legitimate reasons. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most of the seventeen verses of this section deal with hypocrites who had, on false pretexts, secured that permission.

## The arithmetic of the reluctant (42)

"Had it been a near gain and an easy journey, they would have followed you."

The passage opens by pricing their loyalty. Ibn 'Abbas explains *ʿaraḍan qarīban* — "a near gain" — as booty right in front of them. *Safaran qāṣidan*, "an easy journey", Ibn Kathir glosses as travel for only a short distance. He then reads *but the distance was long for them* as the distance to Ash-Sham. Nothing about the truth of the call had changed; only the cost had.

**The oath they are already caught in.** "And they would swear by Allah" — Ibn Kathir specifies the timing: *when you return to them*. Their words are supplied in advance: "If we only could, we would certainly have come forth with you" — meaning, as he puts it, *had there not been a valid excuse, we would have gone out with you*. Before the army has even returned, Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ exactly what they will say and that it is false: "They destroy themselves, and Allah knows that they are liars." They will swear by the very One who has already recorded the lie.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the plea of inability fails. Their absence was down to negligence and lethargy, and "if we only could" is unacceptable "because they did not use the ability given by Allah to pick and choose the right thing to do in His way. Therefore, the excuse of not having that ability is not valid." Pleading incapacity is itself the lie.

## The permission, and the reproach that came softly (43)

"May Allah pardon you! Why did you give them permission…"

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that 'Awn said: "Have you heard criticism softer than this, starting with forgiveness before criticism — *May Allah forgive you. Why did you grant them leave…*?" Muwarriq Al-'Ijli and others said the same.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the same insight. Those with insight into the relationship between Allah and His Prophet ﷺ have said that he had a special attachment to Allah, such that his heart could not simply bear the shock of being subjected to questioning from Him. Had the words *why did you permit them?* come first, "the blessed heart of the Holy Prophet ﷺ would have been simply unable to take it." So the pardon is placed ahead of the question, serving two purposes: it informs him that something has occurred which Allah did not like, and it tells him in advance that he is already forgiven, so that what follows cannot break his heart. A certain displeasure does exist in the outward framework of the words — and it has been "coated with a delightful concern for sensitivities."

**On "pardon" and the Prophet's ﷺ protection from sin.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anticipates the obvious worry: forgiveness is normally given for crimes and sins, and the Prophet ﷺ was *maʿṣūm*, protected from sin — so what is being forgiven here? The answer given is that just as there is forgiveness for sin, there can also be forgiveness for what is contrary to the preferred way (*khilāf al-awlā*) or is simply undesirable — and that does not violate the concept of the ʿiṣmah (infallibility) of a prophet.

**What the better course was.** "…until those who told the truth were manifest to you, and you had known the liars." Ibn Kathir reads *those who told the truth* as those with genuinely valid excuses, and paraphrases the divine question: *why did you not refuse them permission when they asked, so that you would know who truly obeys you, and who the liars are — those intent on remaining behind even if you did not give them permission?*

Mujahid reports that the ayah came down about people who said to one another, "Ask permission from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and whether he agrees or disagrees, remain behind!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: even had permission been refused, they were never going to march. What was lost was the exposure — the permission gave their hypocrisy a cover, so instead of being uncovered they went about congratulating themselves on how smartly they had deceived the Prophet ﷺ, and kept the chance to throw taunts at the Muslims. Hence Maʿārif's conclusion that the real purpose here "is not to show wrath or displeasure"; it is a way of saying that in future the motives and moves of such people should be watched and screened carefully.

**And the ruling was later relaxed.** Qatadah said that Allah criticised him as we read here, then later revealed permission for him to allow people to lag behind if he wished, in Surat An-Nur: "So if they ask your permission for some affairs of theirs, give permission to whom you will of them" [24:62]. 'Ata' Al-Khurasani said similarly.

## The line that runs through the request (44–45)

The same act — asking to be excused — is now traced back to the two hearts it can come from.

Ayah 44 gives the believers' side: those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask to be excused from striving with their wealth and their lives. Ibn Kathir gives the reason in one line: *because they consider Jihad an act of worship*. Nobody asks to be excused from something they experience as a chance to worship — so when Allah called them, they obeyed and hastened to act in His obedience. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it from the other direction: those who believe truly and staunchly do not pick an occasion like that to seek desertion for the sake of love for their lives and wealth. The ayah closes with "Allah is the All-Knower of those who have Taqwa" — and as Maʿārif puts it, He knows those who fear Him perfectly well.

Ayah 45 gives the other side: it is only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day who ask leave, and Ibn Kathir specifies — without a valid excuse. Two causes are named:

- **No hope of reward.** Ibn Kathir: "they do not hope for Allah's reward in the Hereafter for their good actions." Once the Hereafter is not real to a man, sacrifice is pure loss.
- **A doubting heart** — *wa-rtābat qulūbuhum*, "their hearts are in doubt", which Ibn Kathir specifies as doubt "about the validity of what you brought them." The excuse is a symptom; the doubt is the disease.

Then the closing image: *fahum fī raybihim yataraddadūn*, "so in their doubts they waver." Ibn Kathir describes it — they take one step forward and one step back, have no firm stance in anything, unsure and destroyed, "neither belonging to these nor to those." He adds the sobering principle that those whom Allah misguides will never find a way for themselves to guidance.

## Two exposures — what they never prepared, and what they would have done (46–47)

**Preparation is the proof (46).** "Had they really intended to march forth, they would have made preparation for it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the exposure of the falsehood: had they genuinely wished to set out, they would of necessity have made at least *some* preparation — and they made none.

**A working test for excuses.** Maʿārif draws from this a principle reaching far beyond Tabuk. An excuse is acceptable from someone who was ready to carry out orders and was then rendered helpless by some accident; this rule applies to all matters pertaining to the excusable. But a man who made no preparation, did not even make the intention when called, and only afterwards produced a reason — his excuse "will be like the excuse of sin which is worse than the sin." The examples given are exact: a man who has made all his preparations for Jumuʿah and is intending to go when an impediment suddenly stops him has a reasonable excuse, and Allah blesses him with the full reward of that worship; a man who prepared nothing and then happened upon an excuse is offering nothing but a ruse and a pretext.

Maʿārif grounds this in the night the Prophet ﷺ camped late on a journey (*lailat al-taʿrīs*). To be sure of waking for Fajr he arranged with Sayyidna Bilal (may Allah be pleased with him) that he would sit the night out and wake everybody at morning — but sleep overtook him too, and the company woke only after the sun had risen. Consoling his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), the Prophet ﷺ said that there is no negligence in sleep; negligence occurs only when one is awake. The excuse held precisely because, as far as it was possible to do, arrangements had already been made. As Maʿārif concludes, a decision about an excuse being reasonable or unreasonable can be taken only by knowing whether preparation was made — "simply using a lot of words to make a point gets nothing done."

**"But Allah was averse to their being sent forth."** Ibn Kathir: Allah hated that they should go out with you — *fa-thabbaṭahum*, so He made them lag behind and stay away. Then "it was said to them: Sit among those who sit at home." Ibn Kathir adds a careful qualification to those words: this was "as a part of what was decreed for them" — and, in his own words, *not that He legislated that they stay behind*.

**Why their absence was a mercy (47).** Allah then explains why He disliked their marching: "Had they marched out with you, they would have added to you nothing except disorder."

- *Khabāl* — disorder. Ibn Kathir's reason: "because they are cowards and failures." Numbers are not strength if the numbers break.
- "They would have hurried about in your midst… sowing sedition among you." Ibn Kathir: they would have rushed to spread false stories, hatred and discord among you.
- "And there are some among you who would have listened to them." Ibn Kathir names the danger: some would have obeyed them, given preference to their speech and words, and asked them for advice, unaware of the true reality of these hypocrites — which might have caused corruption and great evil between the believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: among the Muslims there were also simple people, who could be easily taken advantage of and were likely to be affected by their false rumours.

Muhammad bin Ishaq identifies the weight of the men involved: those who sought permission to lag behind included some of the chiefs, such as 'Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul and Al-Jadd bin Qays, who were masters of their people. Allah made them lag behind because He knew that if they went along with the Messenger ﷺ they would sow sedition in his army. There were some in the Prophet's ﷺ army who liked these chiefs and were ready to obey them, because they considered them honourable.

**"And Allah is the All-Knower of the wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir draws a point of belief from the closing phrase: Allah knows what occurred, what will occur, and — for what never occurred — how it would have occurred had it happened. He cites parallels: "But if they were returned to the world, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden" [6:28]; "Had Allah known of any good in them, He would indeed have made them listen" [8:23]; and 4:66–68, where very few would have obeyed a harder command, though obeying would have been better for them and would have strengthened their conviction.

## Not a new lapse but an old habit (48)

"They had already sought to spread discord before and devised plots against you."

Ibn Kathir places it in history: for a long time these men had thought and plotted against the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, as well as attempting to extinguish his religion. It occurred soon after the migration to Al-Madinah, when the pagan Arabs joined forces and the Jews and hypocrites of Al-Madinah waged war against the Messenger ﷺ. Then Allah gave victory at Badr and raised his word high — and 'Abdullah bin Ubayy and his fellows said, "This is a matter that has prevailed," and embraced Islam outwardly. Ibn Kathir's observation: whenever Allah elevated Islam and its people in might, the hypocrites only increased in rage and disappointment. Their Islam was a calculation about which side was winning, so victory could never make them glad. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that "they sought disorder even earlier" refers to what had happened in the battle of Uhud.

**The comfort in the closing words.** "…until the truth came and the decree of Allah became manifest, though they hated it." Maʿārif reads this ending as an indication that victory is in the hands of Allah. It was proved on earlier occasions when the Prophet ﷺ was blessed with victory, and the same will happen in this campaign too, when all the tricks played by the hypocrites will fail.

## The crowd narrows to one man (49)

"There are some of them who say, 'Exempt me and do not put me to trial.'"

Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Az-Zuhri, Yazid bin Ruwman, 'Abdullah bin Abi Bakr, 'Asim bin Qatadah and several others that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Al-Jadd bin Qays from Bani Salimah, "Would you like to fight the yellow ones (the Romans) this year?" He replied: "O Allah's Messenger! Give me permission to remain behind and do not cause Fitnah for me. By Allah! My people know that there is not a man who is more fond of women than I. I fear that if I see the women of the yellow ones, I would not be patient." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and said, "I give you permission." Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and several others that the ayah was revealed in his case; he was among the chiefs of Bani Salimah.

Look at the shape of that excuse: desertion dressed in the language of piety. Allah's answer cuts straight through: "Surely, they have fallen into trial." Ibn Kathir: they fell into it because of the statement they uttered, and the Fitnah he fell into by not joining the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, preferring his own safety to the safety of the Messenger ﷺ, is worse than the Fitnah he falsely claimed to fear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: such people were not very smart — trying to hide behind an imaginary ordeal, they did not realise they had already fallen into a certain one, the ordeal of acting against the command of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and of deserting the campaign, right there on the spot.

Ibn Kathir adds a report about the same man, noting that it is also recorded in the Sahih: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, "Who is your chief, O Bani Salamah?" They said, "Al-Jadd bin Qays, although we consider him a miser." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "There is not a disease worse than stinginess! Therefore, your chief is the white young man with curly hair, Bishr bin Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur."

**"And verily, Hell is surrounding the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir: they will never be able to avoid, avert, or escape from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possible meanings: either Hell will encircle them in the Hereafter, or the very chain of causes now operating to take them there, which has them encircled even now, is what is being equated with Hell — so that they happen to be, already, within the larger circle of nothing but the Fire.

## Living it

**Test your excuses by your preparation, not by your reasons.** This is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's principle from ayah 46. Before deciding whether an obstacle excused you, ask honestly what you had arranged before it appeared. The man who prepared and was stopped has his full reward; the man who prepared nothing and then found a reason has only a reason.

**Do not sanctify your own reluctance.** Al-Jadd ibn Qays turned reluctance into a piety claim. When we decline an obligation in the language of religion — protecting ourselves from a trial we invented — ayah 49 is speaking to us: the ordeal you are avoiding may be nothing next to the one you are stepping into.

**Watch what you find easy.** Ayah 42 does not accuse them of refusing to serve; it observes that they would have served for a short trip and a quick gain. Measure your commitment where it costs, not where it pays.

**Guard your ear.** Ayah 47 puts the blame on the whisperers, but it also names *listeners* among the believers — men who admired prominent voices and were ready to obey them because they thought them honourable, unaware of what those men really were. Respect given to the wrong person is a door.

**And take the comfort of ayah 48.** Victory is in the hands of Allah; the decree of Allah becomes manifest, though they hate it.

passages.title: Their glee at misfortune answered by destiny
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat catch the hypocrites at the exact moment they give themselves away — not by what they say in public, but by how they react to what happens to the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 50 exposes the reflex; ayah 51 gives the Prophet ﷺ the reply he is told to make, the creed that renders that reflex harmless; ayah 52 turns the whole thing around and shows that the believer's ledger has no losing column in it at all. The unit moves from *their* glee, to *our* certainty, to *their* dead end.

## Ayah 50: a heart read by its reactions

Ibn Kathir opens with the plain point: here "Allah emphasizes the enmity that the hypocrites have for the Prophet ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this particular test is so revealing. These people "live among Muslims giving the outward impression that they are one of them, but they are soon exposed by their inner reactions to what happens to the Holy Prophet ﷺ."

Look at the shape of the ayah. If a **ḥasanah** reaches you — Ibn Kathir glosses it as "a blessing, such as victory and triumph over the enemies," the sort of thing that pleases the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions — then *tasu'hum*: Ibn Kathir renders it "it grieves them," Maʿārif "it annoys them." And if a **muṣībah**, a calamity, reaches you, they start talking.

The Arabic uses one and the same verb for both arrivals: *tuṣibka* — the blessing "strikes" you and the calamity "strikes" you. That verb then carries straight through the passage: *lan yuṣībanā* in ayah 51 ("nothing will strike us"), *yuṣībakum* in ayah 52 ("that Allah strike you"). Nothing in these three ayat merely happens; things *land*. The only real question the passage asks is who sends them — and ayah 51 answers it.

**"We had already taken care of our problem."** Their line when bad news comes is قَدْ أَخَذْنَا أَمْرَنَا مِن قَبْلُ. Ibn Kathir unpacks it in one sentence: "they say, we took precautions when we did not join him" — i.e. we saw this coming, we kept our distance, we hedged. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: "They would take it as expedient in their favour that they did not go along with Muslims and found the results satisfying enough to go away delighted."

**And the tell is the final word.** وَيَتَوَلَّوا وَّهُمْ فَرِحُونَ — "and they turn away *rejoicing*." Not merely relieved. Escaping harm brings anyone a quiet relief; that is nature. This is something else. The community's wound has become their vindication, and being proved right feels better to them than the ummah being safe. That is the diagnostic Maʿārif is pointing at: you cannot always read a heart from its statements, but you can often read it from its inner reactions — from what makes it happy.

## Ayah 51: the reply he is told to give

Ibn Kathir says that in the face of "the perfect enmity they have towards him," "Allah directed His Prophet ﷺ to reply." The reply is not an argument about their loyalty or a rebuke of their glee. It is a statement about who runs the world.

**Notice a small grammatical shift.** In ayah 50 the address is singular: if *you* are struck, if *you* are afflicted — it is the Prophet ﷺ alone in their sights. But the answer he is told to give is plural: *lan yuṣībanā*, "nothing will ever strike **us**"; *mawlānā*, "**our** Master." He does not answer as an individual. He answers as a body — the believers stand inside the sentence with him, and the ayah widens further at its close to "the believers" as a whole.

**"Except what Allah has written for us."** The verb is *kataba*, "has written," as Maʿārif renders it: "Nothing can ever reach us except what Allah has written for us." Ibn Kathir's comment is short and total: "for we are under His control and decree." What reaches a believer was written before it arrived. Which means the hypocrite's calculation — *we kept clear and it paid* — was never the calculation he thought it was. Maʿārif's word for that whole way of reading events is unsparing: those who lean on material causes this way "were in a serious deception."

**"He is our Mawla."** Ibn Kathir glosses *Mawlā* as "Master and protector," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "our Master, Guardian and Helper." The word carries both halves at once: the One who owns and disposes, and the One who stands by you. This matters here, because a decree from a distant power would be something merely to be endured. A decree from your *Mawlā* is something else entirely: it comes from the One whose protection you are already under. Ibn Kathir closes the ayah on that note — "we trust in Him. Verily, He is sufficient for us and what an excellent guardian."

**"And in Allah let the believers put their trust."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this is aimed at. The Prophet ﷺ is being asked to tell "those, who worship material causes such as these, that they were in a serious deception. These material causes were no more than a curtain. The power that moves inside them belongs to none but Allah." Ayah 51 does not deny that causes exist. It denies that they are the ones deciding. As Maʿārif puts it, Muslims "must see material causes as no more than effective agents and signs while never taking them to be the real dispensers of any good or evil."

## Tawakkul is not sitting down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah as the place where the twin issues of **taqdīr** (destiny) and **tawakkul** (trust in Allah) come into sharp focus — and it spends its energy on the misunderstanding, because the mistake runs in two opposite directions. Speaking generally, it notes, "people around the world are found in great confusion about the religious problem of Taqdir and Tawakkul."

Some of them, it says, "are plain irreligious. They just do not recognize the very possibility that something like that exists. They are content with material means as the deity they are comfortable with."

Others "lack proper awareness. They have turned destiny and trust into a pretext for their sloth and inertia." Maʿārif is blunt that this is no virtue: "The outcome of believing in Taqdir and Tawakkul should never be that one goes home, sits tight, does nothing and says what will be will be. This is no belief in destiny and this is no practice of trust."

**The correct order is both, in sequence.** "One should devote full personal energy and courage to put together whatever lawful material means one can arrange for — within the range of what lies in control. After this has been done, the matter should be resigned to destiny and trust." And then the caveat, in Maʿārif's own words: "one has to keep his or her sight trained toward Allah alone — for it is He who has the ultimate outcome of everything one does under His absolute power and control."

**And the timing of the revelation teaches it.** Maʿārif notes that the Prophet ﷺ "made full preparation for Jihad, after which, the revelation of this verse put an end to this cycle of excess and deficiency and showed the right way." The ayah did not come down instead of the preparation. It came down *after* it — the effort first, and then the heart told where the outcome actually lives. Maʿārif quotes the Persian saying for it: **بر توکل زانوے اشتر بہ بند** — "With Tawakkul [trust], do tie the knees of the camel."

The summary is worth keeping in the front of the mind: "means which you have the option to utilize, are nothing but blessings given by Allah Taʿālā. Not taking advantage of these means is ingratitude, even stupidity. Of course, do not give means the status they do not have and believe that results and outcomes are not subservient to these means — instead of all that, they obey the command of Allah Almighty."

## Ayah 52: two goods, and no third

Now the argument reverses. The hypocrites had been *waiting* — watching to see what would land on the Muslims. Ayah 52 takes their own word and hands it back to them four times over: *tarabbaṣūn* (you wait), *natarabbaṣu* (we wait), *fa-tarabbaṣū* (so wait!), *mutarabbiṣūn* (we too are waiting). Both sides are standing at the same window. Only the view differs.

**"Except one of the two best things."** إِحْدَى الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ is a dual — literally *one of the two best-things*. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as "martyrdom or victory over you," reporting this "according to the meaning given by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others." Maʿārif renders the pair the same way: "the two good things [martyrdom and victory]."

Read that carefully. The word covering both outcomes is *ḥusnā*, "the best." The believer's two possible results are not *win* and *lose*, nor even *good* and *acceptable*. Death in Allah's path and victory in Allah's path are both filed under the same superlative. Whatever the hypocrites are hoping to see is not on the list, because there is no third column for them to hope for.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes exactly this the answer to their glee: "the thing that hypocrites take as suffering for Muslims and which makes them happy is really no suffering for them. In fact, it is another form of comfort and success," because "a man of true faith becomes deserving of eternal returns and rewards even after having failed in his strong resolve, something that is the real objective of all his successes." Its conclusion is one of the finest lines in the passage: **"Therefore, he succeeds, even in failure and gains, even in loss."**

**What the believers are waiting for, on their side.** أَن يُصِيبَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِعَذَابٍ مِّنْ عِندِهِ أَوْ بِأَيْدِينَا — "either that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or at our hands." Ibn Kathir explains "at our hands" as "either capture or killing." So their two possibilities are the mirror image of ours: not two goods but two forms of punishment, one direct from Allah, one delivered through the believers.

Maʿārif spells out how tightly that closes: "Either, they would be punished at the hands of Muslims right here in this world, in which case, they will taste the punishment in the mortal and the eternal world both. And, in case, they somehow escaped unscathed in the mortal world, there is no possibility of deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter." Escaping in this life is not an exit; it only removes one of the two instalments.

**"So wait — we too are waiting with you."** The ayah ends without threat or argument. It simply lets time be the judge, and the confidence in that closing line is the whole point: a man who knows both of his outcomes are called *the best* can afford to be patient.

## Living it

**Watch what gladdens you.** Ayah 50 does not test people by their words but by their reflex when someone else's affair goes well or badly. Secret satisfaction at another believer's setback — that the thing you warned against went wrong, that you were proved right — is the very reflex being exposed here.

**Refuse the hedge.** The hypocrite's phrase, "we took our precaution beforehand," is the voice of the person who never fully commits so that he can never fully lose. Ayah 51 dismantles it: nothing reaches you but what was already written, so the hedge bought nothing.

**Work fully, then hand it over.** Tie the camel *and* trust. Take every lawful means — Maʿārif calls neglecting them ingratitude and even stupidity — and then refuse to let those means become the thing you actually rely on. They are the curtain; Allah is the power moving behind it.

**Reprice loss.** If both of your outcomes are *ḥusnā*, then the worst that hostility can do to you is deliver one of the two things you wanted. That, not bravado, is the source of the believer's steadiness in this passage.

Held together, the three ayat make one point from three directions. Events do not arrive at random and they are not steered by the clever positioning of men. The passage does not promise the believer an easy road; it tells him Whose writing decides what reaches him, and Who is his *Mawlā* when it does.

passages.title: Their spending refused, their hearts exposed
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** these five ayat take the hypocrites at their most respectable — contributing to the cause, coming to the prayer, swearing loyalty by the name of Allah — and quietly turn the whole picture inside out. What holds the passage together is a single question: not *what did you give?* but *was it accepted?* Ayat 53–54 refuse their money and name the reason; ayah 55 refuses the envy their wealth and children provoke; ayat 56–57 refuse their oaths, showing that the loyalty behind them is fear, not love.

## Where we are

The verse just before this (ayah 52) sets the tone. The hypocrites were delighted at the discomfort of the Muslims, waiting for misfortune to strike them. The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer: *"Do you wait for us (anything) except one of the two best things"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others, **martyrdom or victory**. Either outcome is a win. Meanwhile the believers wait to see what will reach the other side: *"either that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or at our hands"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as capture or killing.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the beauty of this reply. What the hypocrites take as suffering for the Muslims is really no suffering at all; it is another form of comfort and success, because a man of true faith becomes deserving of eternal reward even after failing in his strong resolve. He succeeds even in failure, and gains even in loss. The disbelievers' position is the exact reverse: punished at the hands of the Muslims right here in this world — in which case they taste punishment in both worlds — and if they somehow escape unscathed here, there is no possibility of deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter.

That is the frame. Now Allah turns from what the hypocrites are waiting for to what they are offering.

## Ayah 53 — "Spend willingly or unwillingly"

*"Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you. Verily, you are ever a people who are rebellious."*

Notice the two words in the middle: **ṭawʿan aw karhan** — willingly or unwillingly. The verse deliberately covers both cases so that no loophole is left. Ibn Kathir's comment is one short line: *for whatever you spend either way* — it will not be accepted. The hypocrite who gives cheerfully and the hypocrite who gives through gritted teeth end at the same place.

And note what is *not* said. The verse does not say their money is worthless in itself. It says **lan yutaqabbal minkum** — "it will not be accepted **from you**." Acceptance is Allah's to grant, and the phrase puts the refusal on the giver, not on the amount or the manner of the giving. Nothing about how much was handed over, or how graciously, changes the answer.

Then the reason in summary: *"you are ever a people who are rebellious"* — **fāsiqīn**, a people settled in defiance of Allah. It is not the coins that were rejected; it was the people.

## Ayah 54 — the reason spelled out

Ayah 54 opens the file and shows the three entries written inside it: *"And nothing prevents their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and in His Messenger, and that they came not to the Salah except in a lazy state, and that they offer not contributions but unwillingly."*

**First, the root cause: disbelief.** Ibn Kathir's principle here is worth memorising: *the deeds are accepted if they are preceded with faith.* Faith is not one good deed among many; it is the condition on which every other deed is even eligible to be weighed. A building with no foundation is not a short building — it is not a building.

**Second, the prayer.** They came to the Salah, but "in a lazy state" — **kusālā**. They are physically present. What is missing is on the inside.

**Third, the giving.** They gave, but "unwillingly" — **kārihūn**, resenting it as it left their hands.

Ibn Kathir ties this together in a single verdict: *they neither have good intention nor eagerness to perform the acts of faith.* That is the anatomy of the disease. Intention is the heart's direction; eagerness is the heart's appetite. Strip both away and what remains is the outward shape of worship performed by someone who would rather be elsewhere.

## Why acceptance is not automatic

Ibn Kathir closes this section by recalling the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ — whom he calls "the Truthful, to whom the Truth was revealed" — that **Allah does not stop giving rewards until you (believers) stop performing good deeds**, and that **Allah is Ṭayyib (Good and Pure) and only accepts what is Ṭayyib.** (The commentary conveys this teaching without naming the collection it comes from, so it is passed on here in the same way.)

Two things are being said at once, and they balance each other.

The first is pure generosity: the flow of reward from Allah has no ceiling and no fatigue in it. It stops only when *you* stop. Nobody is ever rationed out.

The second is the standard: Allah is Ṭayyib — Good and Pure, in a way that belongs to Him alone, without resemblance to anything in creation and without our explaining the attribute away — and He accepts only what is Ṭayyib. A pure hand and an impure heart do not produce a pure offering. This, Ibn Kathir concludes, is exactly why Allah does not accept the charity or good deeds of the people described in these ayat: *He only accepts it from those who have Taqwā* — mindfulness of Allah.

So acceptance is not a transaction we can force. It is a gift, and the passage tells us plainly what makes a heart fit to receive it.

## The warning is aimed at us too

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the practical turn explicit. In ayah 54 two signs of the hypocrites are named:

1. they come to the Salah lazily and listlessly;
2. they spend in the way of Allah unwillingly.

And then the warning, addressed to Muslims: **sloth in Salah, and being sour at heart while spending in the way of Allah — that is, Zakah and Sadaqah — are signs of nifāq (hypocrisy). All Muslims should make conscious effort to stay safe from these signs.**

This deserves care. The commentary does not say that every believer who feels sluggish at prayer is a hypocrite; the people of ayah 54 are people whose foundation was disbelief in Allah and His Messenger. But it does say these are the *marks* of that disease, and marks are things you check yourself for. Two honest questions fall out of it:

- When it is time to pray, what happens inside me — movement, or dragging?
- When the Zakah is calculated or the appeal is made, does something in me wince as the money leaves?

If the answer is uncomfortable, the response is not despair. It is the very thing the passage identifies as missing: intention and eagerness. Rebuild those, and the same outward act becomes a different thing entirely.

## Ayah 55 — do not be impressed by what they have

*"So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart (die) while they are disbelievers."*

The address turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and through him to every believer who has ever looked across at a comfortable, well-provided-for opponent of the truth and felt a flicker of *why them?*

Ibn Kathir places two similar passages of the Qur'an alongside it. First: *"And strain not your eyes in longing for the things We have given for enjoyment to various groups of them, the splendor of the life of this world, that We may test them thereby. But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting"* (20:131) — where Ibn Kathir notes that the provision meant is the good reward in the Hereafter. Second: *"Do they think that in wealth and children with which We enlarge them, We hasten unto them with good things? Nay, but they perceive not"* (23:55–56). Read together, they say: the abundance you are looking at is not a verdict in their favour. It is a test — and they do not perceive it.

**How is wealth itself a punishment?** Al-Hasan Al-Baṣrī, as reported by Ibn Kathir, gives one concrete answer: by the Zakah due on their money being taken from them and spent in Allah's cause.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes a different and equally piercing angle: love for and engrossment in worldly life becomes a punishment right here in this world. Look at the shape of that life. First the desires to acquire worldly wealth; then a series of hard work to establish the necessary channels, day in and day out, sacrificing sleep, comfort and family life. Then, if one succeeds, come the concerns of increasing it and retaining it — a round-the-clock punishment indeed. A serious loss or sickness could become an unwelcome can of worries. And if a man does get everything he wants, the vicious circle continues, either through apprehensions of decreasing wealth or cravings of increasing it further. There is just no respite at any time.

Then, in the end, these things go out of his hands — at death, or much earlier — and despair takes over. "What is this," the commentary asks, "if not punishment?" Its verdict is unforgettable: man surrounds himself with articles of comfort and calls it comfort, while real comfort — the peace and comfort of the heart — is something man has yet to find. Meanwhile the material things he leans on for satisfaction keep snatching away his share of peace in this world, and become the prelude to the punishment in the world to come.

**The final clause is the worst of it.** *"...and that their souls shall depart while they are disbelievers."* Ibn Kathir explains: so that when Allah brings death to them, they will still be disbelievers — which makes matters worse for them and the torment more severe. Then he adds a prayer, and the reader should say it with him: *we seek refuge from such an end.* Part of what he is seeking refuge from is being **led astray gradually** by the very things they have: the slow, comfortable slide in which nothing appears to be going wrong right up until the end.

So ayah 55 quietly redefines what a blessing is. Wealth and children are not the measure. The measure is the state of the soul on the day it leaves.

## Ayat 56–57 — oaths on the surface, flight underneath

*"They swear by Allah that they are truly of you while they are not of you, but they are a people (hypocrites) who are afraid (that you may kill them)."*

Ibn Kathir titles this section *Exposing Hypocrites' Fright and Fear*: Allah is describing to His Prophet ﷺ the fright, fear, anxiety and nervousness of these people. They swear a sure oath that they belong to the community. Allah answers: *"while they are not of you"* — in reality. And then He names the motive: **"but they are a people who are afraid"** (*yafraqūn*). Ibn Kathir's comment is the key to the whole scene: *and this is what made them swear.* The oath is not a statement of belonging; it is a symptom of fear.

Ayah 57 then shows what they would do if fear were removed — and the Arabic piles up hiding places one on top of another, each explained by Ibn Kathir on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah:

- **malja'** — a refuge: a fort in which they hide and fortify themselves;
- **maghārāt** — caves, in some mountains;
- **muddakhal** — a place of concealment: a tunnel or a hole in the ground.

A fortress, a cave, a hole. The list descends from the dignified to the desperate: any of them would do. And then the verb — *"they would turn straightway thereto with a swift rush"* (**yajmaḥūn**), away from you.

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion with real psychological precision: they associate with the believers *unwillingly, not because they are fond of you.* They would prefer not to have to mix with them at all — "but necessity has its rules!" It is because of this, he says, that they feel grief, sadness and sorrow at the sight of Islam and its people enjoying ever more might, triumph and glory. Whatever pleases Muslims brings them grief; that is precisely why they prefer to disassociate themselves from the believers.

That is the deepest exposure in the passage. A person can be counted among the community, present at the prayer, contributing to the fund, swearing by the name of Allah — and the true test is what his heart does when the community he claims is doing well.

## A ruling raised here: can Sadaqah be given to a disbeliever?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the hypocrites used to receive a share from the properties available as **Ṣadaqāt** (plural of *ṣadaqah*: a donation through which one seeks reward with Allah, usually referred to as alms or charity), and that when they did not get these as they wished, they became angry and started accusing and cursing. That raises an obvious question, and the commentary answers it on two readings:

- If *ṣadaqāt* here is taken in its **general** sense — covering both necessary (*wājib*) and voluntary (*nafl*) giving — there is no problem, since non-Muslims can be given out of the voluntary ṣadaqāt. This is permissible on the basis of the consensus of the Muslim Ummah and stands proved from the Sunnah.
- If it means specifically what is obligatory, such as Zakah and 'Ushr, then the hypocrites were given a share on the basis that they *claimed* to be Muslims. Since they claimed to believe in all the necessary articles of faith and their kufr was hidden in their hearts, with no conclusive proof in their apparent claims, they were treated as Muslims to the extent of this worldly life — and Allah, in His wisdom, had given the orders that they be treated so. (*Bayān al-Qur'an*)

Notice what that leaves standing. What was hidden in their hearts was known to Allah, and it is Allah who discloses it here. In the dealings of this world, their outward claim was what the community had to go on.

## Living it

The passage is stern, but its practical demand on a believer is warm and simple, and it is all about the inside of the act:

- **Give as though acceptance is the goal, not the giving.** Ayah 53 has already priced the alternative at zero.
- **Guard the two marks of ayah 54.** Come to the Salah with something moving inside you; let the money leave your hand without your heart clinging to it.
- **Stop measuring people by ayah 55's yardstick.** Wealth and children in the hands of those who oppose Allah are a test they do not perceive, not a favour.
- **Take heart from the promise.** Allah does not stop giving rewards until we stop performing good deeds.
- **And pray Ibn Kathir's prayer.** We seek refuge in Allah from a soul departing in that state — and from being led astray gradually by the very things we are enjoying.

passages.title: Complaints over the alms and its eight recipients
passages.tafsir:
Some of the hypocrites attacked the Prophet's ﷺ integrity in distributing the alms. Ayah 58 exposes the charge and the motive behind it, ayah 59 shows them what they should have said, and ayah 60 answers by declaring that the assignment was never the Prophet's ﷺ to make — naming, in Allah's own words, the eight categories to whom the alms belong.

## The accusation, and what gave it away (ayah 58)

The key word is **yalmizuka**. Ibn Kathir glosses it as to "accuse you" — to question your integrity — in the *division* of the alms. His comment is withering: "They question your fairness, even though it is they who deserve that their integrity be questioned. The hypocrites do not do this in defense of the religion, but to gain more for themselves."

The ayah supplies the proof: *if they are given part thereof, they are pleased, but if they are not given thereof, behold! They are enraged.* Their verdict on justice tracks their own share exactly. Ibn Kathir notes they were "angry for themselves."

## Said to his face

Qatadah relates that a bedouin newly come to Islam approached the Prophet ﷺ while he was dividing gold and silver and said, "O Muhammad! Even though Allah commanded you to divide in fairness, you have not done so." The Prophet ﷺ answered, **"Woe to you! Who would be fair to you after me then?"** He then said, in the wording Ibn Kathir transmits: **"Beware of this man and his likes! There are similar persons in my Ummah who recite the Qur'an, but the Qur'an will not go beyond their throat. If they rise (against Muslim rulers) then kill them, if they rise, kill them, then if they rise kill them."**

Qatadah also reports that the Prophet ﷺ used to say: **"By He in Whose Hand is my life! I do not give or withhold anything; I am only a keeper."**

## What they should have said (ayah 59)

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah now directs these very people "to what is more beneficial for them than their behavior." Ayah 59 is phrased as a wish over them — *would that they had been content* — and hands them the sentence they failed to speak. Ibn Kathir calls it "a gracious type of conduct and an honorable secret," and lists what Allah folded into it:

- **Contentment** with what Allah and His Messenger gave them.
- **Trusting in Allah alone**: *ḥasbunā-Llāh*, "Allah is sufficient for us."
- **Hoping in Allah alone**: "We implore Allah (to enrich us)."
- And Allah made these the indications of **obedience to the Messenger ﷺ** — adhering to his commands, avoiding his prohibitions, believing his narrations, following his footsteps.

Notice how the ayah divides its terms: what is *given* is attributed to Allah and His Messenger together, while sufficiency and longing are voiced toward Allah alone.

**Why were hypocrites receiving anything at all?** Because they *claimed* Islam: they professed belief in the necessary articles of faith, their kufr hidden in their hearts, and Allah in His wisdom had ordered that they be treated as Muslims to the extent of this worldly life (Bayān al-Qurʼān, via Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

Maʿārif recalls that **in verse 54** two signs of the hypocrites had been given: they come to salah lazily and listlessly, and they spend in the way of Allah unwillingly. These are marks of *nifāq* (hypocrisy), and every Muslim should make a conscious effort to stay safe from them.

## Ayah 60: Allah settles it Himself

Ibn Kathir states the logic plainly: "He stated that it is He who divided the alms, explained its rulings and decided in its division; He did not delegate this decision to anyone else." Maʿārif puts it from the other side: by listing the recipients category by category, Allah told them that He Himself has determined who should receive — the Prophet ﷺ "doing nothing on his own or with his personal opinion."

Maʿārif records a hadith reported in Abu Dawud and Daraqutni from Ziyād ibn Ḥārith al-Sudāʼī: a man came in asking for something, and the Prophet ﷺ told him: **"Allah has never handed over the distribution of Sadaqat to any prophet, even to anyone other than a prophet. Instead of that, He has Himself determined eight categories for it. If you are included under one of those eight, I can let you have it."**

**The grammar carries the argument.** The ayah opens with *innamā*, the particle of restriction (*ḥaṣr* and *inḥiṣār*) — "only," and nothing besides — so its first word announces a closed list. Then comes *li'l-fuqarāʼ*, where the *lām* carries particularisation: all the ṣadaqāt rightfully *belong* only to those named after it.

**Which ṣadaqah is meant?** Maʿārif reports the consensus of the Muslim Ummah — and of the Ṣaḥābah and Tābiʿīn — that this verse refers only to the *obligatory* ṣadaqāt, citing al-Qurṭubī's verification that wherever the Qur'an uses "ṣadaqah" in an absolute sense, it invariably means the obligatory kind. Voluntary ṣadaqāt have a far wider range.

And it is a right, not a kindness. Allah has promised sustenance to every creature — *there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision* (11:6) — yet did not make all equal in provision, fixing a share for the poor and needy in the riches of the rich: *and in their wealth there is a share fixed for the asking and the deprived* (70:24). So taking ṣadaqah from the wealthy is no favour from them; it is a right of the needy, fixed in the sight of Allah, which no one may increase or decrease at will.

## The eight

**1. Al-Fuqarāʼ (the poor).** Allah began here, Ibn Kathir notes, because they have more need than the other categories. He reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Zayd and others that the *faqīr* is a graceful person who does not ask anyone for anything, while the *miskīn* follows after people, begging; Qatādah said the faqīr is the ill person and the miskīn the physically fit. Ibn ʿUmar reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"The alms should not be given to the wealthy and the physically fit"** (Ahmad, Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi collected it).

**2. Al-Masākīn (the needy).** Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"The needy person is not the one who goes round the people and asks them for a mouthful or two, or a date or two."** They asked, "Then who is the needy person, O Allah's Messenger?" He said, **"The one who does not have enough to satisfy his needs and whose condition is not known to others, that others may give him something in charity, and who does not beg of people."** The Two Shaykhs collected it.

Maʿārif adds the fiqh. Scholars differ over the precise sense of *faqīr* and *miskīn* — a faqīr being one who has nothing, a miskīn one who has less than the *niṣāb* — but under the injunction of zakah no difference remains between them. Whoever does not own wealth to the value of the niṣāb in excess of his basic needs (house, clothes, furniture) may be given zakah. The niṣāb is 7½ tolas of gold (87.48g), 52½ tolas of silver (612.36g), or the equivalent in cash — provided he is not in debt. One may lawfully be *given* while still being forbidden to *ask*: a person below the niṣāb who is healthy enough to earn may be given, but stretching his hand before others is not permissible, and what such a person acquires by soliciting the Prophet ﷺ equated with an ember from Hell (Abu Dawud, from a report of ʿAlī, cited via al-Qurṭubī).

Zakah proper goes only to the Muslim poor: sending Muʿādh ibn Jabal to Yemen, the Prophet ﷺ instructed that it be taken from the rich among the Muslims and spent on their poor. Other charity is wider — he ﷺ said, **"Give ṣadaqah to people of all religions"** — and with the exception of zakah, other ṣadaqāt, even Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr, may be given to a non-Muslim faqīr (Hidāyah).

**3. Those employed to collect it (al-ʿāmilīn).** These are people appointed by the Islamic government to collect the zakah and *ʿushr* for the *Baytul-Māl*, the state treasury. Because the work consumes all their time, the verse assigns their payment from zakah — the one head of the eight where the money is *compensation for service rendered*, not charity, which is why a wealthy man may take it.

Maʿārif explains why this breaks no rule. The collectors stand as authorised representatives of the poor, and possession by a representative counts as possession by the principal — so the payer's zakah is discharged the moment they receive it, and what they are paid is compensation given, in effect, by the poor. Their salaries must not exceed half of the total collected (Tafsīr Maẓharī, Ẓāhiriyyah).

Many jurists held that wages for an act of worship are impermissible, while collecting the alms is itself a religious duty. Yet this verse declares such payment permissible. Imam al-Qurṭubī resolves it: compensation for worship that is *farḍ* or individually obligatory is unlawful, but compensation for a *farḍ al-kifāyah* — a duty on the community as a whole, discharged for all if some fulfil it — is permissible on the authority of this very verse.

They may not, however, be relatives of the Messenger ﷺ. Muslim recorded that ʿAbdul-Muṭṭalib bin Rabīʿah bin al-Ḥārith and al-Faḍl bin al-ʿAbbās went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asking to be employed on the alms, and he replied, **"Verily, the alms are not allowed for Muhammad nor the relatives of Muhammad, for it is only the dirt that the people discard."**

A live consequence Maʿārif stresses: those who collect zakah for religious schools and organisations *without* being appointed by an Islamic state are **not** the *ʿāmilīn* of this verse; they are agents of the donor. So they may not draw salaries from zakah, and the donor's obligation is not discharged until the money actually reaches someone entitled to receive it.

**4. Those whose hearts are to be won (al-muʼallafatu qulūbuhum).** Ibn Kathir lists the types: those given so they embrace Islam; those given so they become firmer in faith; and those given to collect alms from surrounding areas or to defend Muslim outposts. Of the chiefs of the Ṭulaqāʼ, whom he gave a hundred camels each after Ḥunayn, the Prophet ﷺ said, **"I give a man while another man is dearer to me than him, for fear that Allah might throw him on his face in the fire of Jahannam."** Ibn Kathir also cites Ṣafwān bin Umayyah, who attended Ḥunayn while a *mushrik*: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave me from Ḥunayn while he was the most hateful person to me. He kept giving me until he became the most beloved person to me" (Imam Ahmad recorded it; Muslim and At-Tirmidhi collected it as well).

Ibn Kathir presents Ṣafwān — then still a mushrik — as an instance of this category. Maʿārif holds the most authentic position to be that non-Muslims were never given a share from ṣadaqāt: al-Qurṭubī's list of those the Prophet ﷺ gave under this head ends by noting that all were believers; and Tafsīr Maẓharī states that no report establishes the Prophet ﷺ giving any disbeliever from zakah property. On Ṣafwān, Maʿārif reports from Imam al-Nawawī — with al-Bayhaqī, Ibn Sayyid al-Nās and Ibn Kathir concurring — that his gift came from the *khums* of the Ḥunayn spoils, not from zakah.

Because this head lapsed under Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, some jurists called it abrogated — attributed to ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Abu Ḥanīfah and Mālik ibn Anas. Others — al-Zuhrī, Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, Ibn al-ʿArabī, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad — held that it merely lapsed for want of need and may be given again if the need returns. All are unanimous that poor new Muslims are eligible, and Maʿārif concludes that all agree the category itself still holds.

**5. Fī'r-riqāb (in freeing necks).** *Riqāb* is the plural of *raqabah*, the neck, used for a person shackled in the chains of slavery. Ibn Kathir reports from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān, ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, an-Nakhaʿī, az-Zuhrī and Ibn Zayd that it means the slave who has contracted with his master to pay a set ransom for his freedom — the *mukātab* — helped from zakah to pay off what stands against him. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan held that zakah funds may also buy a slave's freedom outright.

Maʿārif reports the consensus on the mukātab, and that the majority — Abu Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others — do not permit buying a slave from zakah funds to free him: zakah requires that a deserving person be made the *owner* of what is given, whereas here the money passes to the master, who is neither deserving nor giving it up for nothing. One narration from Mālik restricts the phrase to the mukātab; another permits buying and freeing.

**6. Al-ghārimūn (the debt-burdened).** Ibn Kathir includes several types: those who incur expenses solving disputes between people, those who guaranteed a loan that fell due and strained them, those whose funds do not cover their debts, and those who indulged in a sin and repented from it. Maʿārif adds two conditions: the debtor must not have enough funds to clear the debt himself — that is what *ghārim* means — and some Imams add that he should not have borrowed for something impermissible, lest zakah encourage him in sin.

**7. Fī sabīlillāh (in the way of Allah).** Ibn Kathir restricts this to the fighters in jihad who do not receive compensation from the Muslim Treasury. Maʿārif notes that Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Kathir both particularise it to *mujāhidīn* and *ḥujjāj* who lack the wherewithal for jihad or Hajj; jurists who admitted students of religious learning and servants of good causes did so on the condition that they be poor and needy, which would qualify them in any case.

It cautions against taking the phrase in its broad literal sense — spacious enough to cover mosques, schools, hospitals, wells, bridges, roads and the running costs of public institutions. Maʿārif calls this against the consensus of the Ummah and against what is transmitted from the Ṣaḥābah and the Tābiʿīn — all of whom restrict the expression to *ḥujjāj* and *mujāhidīn*. And if this head could absorb every act of worship and virtue, naming the eight recipients would be redundant.

**8. Ibn as-sabīl (the wayfarer).** Literally "son of the road": Arab usage applies *ibn* (son) to things a person is deeply bound up with, and a traveller is bound up with traversing distances. As a term of zakah, he is the traveller who lacks the funds he needs where he is, *even if he is a wealthy man back home*, and he takes what suffices him to reach his destination and return home in peace.

The ayah ends *farīḍatan mina-Llāh* — which Ibn Kathir explains as a decision, decree and division ordained by Allah — and names two attributes: *ʿAlīm*, knowledgeable of all things and of what benefits His servants, and *Ḥakīm*, wise in all He legislates and decides.

## Living it

**Ownership must actually transfer (tamlīk).** The majority of Muslim jurists hold that zakah is validly paid only when someone deserving is given possession of it *as its owner*; spend on their benefit without that, and the zakah remains unpaid. Hence the agreement of the four Imams that zakah funds may not be spent on building or running mosques, religious schools, hospitals or orphanages: the benefit reaches the poor, but nothing passes into their ownership. Where ownership does transfer — meals and clothes given to orphans as their own — that expenditure may come from zakah. Abū ʿUbayd in *Kitāb al-Amwāl*, with Sufyān al-Thawrī concurring, ruled likewise on a dead person's debts, funeral costs, building masjids and digging public canals; and al-Muwaffaq in *al-Mughnī* on bridges, roads, shrouds and feeding guests — reward-worthy deeds, but not among the eight heads.

**Give near home, and to relatives first.** From the instruction to Muʿādh, jurists derived that a town's zakah should not be sent elsewhere without need; its own poor have the better claim. But poor relatives in another city may be sent it, for the Prophet ﷺ gave glad tidings of a two-fold reward there; and where another township's hunger is more acute it may be sent there too (al-Qurṭubī, with reference to Daraqutni). Giving to poor relatives is more reward-worthy — one reward for the ṣadaqah and one for kinship — and it may be given as a gift, so the one who takes it is not humiliated. But husband and wife may not give zakah to each other, nor parents and children (nor grandchildren, grandfather or great-grandfather), since their expenses are generally combined.

**And do not interrogate the poor.** Where the obvious state of a person makes it overwhelmingly likely that he is genuinely needy, zakah may be given without investigating his background — as when some people came to the Prophet ﷺ in a very broken-down condition and he asked people to collect ṣadaqāt for them, without probing further (al-Qurṭubī). If it later turns out the recipient was wealthy, or a Hashimite descendant of the Prophet ﷺ, or one's own parent, child or spouse, the zakah need not be paid again — it has reached its place of reward. But if he turns out to have been one's own slave, or a disbeliever, the zakah remains unpaid and must be given again (*al-Durr al-Mukhtār*).

Allah's answer to the men who demanded a larger cut and impugned the one distributing was to show the Ummah that this wealth was never anyone's to allocate by preference: it is a fixed right, assigned by the One who is *ʿAlīm* and *Ḥakīm*.

passages.title: Injuring the Prophet and mocking the revelation
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These six ayat expose a single pattern of behaviour among the hypocrites: they hurt the Prophet ﷺ with their tongues, then swore oaths to smooth it over, then lived in dread that a surah would be revealed about them, and when confronted said they had only been joking. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the thread — like the ayat before them, these "chastise hypocrites for their absurd objections, hostility to the Holy Prophet ﷺ and their feigned professions of Faith on false oaths." Ayah 61 gives the insult, ayat 62–63 the oath used to cover it, ayah 64 the fear underneath it, and ayat 65–66 the excuse that is refused.

## "He is (lending his) ear" (ayah 61)

The taunt itself is short: **هُوَ أُذُنٌ** — rendered "He is (lending his) ear (to every news)." They do not accuse him of a crime. They reduce him to his listening.

Ibn Kathir explains what they meant by it: some hypocrites bothered the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by questioning his character, saying he lends his ear to those who say anything about us, and believes whoever talks to him — "therefore, if we went to him and swore, he would believe us." Ibn Kathir notes that similar was reported from **Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah**.

Notice what the insult reveals about them. They had read the Prophet's ﷺ gentleness as gullibility, and then built a strategy on the mistake: *he takes people at their word, so our oaths will always work.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly this. They thought that since he hears and believes everything, they had nothing to worry about; if a conspiracy of theirs was exposed, they would simply tell him on oath that they had nothing to do with it. Allah corrected them: His Messenger ﷺ "preferred silence against baseless hostilities because of his high morals. He did not believe in what they said. He himself knew reality as it was. He simply avoided refuting them on their faces because of his inherent gentleness of nature."

## Allah's answer: "He listens to what is best for you"

The reply is one of the most beautiful turns in the Qur'an. Allah does not deny the word — He keeps it and transforms it. **قُلْ أُذُنُ خَيْرٍ لَّكُمْ** — "Say: 'He listens to what is best for you.'" Yes, he listens; and what he listens to is what is best *for you*. The very trait they threw at him as a defect is turned toward their own good.

Then three descriptions, each answering the slander.

**"He listens to what is best for you"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this with a single decisive line: **he knows who's saying the truth and who is lying.** Their whole calculation was wrong from the start. What they read as credulity was not credulity at all.

**"He believes in Allah; has faith in the believers"** — Ibn Kathir's gloss of the second phrase is brief: "he believes the believers." His faith is in Allah; the believers he takes at their word.

**"And is a mercy to those of you who believe"** — Ibn Kathir completes the thought with a striking counterweight: he is a mercy to those who believe, "and a proof against the disbelievers." The same person is mercy on one side and evidence on the other. What you receive from him depends on what you bring to him.

The ayah closes with the warning that gives the passage its weight: **"But those who annoy Allah's Messenger, will have a painful torment."** Hurting him is not a social offence with a social penalty. It carries a punishment from Allah.

## The oath as a tool (ayat 62–63)

Ayah 62 exposes the mechanism: "They swear by Allah to you (Muslims) in order to please you." The oath is not aimed at truth; it is aimed at an audience. And Allah answers not by disproving the oath but by moving the question: **"but it is more fitting that they should please Allah and His Messenger, if they are believers."** You are working hard to be acceptable to the wrong court.

Ibn Kathir preserves the incident **Qatadah** reported about this ayah. A hypocrite man said: "By Allah! They (hypocrites) are our chiefs and masters. If what Muhammad says is true, they are worse than donkeys." A Muslim man heard him and declared: "By Allah! What Muhammad says is true and you are worse than a donkey!" The Muslim conveyed what happened to the Prophet ﷺ, who summoned the hypocrite and asked him:

> **مَا حَمَلَكَ عَلَى الَّذِي قُلْتَ؟** — "What made you say what you said?"

That man invoked curses on himself and swore by Allah that he never said it. Meanwhile the Muslim man made a du'a that deserves to be memorised: **"O Allah! Assert the truth of the truthful and expose the lies of the liar."** Then Allah revealed this ayah.

Read the scene closely and ayah 61 comes alive. The Prophet ﷺ asks one open question. He does not accuse. The hypocrite, exactly as ayah 61 describes, reaches for an oath. The man had staked everything on being believed — and Allah settled the matter over his head, by revelation.

## "Whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger" (ayah 63)

Ayah 63 raises the stakes: **أَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا أَنَّهُ مَن يُحَادِدِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ** — "Know they not that whoever opposes and shows hostility to Allah and His Messenger…" Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean: have they not come to know and realize that those who defy, oppose, wage war and reject Allah, **"thus becoming on one side while Allah and His Messenger ﷺ on another side."** That image of two camps is the heart of it. To take up a position against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is to declare which side of the line you stand on — and the line has only two sides.

The consequence: the fire of Hell, to abide therein — Ibn Kathir adds, "in a humiliating torment" — and then **ذَٰلِكَ الْخِزْيُ الْعَظِيمُ**, "That is the extreme disgrace," which he glosses as "the greatest disgrace and the tremendous misery."

Set that beside ayah 62. There, the oath was sworn in order *to please you* — to win approval. Here, the end described is the greatest disgrace. The two ayat sit side by side deliberately.

## Living in fear of the next surah (ayah 64)

Ayah 64 reaches inside them: "The hypocrites fear lest a Surah should be revealed about them, showing them what is in their hearts."

**Mujahid** described the atmosphere exactly: the hypocrites would say something to each other, then declare, "We wish that Allah does not expose this secret of ours." Imagine that as a way of life — every private exchange shadowed by the possibility that Allah would bring it into the open.

Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere about those who greet the Prophet ﷺ with a greeting Allah never gave and say within themselves, "Why should Allah punish us not for what we say?" — to which the answer is: "Hell will be sufficient for them; they will burn therein. And worst indeed is that destination!" (58:8). He also cites: "Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring to light all their hidden ill-wills?" … "but surely, you will know them by the tone of their speech!" (47:29–30).

And Allah's response to their dread is not reassurance but a challenge: **قُلِ اسْتَهْزِئُوا** — "Say: '(Go ahead and) mock! But certainly Allah will bring to light all that you fear.'" Ibn Kathir explains: He will expose and explain your reality to His Messenger ﷺ through revelation. Their fear was not paranoia. It was accurate.

**Why this surah is called al-Fadihah.** Ibn Kathir reports that, according to **Qatadah**, this surah is called *Al-Fadihah*, "the Exposing," because it exposed the hypocrites. That name is this ayah made into a title.

**One occasion when the promise came true.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives an event that fulfilled "Allah is surely to bring out what you are afraid of": while returning from the battle of Tabuk, some hypocrites had conspired to kill the Messenger of Allah. Allah Almighty informed him about the plan through the angel Jibra'il (peace be upon him), helping him to bypass the spot where the hypocrites were sitting in ambush. (Maʿārif attributes this to Mazhari, with reference to al-Baghawi.)

**A separate report, about what he did not say.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also transmits from **Ibn 'Abbas** that Allah had informed the Prophet ﷺ of the names of seventy hypocrites, complete with their parentage and addresses — "But, being the universal mercy, he did not disclose these before his people." (Mazhari.)

Sit with that second report on its own and the portrait of the Prophet ﷺ in ayah 61 is complete. He had names, parentage, addresses — and he did not announce them. Maʿārif gives the reason in the same word the ayah uses of him: mercy (*raḥmah*). The man they called "an ear" knew far more than they imagined, and said less than he could have.

## "We were only joking" (ayat 65–66)

Ibn Kathir records from **'Abdullah bin 'Umar** what happened during the battle of Tabuk. A man sitting in a gathering said: "I have never seen like these reciters of ours! They have the hungriest stomachs, the most lying tongues and are the most cowardice in battle." A man in the Masjid said: "You lie. You are a hypocrite, and I will surely inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The statement was conveyed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a part of the Qur'an was revealed about it.

Then 'Abdullah bin 'Umar describes the aftermath in a sentence you do not forget: "I have seen that man afterwards holding onto the shoulders of the Messenger's camel while stones were falling on him, declaring, *'O Allah's Messenger! We were only engaged in idle talk and jesting,'* while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was reciting:

> **أَبِاللَّهِ وَآيَاتِهِ وَرَسُولِهِ كُنتُمْ تَسْتَهْزِئُونَ** — 'Was it at Allah, and His Ayat and His Messenger that you were mocking?'"
