The Prophet ﷺ does not argue with him. He recites the ayah, and the ayah is the argument. The man pleads sideways — *it was only talk* — and the recitation keeps naming what he had actually aimed at.

That is the pivot of ayah 65. The excuse is about **intention**: we did not mean anything by it. The reply is about **target**: look at *what* you made the object of your joke. Allah, His Ayat, His Messenger ﷺ. And note where the ridicule in the report was actually pointed — at "these reciters of ours" — while the ayah recited over the man named the target as Allah, His Ayat and His Messenger ﷺ.

Ayah 66 shuts the door: **لَا تَعْتَذِرُوا قَدْ كَفَرْتُم بَعْدَ إِيمَانِكُمْ** — "Make no excuse; you disbelieved after you had believed." Ibn Kathir specifies the cause: it was "on account of your statement and mocking." Not a hidden thought, not a private doubt — a statement, and the mockery in it.

Then a phrase heavy with both justice and hope: "If We pardon some of you, We will punish others among you." Ibn Kathir explains it plainly — not all of you will be forgiven, some will have to taste the torment — "because they were criminals," and they were criminals, he says, "because of this terrible, sinful statement." Even in an ayah that begins "Make no excuse," Allah still names a group who may be pardoned. The excuse is refused; the possibility of pardon is not withdrawn.

## What this asks of us

**Do not mistake forbearance for ignorance.** The hypocrites built their whole scheme on misreading the Prophet's ﷺ silence. Maʿārif answers them in one line: "He did not believe in what they said. He himself knew reality as it was." When someone forbears with you, that is more often mercy than blindness — and ayah 64 warns that Allah brings to light exactly what people most want hidden.

**Guard the tongue where "jokes" are made.** Ayah 65 draws the line at the target, not the tone. In the report Ibn Kathir transmits, words thrown at the reciters were answered with "Was it at Allah, and His Ayat and His Messenger that you were mocking?" — and the plea "we were only engaged in idle talk and jesting" did not move the recitation off its course.

**Oaths are not a substitute for sincerity.** Ayah 62 redirects the whole enterprise of impression management: if you are going to work this hard to be found acceptable, "it is more fitting that they should please Allah and His Messenger, if they are believers."

**And take the believer's du'a from the report on ayah 62 with you** — the words of the man who was contradicted on oath to his face and answered by turning to Allah: *"O Allah! Assert the truth of the truthful and expose the lies of the liar."* He did not have to win the argument. Revelation came down and settled it.

passages.title: Hypocrite men and women against believing men and women
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing.** These six ayat set two communities side by side — the hypocrites, men and women, and the believers, men and women — give each a portrait, then give each its promise. Between the two halves stands a warning drawn from history (69–70): the nations before them who rejected their Messengers, who were mightier in power and more abundant in wealth and children, and whose end is now a story to be learned from.

The unity of the passage is visible in the wording. Ayah 67 opens with *al-munāfiqūna wa'l-munāfiqāt* — the hypocrites, men and women; ayah 71 opens with *al-mu'minūna wa'l-mu'mināt* — the believers, men and women. Ayah 68 begins "Allah has promised the hypocrites — men and women — and the disbelievers, the fire of Hell"; ayah 72 begins "Allah has promised the believers — men and women — Gardens under which rivers flow." The same verb, *waʿada* (to promise), is used for the Fire and for the Gardens.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the believers appear here at all: the previous verses had dealt with the hypocrites — their conspiracies, their hostilities, and the punishment waiting for them. The characteristic style of the Qur'an required that the true believers be mentioned at this very place, giving a view of their way of life, their rewards and their ranks.

## Ayah 67 — the anatomy of hypocrisy

**"They are one from another."** *Baʿḍuhum min baʿḍ* — they are all alike. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to how carefully this differs from what is said of the believers in ayah 71, *baʿḍuhum awliyā'u baʿḍ*, "the believers are friends to each other." Citing Qurṭubī, it explains that this releases a hint about the nature of their mutual relationships: the hypocrites base theirs on functional cooperation between kinsfolk, or on self-interest. Such bonds do not last long, nor do they bring the kind of spiritual benefits that are the hallmarks of a heart-to-heart friendship. Set against them are the true believers, who are sincere friends and wish well of each other.

**The inverted command.** Ibn Kathīr builds his comment on a contrast: Allah admonishes the hypocrites who, *unlike the believers* — who enjoin righteousness and forbid evil — "enjoin evil, and forbid the good." Hypocrisy here is not merely the absence of moral energy. It is moral energy pointed backwards.

**"And they close their hands."** A physical image for stinginess. Ibn Kathīr reads it as withholding *from spending in Allah's cause*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the explanation given in Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: the withheld hand stands for abandonment of jihād and non-compliance with obligatory rights and duties.

## "They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them"

Ibn Kathīr explains "they have forgotten Allah" as: *they have forgotten the remembrance of Allah*. And "so He has forgotten them," he explains as Allah **treating them as if He has forgotten them** — citing the words of Allah, "And it will be said: 'This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours'" [45:34].

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: the words literally mean "they forgot Allah, so He forgot them," but Allah, Most High, is free of forgetfulness. The sense at this place is that those people had abandoned the commandments of Allah as if they had forgotten them; therefore Allah too abandoned their prospects of a better life in the Hereafter, to the extent that there remained just no trace of any good, or reward, in their name.

What is described here is not a failure of memory — it is a deliberate withdrawal, an abandonment answering an abandonment.

**"Verily, the hypocrites are the rebellious."** Ibn Kathīr glosses this as: *the rebellious from the way of truth, who embrace the wicked way*.

## Ayah 68 — the promise that is a threat

Allah has promised the hypocrites — men and women — and the disbelievers, the fire of Hell. Ibn Kathīr ties this directly to what precedes: it is *on account of their evildoing mentioned here*. The hypocrites are named alongside the open disbelievers, and "therein shall they abide" means, he says, **for eternity, they and the disbelievers**.

Three phrases close the ayah, and Ibn Kathīr gives each a word:

- *"It will suffice them"* — that is, **as a torment**.
- *"Allah has cursed them"* — meaning, He expelled and banished them from His mercy.
- *"and for them is the lasting torment."*

## Ayat 69–70 — the road has been walked before

**"Like those before you."** Ayah 69 describes them: mightier than you in power, and more abundant in wealth and children. "They had enjoyed their portion, so enjoy your portion as those before you enjoyed their portion." On the word *khalāq*, "their portion," Ibn Kathīr reports the view of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī that it means their religion — the printed text reads "[they mocked] their religion." And on "you indulged in play and pastime as they indulged in play and pastime," Ibn Kathīr's gloss is short: they *indulged in lies and falsehood*.

"Such are they whose deeds are in vain in this world and in the Hereafter." Ibn Kathīr — their deeds are annulled; they will not acquire any rewards for them, because they are invalid. "Such are they who are the losers."

**Who is being addressed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two exegetical explanations: according to one, the address in ayah 69 is to the hypocrites; according to the other, it is to the Muslims — which is why translations often supply "you are" in parenthesis. On the second reading the sense is: you too are like the people before you. They went for worldly enjoyments and forgot all about the life to come. The result was that they sank into all sorts of sins. So shall you be.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr records that Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You will follow the traditions of those who were before you, a hand span for a hand span, a forearm's length for a forearm's length, and an arm's length for an arm's length. And even if they enter the den of a lizard, you will also enter it." They asked, "Who, O Allah's Messenger, the People of the Book?" He said, "Who else?" Ibn Kathīr notes that this ḥadīth is similar to another ḥadīth collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān narrates the same ḥadīth from Abū Hurayrah and adds what he said after narrating it: that anyone wishing to ascertain the thematic authenticity of this ḥadīth should read this very ayah — *ka'lladhīna min qablikum*, "(You are) like those before you." On hearing this, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said: *mā ashbaha'l-laylata bi'l-bāriḥah* — "how similar is this night to the last night" — meaning that they are the people of Banī Isrā'īl, and we have been likened to them. (Qurṭubī) Ibn Kathīr records the same remark of Ibn ʿAbbās.

**Read the placement.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point worth pausing on. The ḥadīth warns that Muslims too will start following the ways of the Jews and Christians in later times. But this statement appears only *after* a punishment has been announced for the hypocrites, and that placement serves as an indicator that good Muslims would not do that. Only those among them who are weak in īmān may do so, because they are still infected with the germs of hypocrisy. All the good men and women of the Muslim community are instructed in this verse to abstain from such ways themselves, and to help others do the same.

**Ayah 70 — the roll-call.** "Has not the story reached them of those before them?" Ibn Kathīr reads this as Allah advising the hypocrites who reject the Messengers: have you not learned the end of the nations before you who rejected the Messengers? He then walks the list:

- **The people of Nūḥ** — and the flood that drowned the entire population of the earth, except those who believed in Allah's servant and Messenger Nūḥ, peace be upon him.
- **ʿĀd** — who perished with the barren wind when they rejected Hūd, peace be upon him.
- **Thamūd** — who were overtaken by the *Ṣayḥah*, the awful cry, when they denied Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, and killed the camel.
- **The people of Ibrāhīm** — over whom Allah gave Ibrāhīm victory with the aid of clear miracles, destroying their king Nimrod.
- **The dwellers of Madyan** — the people of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, destroyed by the earthquake and the torment of the day of the Shade.
- **The overturned cities** — the people of Lūṭ. Ibn Kathīr connects the word to another ayah, "And He destroyed the overturned cities" [53:53], meaning the people of the overturned cities, in reference to Sadūm (Sodom), their major city. Allah destroyed them all because they rejected Allah's Prophet Lūṭ, peace be upon him, and because they committed the sin that none before them had committed.

Then the summary: "to them came their Messengers with clear proofs" — and unequivocal evidence, says Ibn Kathīr — "so it was not Allah Who wronged them." When He destroyed them, He had already established the proofs against them by sending the Messengers and dissipating the doubts. "But they used to wrong themselves," on account of their denying the Messengers and defying the truth; and this is why they earned the end, torment and punishment, that they did.

## Ayah 71 — the believers, in five strokes

Ayah 71 answers ayah 67 clause by clause. Ibn Kathīr frames it exactly so: after Allah mentioned the evil characteristics of the hypocrites, He then mentioned the good qualities of the believers.

**"Supporters of one another."** Ibn Kathīr: *they help and aid each other*. He cites a ḥadīth he describes as authentic: "The believer to the believer is just like a building, its parts support each other" — and the Prophet ﷺ crossed his fingers together as he said it. And in the Ṣaḥīḥ it is recorded: "The example of the believers in the compassion and mercy they have for each other is the example of one body: if a part of it falls ill, the rest of the body suffers with fever and sleeplessness."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the consequence: since this friendship and concern for each other is for Allah alone, it is always constant. It remains the same under all conditions — open or secret, present or absent — and it is lasting. It is in the very nature of īmān (faith) and *al-ʿamal aṣ-ṣāliḥ* (righteous action) that they generate mutual love and friendship; the Qur'an confirms it at 19:96, which Maʿārif explains to mean that among those who have believed and taken to consistent good conduct in life, Allah creates a friendship deeply rooted in their hearts. The commentary then turns the mirror on our own time: perhaps we are short on the faith in our hearts and the concern for good in our conduct — which is why mutual relationships among Muslims do not seem to be what the Qur'an would like them to be, subservient to worldly needs and interests rather than being for the sake of Allah alone.

**The five marks**, as Ibn Kathīr takes them:

1. **They enjoin good** — exactly inverting ayah 67. He compares 3:104: "Let there arise out of you a group of people inviting to all that is good, enjoining *al-maʿrūf* and forbidding *al-munkar*."
2. **They forbid evil.**
3. **They perform the Salah** and **4. give the Zakah** — in Ibn Kathīr's summary of these two together, they *obey Allah and are kind to His creation*. The open hand, against the closed fist of ayah 67.
5. **They obey Allah and His Messenger** — concerning what he commands, and refraining from what he prohibits.

**"Allah will have mercy on them."** Where the hypocrites' ayah ended in a curse — banishment from mercy — the believers' ayah ends in mercy itself. Ibn Kathīr: Allah will give mercy to those who have these qualities.

**"Surely, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Wise."** On *All-Mighty* (*ʿAzīz*), Ibn Kathīr says: He grants glory to those who obey Him, for indeed might and glory are from Allah, Who gives them to His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. On *All-Wise* (*Ḥakīm*): wise in granting these qualities to the believers, while giving the evil characteristics to the hypocrites. Surely Allah's wisdom is perfect in all His actions; praise and glory be to Him.

## Ayah 72 — the promise kept

The mirror completes: "Allah has promised the believers — men and women — Gardens under which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever, and beautiful mansions in gardens of ʿAdn (Eden)." Ibn Kathīr glosses "beautiful mansions" as *built beautifully in good surroundings*, and gathers around the ayah what the Sunnah says of the place:

- In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, it is recorded that Abū Mūsā, ʿAbdullāh bin Qays al-Ashʿarī, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Two gardens, their pots and whatever is in them are made of gold; and two gardens, their pots and whatever is in them are made of silver. Only the Veil of Pride of Allah's Face separates the people from gazing at Him, in the garden of Eden."
- He also narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "For the believer in Paradise there is a tent like a hollow pearl which is sixty miles high in the sky, and in the tent the believer will have so large a family that he visits them all, and some of them would not be able to see the others." The Two Ṣaḥīḥs collected this ḥadīth.
- It is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger, offers prayer perfectly and fasts the month of Ramaḍān, will rightfully be granted Paradise by Allah, no matter whether he emigrates in Allah's cause or remains in the land where he is born." The people said, "O Allah's Messenger! Shall we acquaint the people with this good news?" He said: "Paradise has one hundred grades which Allah has prepared for the Mujāhidīn who fight in His cause; the distance between each two grades is like the distance between the heaven and the earth. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, which is the best and highest part of Paradise; from it gush forth the rivers of Paradise, and above it is the ʿArsh (Throne) of the Most Beneficent."
- Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If you invoke Allah for blessings upon me, then also invoke Him to grant me al-Wasīlah." He was asked, "What is al-Wasīlah, O Allah's Messenger?" He said: "The highest grade in Paradise; it will be for only one man, and I hope I am that man."
- The Musnad contains a ḥadīth from Saʿd bin Mujāhid aṭ-Ṭā'ī, that Abū al-Mudillah said, that Abū Hurayrah said: "We said, 'O Allah's Messenger! Talk to us about Paradise — what is it built of?' He said: 'A brick of gold and a brick of silver. Its mortar is from musk, its gravel is pearls and rubies, its sand is saffron. Whoever enters it will enjoy the delights, will never be hopeless, and will live forever and will not die. His clothes will never decay, nor will his youth ever end.'"

**And then the ayah dwarfs all of it.** "But the greatest bliss is the good pleasure of Allah." Ibn Kathīr: Allah's pleasure is more grand, greater and better than the delight the believers will be enjoying in Paradise. Imām Mālik narrated, that Zayd bin Aslam said, that ʿAṭā' bin Yasār said, that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted and Ever High, will say to the people of Paradise, 'O residents of Paradise!' They will say, 'Labbayk, our Lord, and Saʿdayk, and all the good is in Your Hand.' He will ask them, 'Are you pleased?' They will say, 'Why would we not be pleased, O Lord, while You have given us what You have not given any other of Your creation?' He will say, 'Should I give you what is better than all this?' They will say, 'O Lord! What is better than all this?' He will say, 'I will grant you My pleasure, and will never afterwards be angry with you.'" The Two Ṣaḥīḥs collected the ḥadīth of Mālik.

Set that final line beside ayah 68. The hypocrites' end was that Allah *cursed* them — expelled and banished them from His mercy. The believers' end is that Allah is *pleased* with them, and will never afterwards be angry with them. "That is the supreme success."

## Living it

- **Watch the direction of your influence.** The two groups are distinguished here not by belief alone but by what they urge on others. What does your presence make easier for those around you?
- **Open the hand.** Ibn Kathīr reads the closed fist as withholding from spending in Allah's cause; Qurṭubī, as reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reads it as abandoning jihād and failing to comply with obligatory rights and duties. Generosity sits here as a marker of faith, not an extra.
- **Keep the remembrance alive.** Forgetting Allah, as Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both explain it, is not a lapse of memory but the abandonment of His commandments — and the remedy runs the same way: the five marks of ayah 71 are all *practices*.
- **Build the bond.** Believing men and women are described as supports in one building and limbs in one body — a duty before it is a comfort. And note Maʿārif's condition: it lasts only when it is for the sake of Allah alone, the same in public and in private, in a person's presence and in their absence.
- **Aim high, and higher.** The Prophet ﷺ told us to ask specifically for al-Firdaws. Ayah 72 teaches us to ask beyond the Garden itself, for the good pleasure of the One who made it.

passages.title: Striving against hypocrisy and the word of blasphemy
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat turn from *describing* the hypocrites to *instructing* the Prophet ﷺ how to deal with them. Ayah 73 is the command — strive against disbelief and hypocrisy, and do not go soft. Ayah 74 is the case file: men who said something that was disbelief, swore by Allah they had never said it, and resolved on something they could not carry out. Running through both is the oath. It shields the hypocrite from people; ayah 74 shows it does not shield him from Allah — and then, remarkably, holds the door of repentance open.

## Ayah 73: one command, two very different groups

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and to be harsh against them. Allah also commanded him to be merciful with the believers who followed him, informing him that the destination of the disbelievers and hypocrites is the Fire in the Hereafter.

One command covers two groups who could not be more different — open disbelievers, and men living inside the Muslim community. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to wage jihād (striving, struggle) against disbelievers and hypocrites both, and to be strict in the case of both. The early authorities read the difference between them into the command rather than flattening it:

- **Ibn Masʿūd** said of "strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites": "With the hand, or at least have a stern face with them."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: "Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to fight the disbelievers with the sword, to strive against the hypocrites with the tongue and annulled lenient treatment of them."
- **Ad-Daḥḥāk** said: "Perform Jihad against the disbelievers with the sword and be harsh with the hypocrites with words, and this is the Jihad performed against them." **Muqātil** and **Ar-Rabīʿ** said something similar.
- **Al-Ḥasan** and **Qatādah** said, "Striving against them includes establishing the (Islamic Penal) Law of equality against them."

Ibn Kathir does not pick a winner among these. He combines them: Allah causes punishment of the disbelievers and hypocrites with all of these methods in various conditions and situations — "and Allah knows best."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the point about the hypocrites specifically. The need to fight belligerent disbelievers is self-evident, it says; but the meaning of carrying out jihād against the hypocrites is explained by the very conduct of the Prophet ﷺ. That conduct proves that jihād against them signifies a **vocal** jihād, through which they should be induced to understand the veracity of Islam, to start to feel for it, and thus to become sincere in their adherence to Islam (citing Qurṭubī and Maẓharī).

## "And be strict with them" — what *ghilẓah* actually means

The real meaning of the word **ghilaẓ / ghilẓah** used in "and be strict with them," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is that **one should not show any leniency or grant any concessions in taking a course of action which the person addressed deserves**. The word is used as an antonym to **raʼfah** — mercy and kindheartedness. So the command is: do not soften what is owed.

Imām al-Qurṭubī, as quoted there, makes this explicit: the use of *ghilẓah* (strictness) in this place means that leniency should not be shown and concessions should not be granted **when the injunctions of the Sharīʿah (Islamic law) are enforced on them**. This approach has nothing to do with being vocally strict — because that is against the favoured practice of the blessed prophets. They are never harsh in speech, nor do they curse and swear.

Qurṭubī supports this with a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays as a hadith without naming any collection: "If a bondwoman of anyone among you commits fornication, just enforce the Islamic legal punishment for it on her — but do not denounce her verbally." The penalty is carried out in full; the tongue is still held. That is *ghilẓah*, and there is no cruelty in it.

Allah has Himself described the manner of His Prophet ﷺ — the image he exuded before people: *"and had you been rough and hard hearted, they would have dispersed from around you"* (3:159). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that there is no evidence even from the actual dealings of the Prophet ﷺ that he ever demonstrated any harsh attitude in conversation or address before disbelievers and hypocrites.

**A warning the commentary itself raises.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a matter of regret that harshness in address and conversation — something Islam never took to even against rigid and hostile disbelievers — is used by contemporary Muslims **against other Muslims** without a second thought, with some congratulating themselves as though it were a service to their religion.

## Ayah 74: the oath that was a lie

Now the reason for the command.

**Ibn Kathir's account.** Al-Amawī said in his Book on Battles that Muḥammad bin Isḥāq narrated that az-Zuhrī said that ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin ʿAbdullāh bin Kaʿb bin Mālik narrated from his father, from his grandfather: among the hypocrites who lagged behind from the battle, and concerning whom the Qur'an was revealed, was **Al-Julās bin Suwayd bin aṣ-Ṣāmit**. He was married to the mother of **ʿUmayr bin Saʿd**, and ʿUmayr was under his care. When the Qur'an was revealed about the hypocrites, exposing their practices, Al-Julās said: *"By Allah! If this man (Muhammad) is saying the truth, then we are worse than donkeys."*

ʿUmayr heard him, and what he said back is one of the most human lines in the whole account: "By Allah, O Julas! You are the dearest person to me … and I would hate that harm should touch you, more than I do concerning anyone else! You have uttered a statement that if I exposed, will expose you, but if I hide, it will destroy me. One of them is a lesser evil than the other." So ʿUmayr went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him. Al-Julās came to the Prophet ﷺ and **swore by Allah** that he had not said it: "He lied on me." Allah then sent down this verse in his case. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ conveyed the ayah to Al-Julās, who — they claim — repented, and his repentance was sincere, prompting him to refrain from hypocrisy.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account** fills in the courtroom. Reporting from al-Baghawī, it says the Prophet ﷺ gave an address on the occasion of the battle of Tabūk. He talked about the sorry state of affairs the hypocrites were in and warned them of their sad end. Jullās, a hypocrite, was present; when he returned to his people he said, "If whatever Muḥammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." By chance a Companion named **ʿĀmir ibn Qays** heard the comment, and told him there was no doubt about what the Prophet ﷺ said, for it is true — "and you are really worse than donkeys."

When the Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah from Tabūk, ʿĀmir told him about it. Jullās flatly disowned what he had said, and on top of that charged ʿĀmir with accusing him falsely. The Prophet ﷺ ordered both of them to stand close to the Mimbar (the stepped platform in the masjid from which the Friday address was delivered, originally occupied by the Prophet ﷺ and traditionally regarded as a symbol of his message) and take an oath. Jullās was quick to take a false oath: he never said it, and ʿĀmir is lying. Then ʿĀmir took his oath, raised his hands in prayer and said: *"O Allah, let Your Messenger know about the reality of this matter through a revelation to him."* The Prophet ﷺ said "Āmīn" (amen) following his prayer, and so did all the Muslims present. **These people had yet to move from there** when Jibrīl (Gabriel, peace be upon him) came with the revelation which included this verse.

Jullās stood up immediately: "Yā Rasūlallāh, now I confess that I was the one in the wrong and that which was said by ʿĀmir was the truth. But this very verse has also given me the right of making Taubah (repentance). Hence, I seek forgiveness from Allah and repent for what I did earlier." The Prophet ﷺ accepted his repentance, after which he stayed firm in it and things turned towards the better in his life. (Maẓharī)

**A third report.** Imām Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Jarīr recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting under the shade of a tree when he said, "A man will now come and will look to you through the eyes of a devil. When he comes, do not talk to him." A man who looked as if he was blue (so dark) came, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned him and said, "Why do you curse me, you and your companions?" That man went and brought his friends, and **they swore by Allah that they did nothing of the sort**, and the Prophet ﷺ pardoned them. Then Allah revealed, *"They swear by Allah that they said nothing (bad)…"*

They lied under oath in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and he pardoned them — and then revelation came down naming what they had done. An oath can settle a matter among people; it settles nothing with Allah.

## "They said the word of disbelief"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the pattern the verse is addressing: the text reverts to the hypocrites who keep uttering words of infidelity in their gatherings but, should Muslims come to know about it, promptly declare on oath that they had nothing to do with it. That is exactly what both accounts show — a sentence spoken among his own people, denied under oath the moment it reached the Prophet ﷺ.

Then: *"and they disbelieved after accepting Islam."* The men in these reports had entered Islam outwardly and lived among the believers. The ayah records what such a statement amounted to when it came from them.

## "And they resolved that which they were unable to carry out"

Ibn Kathir gathers several reports about what was resolved:

- It was said the ayah was revealed about **Al-Julās bin Suwayd**, who tried to kill his wife's son when the young man said he would inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
- It was also said it was revealed in the case of **ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy**, who plotted to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
- **As-Suddī** said: "This verse was revealed about some men who wanted to crown ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy even if the Messenger of Allah did not agree."
- It was reported that some hypocrites — a group of more than ten men — plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ while he was at the battle of Tabūk, riding one night. **Ad-Daḥḥāk** said, "This Ayah was revealed about them."

**The night of al-ʿAqabah.** Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī recorded in his book *Dalāʼil an-Nubuwwah* that **Ḥudhayfah bin al-Yamān** said: "I was holding the bridle of the Messenger's camel while ʿAmmār was leading it, or vice versa. When we reached al-ʿAqabah, twelve riders intercepted the Prophet ﷺ. When I alerted the Messenger ﷺ, he shouted at them and they all ran away." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them, "Did you know who they were?" They said, "No, O Allah's Messenger! They had masks. However, we know their horses." He said, **"They are the hypocrites until the Day of Resurrection. Do you know what they intended?"** They said, "No." He said, **"They wanted to mingle with the Messenger of Allah and throw him from the ʿAqabah (to the valley)."**

They said, "O Allah's Messenger! Should you ask their tribes to send the head of each one of them to you?" He said: **"No, for I hate that the Arabs should say that Muhammad used some people in fighting and when Allah gave him victory with their help, he commanded that they be killed."** He then said, "O Allah! Throw the Dubaylah at them." They asked what the Dubaylah was, and he said, "A missile of fire that falls on the heart of one of them and brings about his demise."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records an incident of this kind with a slightly different turn: during the return from this very battle of Tabūk, twelve men from among the hypocrites sat in ambush behind a mountain pass intending to take the Prophet ﷺ by surprise and kill him; Jibrīl (peace be upon him) informed him of their intention, he took a different route, and their conspiracy went to dust. It adds that several other events of this nature are on record, and that there is no element of contradiction or improbability in the likelihood that the verse refers to all of them.

Abū aṭ-Ṭufayl relates that Ḥudhayfah, pressed once about how many the Companions of al-ʿAqabah were, said: "We were told that they were fourteen men, unless you were one of them, then the number is fifteen!" He testified by Allah that twelve of them are at war with Allah and His Messenger in this life and when the witness comes forth for witness. Three of them were pardoned, for they said they did not hear the person the Messenger ﷺ sent to announce something, and did not know what the people had plotted.

And ʿAmmār bin Yāsir narrated, in a hadith **collected by Muslim**, that Ḥudhayfah told him the Prophet ﷺ said: "Among my Companions are twelve hypocrites who will never enter Paradise or find its scent, until the camel enters the thread of the needle. Eight of them will be struck by the Dubaylah, which is a missile made of fire that appears between their shoulders and pierces their chest."

This, Ibn Kathir notes, is why Ḥudhayfah was called the holder of the secret: he knew who these hypocrites were, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave their names to him and none else.

Two things in *"which they were unable to carry out"* deserve a pause. The resolve is recorded against them though the deed never came off — in the incident Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, because Jibrīl (peace be upon him) informed the Prophet ﷺ and he took another road. And when the Companions offered to settle it by demanding their heads, he refused, giving as his reason what the Arabs would then say about him.

## "They found no cause except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them"

This is the moral centre of ayah 74, and Ibn Kathir puts it with force: the Messenger ﷺ did not commit an error against them, other than that Allah has enriched them on account of the Prophet's blessed and honourable mission. And had Allah guided them to what the Prophet ﷺ came with, they would have experienced its delight completely.

The Prophet ﷺ once said to the Anṣār (the Muslims of Madinah): "Have I not found you misguided and Allah guided you through me, divided and Allah united you through me, and poor and Allah enriched you through me?" And whenever the Messenger ﷺ asked them a question like that, they replied, "Allah and His Messenger have granted the favour."

Ibn Kathir points out that this kind of statement — where the only "fault" named is in fact a good — is uttered when there is no wrong committed at all. He gives the parallel: *"And they had no fault except that they believed in Allah…"* (85:8). Read ayah 74 that way and the sting lands: the only charge that could be brought against the Prophet ﷺ was that Allah had enriched them through him.

## "If then they repent…"

After the words of disbelief, after a false oath sworn by Allah's own name, after what was resolved against the Prophet's ﷺ life — the ayah does not slam shut. Ibn Kathir says it plainly: **Allah called the hypocrites to repent.** *"If then they repent, it will be better for them."*

And that is exactly how Jullās heard it in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account. The verse that exposed him was the verse he took hold of: *this very verse has also given me the right of making Taubah (repentance).*

The alternative is stated without softening: *"but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful torment in this worldly life and in the Hereafter."* Ibn Kathir explains: if they persist on their ways, Allah will inflict a painful torment on them in this life, by killing, sadness and depression, and in the Hereafter with torment, punishment, disgrace and humiliation.

And the last clause: *"And there is none for them on earth as a protector or a helper"* — Ibn Kathir: none who will bring happiness to them, aid them, bring about benefit or fend off harm. Hypocrisy is a bid to keep a foot in both camps so that some protector remains whichever way things go; the verdict of ayah 74 is that it ends with no protector at all.

## What the passage asks of us

**Be firm without being cruel.** The *ghilẓah* of ayah 73 is refusing to water down what is due — not a sharp tongue. As Qurṭubī explains it, as relayed by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: enforce what the Sharīʿah requires, and do not let that become verbal abuse.

**Watch what is said in the private gathering.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes hypocrites uttering words of infidelity in their gatherings and denying it on oath when word gets out. One such sentence, said among his own people, is what ayah 74 records and what we still recite.

**An oath is not a shield.** They swore by Allah — one of them beside the Prophet's own Mimbar — and were believed by men, and answered by revelation.

**Ingratitude is at the root of it.** They were guided, united and enriched, and what came back was resentment. When you find yourself resenting the very source of a blessing, ayah 74 is describing you.

**The door stays open until you walk away from it.** *"If then they repent, it will be better for them."* Jullās is the proof: exposed by revelation, and rescued by the same words.

passages.title: Broken vows and the mockery of the givers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat put money in the witness box. A man promises Allah that if he is made rich he will give — and when the wealth arrives he clutches it and turns away (75–76). Allah's response is terrifying: the broken promise leaves hypocrisy embedded in the heart (77), and no private calculation hides it, because Allah knows their secret ideas and their secret counsels alike (78). The same disease then shows its other face: those who give nothing sneer at those who do — mocking the large gift as showing off and the small one as beneath Allah's need (79). And seeking forgiveness for such people, even seventy times, changes nothing (80).

## A vow made in need, broken in plenty (75–76)

Ibn Kathir reads the opening straightforwardly: "some hypocrites give Allah their strongest oaths that if He enriches them from His bounty, they will give away alms and be among the righteous. However, they did not fulfill their vows or say the truth with their words." He renders the two ayat together: *"And of them are some who made a covenant with Allah (saying): 'If He bestowed on us of His bounty, we will verily, give Sadaqah and will be certainly among the righteous.' Then when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy, and turned away, averse."*

Notice what is promised: not only to give, but to "be certainly among the righteous." They are asking for wealth on credit against a version of themselves that does not yet exist. And notice who the promise is made to — *ʿāhada Allāh*, "made a covenant with Allah," not with someone who might forget.

Ayah 76 does not describe one failure but three, in sequence: they *withheld* it, they *turned away*, and they were *averse*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's paraphrase catches the real injury: "when Allah blessed them with wealth, out of His grace, they became misers overnight and turned away from their pledge of obedience to Allah and His Messenger." The stinginess is the visible symptom. The turning away is the wound. It was never only about the goats.

**The story behind it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects ayah 75 to a particular event, reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Marduwayh, al-Tabarani and al-Baihaqi on the authority of Abu Umamah Bahili (may Allah be pleased with him).

A man called Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib al-Ansari came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him to pray that he become rich. The Prophet ﷺ discouraged him: by the Being who holds my life in His hands, he said, if I had wished, the mountains of Madinah would have turned into solid gold and followed behind me on my walkways — but I do not like being that wealthy. The man went away. Later he returned and repeated the request, this time pledging that if he received the wealth he prayed for, he would give every deserving person his share from it. The Prophet ﷺ made the prayer.

The effect was immediate and enormous: an unprecedented increase in the number of goats he owned. First, Madinah became too small for him, so he moved to the outskirts — coming into the city for Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr with the Prophet ﷺ and praying the rest out in the wilderness where his herd was. Then the flock grew again, that space too became insufficient, and he moved farther out — now coming to Madinah only on Fridays for Jumuʿah, and performing all five daily prayers where he was stationed. Then his wealth increased again, he left that spot too, and went so far from Madinah that he sat deprived of Jumuʿah and congregation both.

**His prayers did not vanish; they retreated.** Each increase in the blessing bought another step away from the One who gave it. After some time the Prophet ﷺ asked people about him, was told his wealth had grown so large that he had gone far from the city, and said three times: *Wayḥa Thaʿlabah* — "Alas for Thaʿlabah."

**The test arrives.** By chance this was the time of the revelation of the verse of ṣadaqāt (ayah 60 of this sūrah), commanding the Prophet ﷺ, "Take from their wealth a charity." He had the whole law of ṣadaqah committed to writing, appointed two men as collectors, and sent them to collect what was due on livestock — with orders to go to Thaʿlabah, and to another man from the tribe of Bani Sulaym.

When the collectors reached Thaʿlabah and presented the order, he said this thing had become a sort of *jizyah* — the levy taken from non-Muslims. Then he hedged: leave for now, call on me on your way back. When they returned he asked to see the written law of ṣadaqah, looked at it, said exactly what he had said before, and told them: all right, you can go for now, I have to think about it first, I will decide later. Not a refusal, exactly. Delay dressed as deliberation.

The man from Bani Sulaym did the opposite. Hearing the order, he went out to meet the two emissaries himself, carrying the **best** of his camels and goats, precisely according to what was due from him. They told him their orders were not to pick out the best animals but to take the average ones, so they could not accept these — and he insisted, saying it was his pleasure to present those very animals, and asked that they be taken as they were.

When the two collectors reached Madinah, before hearing a word of their report the Prophet ﷺ repeated three times, "Alas for Thaʿlabah." Then he was pleased to hear about the Sulaymi, and prayed for him. Thereupon, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, came the ayah: "And among them there are those who made a pledge with Allah."

Ibn Kathir does not tie the ayah to that incident and speaks of the hypocrites in general. The ayah describes a type, and the historical report gives the type a face.

## The punishment that is the disease (77–78)

*Fa-aʿqabahum nifāqan fī qulūbihim* — Ibn Kathir renders it, "So He punished them by putting hypocrisy into their hearts till the Day whereon they shall meet Him." Two things deserve care.

**First, the cause.** The ayah names it twice: "because they broke that covenant with Allah which they had promised to Him and because they used to tell lies." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the ayah "points out to its cause which lies in their lying and pledge breaking." Ibn Kathir puts it as plainly: "He placed hypocrisy in their hearts because they broke their promise and lied." The broken promise did not merely earn a penalty later; it *became* a condition now. Having said it, Ibn Kathir breaks off: "We seek refuge with Allah from such an end."

**Second, the horizon.** "Till the Day whereon they shall meet Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the sober conclusion: Allah made the hypocrisy of their hearts deep and firm, so that "they would just not have the ability to make Taubah itself" — tawbah being the turning back to Allah in repentance. It adds a warning worth pinning up: *there are occasions when the curse of evil deeds assumes alarming proportions, so much so that one is deprived of the very ability (tawfīq) of making tawbah. May Allah protect us from this misfortune.*

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *There are three signs for a hypocrite: if he speaks, he lies; if he promises, he breaks the promise; and if he is entrusted, he betrays the trust.* Set it beside the ayah and the match is exact — two of the three signs. A promise, in this religion, is not a mood. It is a report about the future that you are obliged to make true.

**How the story ended.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues the narrative, noting what Ibn Jarir writes at the end of it. When the Prophet ﷺ said "Alas for Thaʿlabah" three times, some of the man's relatives were in the gathering; one of them travelled to him at once, reproached him for his behaviour, and told him it had caused the revelation of a verse of the Qurʼan. Thaʿlabah grew nervous, reached Madinah, and requested that his ṣadaqah be accepted. The Prophet ﷺ told him that Allah had told him not to accept it. Hearing this, Thaʿlabah was so overcome with disappointment that he started throwing dust on his head. The Prophet ﷺ said: *this is something you have chosen to do on your own; I ordered you and you did not obey — now your ṣadaqah cannot be accepted.*

He tried again after the Prophet ﷺ departed this world. Abu Bakr refused: "when the Holy Prophet ﷺ did not accept it, how can I do it?" ʿUmar gave the same answer. So did ʿUthman, during whose caliphate Thaʿlabah died. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazharī) closes with the same shudder Ibn Kathir showed: we seek the protection of Allah from all evil deeds.

**But why was his repentance not accepted?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection and answers it (citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*): the Prophet ﷺ was informed through revelation that the man was not making his tawbah with absolute sincerity — hypocrisy was concealed in his heart, and he was simply trying to put matters right with the Muslims for the time being. And once the Prophet ﷺ had himself declared him a hypocrite, the caliphs who succeeded him had no right to accept his ṣadaqah, since being a Muslim is a condition for zakāh.

**And the rule that follows for us.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: after the Prophet ﷺ, no one knows the hypocrisy hidden in the heart of a person. Therefore the rule to follow in future is that **anyone who makes tawbah and confesses to his Islam and īmān should be treated as Muslims are treated — no matter what lies in his heart.** Thaʿlabah's case rested on revelation, and revelation ended with prophethood.

**Which is exactly where ayah 78 lands** — a rhetorical question aimed at the private arithmetic behind all of this: "Know they not that Allah knows their secret ideas, and their Najwa (secret counsels), and that Allah is the All-Knower of things unseen?" Ibn Kathir comments that Allah "knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret," and has full knowledge of what is in their hearts — even at the moment they are pretending that they will give away alms if they acquire wealth and be grateful to Allah for it.

We affirm this as it came, without likening Allah's knowledge to ours and without explaining it away: it is real and total, "for He is the All-Knower of all unseen and apparent things, every secret, every session of counsel, and all that is seen and hidden." As Ibn Kathir puts it, "Truly, Allah knows them better than they know themselves." A man can hide his intention from a charity collector. He cannot hide it from the One he made the covenant with.

## Mockery, and the door that closes (79–80)

Ayah 79 turns to the second symptom of the same disease: *"Those who defame such of the believers who give charity voluntarily, and such who could not find to give charity except what is available to them – so they mock at them; Allah will throw back their mockery on them, and they shall have a painful torment."* Ibn Kathir renders *al-muṭṭawwiʿīn* as "the volunteers"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies that what is meant is charity given on a voluntary basis (nafl ṣadaqah) — beyond what is obligatory.

Ibn Kathir captures the logic exactly: it is among the traits of the hypocrites that they "will not leave anyone without defaming and ridiculing him in all circumstances," even those who give charity. Give a large amount, and they say he is showing off. Give a small amount, and they say Allah stands not in need of this man's charity. The mockery is not a judgement about the gift; it is a fixed posture that will find its reason either way.

**What the companions were actually doing.** Al-Bukhari recorded, through a chain ending with Abu Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): "When the verses of charity were revealed, we used to work as porters. A man came and distributed objects of charity in abundance and they said, 'He is showing off.' Another man came and gave a Ṣāʿ" — a small measure of food grains — "they said, 'Allah is not in need of this small amount of charity.' Then the Ayah was revealed." Muslim collected this hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ as well.

Ibn Kathir gives a fuller scene, narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbas. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out and called the people to bring forth their charity. Among the last to come was a man with a ṣāʿ of dates, who said: "O Allah's Messenger! This is a Ṣāʿ of dates. I spent the night bringing water and earned two Ṣāʿ of dates for my work. I kept one Ṣāʿ and brought you the other." The Prophet ﷺ ordered it added to the charity — and some men mocked him: Allah and His Messenger are not in need of this charity; what benefit would this ṣāʿ of yours bring?

In the same gathering ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ whether anyone else was still giving. He was told, *"None besides you."* So he said: I will give a hundred ūqiyah of gold as charity. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him, "Are you crazy?" He answered that he was not, and explained: I have eight thousand dirhams — four thousand I give as a loan to my Lord, and four thousand I keep for myself. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: *May Allah bless you for what you kept and what you gave away.* The hypocrites then defamed him too — "By Allah, ʿAbd al-Rahman gave what he gave just to show off." "They lied," says Ibn Kathir; he gave it willingly, and Allah revealed his innocence and the innocence of the poor man who brought only a ṣāʿ of dates.

A similar story was narrated from Mujahid and several others. Ibn Ishaq names the people involved: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, who gave four thousand dirhams, and ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdi of Bani ʿAjlan, who gave a hundred wasaq of dates — both defamed as showing off. And as for the man who gave the little that he could afford, Ibn Ishaq names him: Abu ʿAqīl, of Bani Anīf al-Arashi, an ally of Bani ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, who brought a ṣāʿ of dates and added it to the charity, and was laughed at — "Allah does not need the Ṣāʿ of Abu ʿAqīl." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, gives Abu ʿAqīl's offering as half a ṣāʿ, approximately 1.75 kilos; the sources differ on the exact measure, and neither version changes what was done to him for it. Allah Himself answers the joke, in a Book still being recited.

**"Allah will throw back their mockery on them."** *Sakhira Allāhu minhum.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: the word "mocked" stands for "punished for their mockery." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is rebuking them for their evil actions and for defaming the believers — "Truly, the reward, or punishment, is equitable to the action. Allah treated them the way mocked people are treated, to aid the believers in this life." And beyond this life, He has prepared for them "a painful torment."

Then ayah 80 speaks to the Prophet ﷺ himself: whether he asks forgiveness for them or does not, and even if he asks seventy times, "Allah will not forgive them because they have disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger. And Allah guides not those people who are rebellious."

Ibn Kathir explains the number: seventy "was mentioned to close the door on this subject, for Arabs use this number when they exaggerate, not that they actually mean seventy or more than seventy." It is the Arabic way of saying *no number of times*.

**The Prophet ﷺ and the closed door.** Ibn Kathir relates from ash-Shaʿbī that when ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy was dying, his son went to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "My father has died, I wish you could attend him and pray the funeral prayer for him." The Prophet ﷺ asked his name; he said, "al-Hubab ibn ʿAbdullah." The Prophet ﷺ said: *Rather, you are ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbdullah, for al-Hubab is a devil's name.* He went along with him, attended the funeral, gave his own shirt as a shroud, and prayed the funeral prayer. He was asked, "Would you pray on him, when he is a hypocrite?" He said: Allah said, "…(and even) if you ask seventy times for their forgiveness…" — *verily, I will ask Allah to forgive them seventy times and seventy more and seventy more.* Ibn Kathir notes that similar narrations were collected from ʿUrwah ibn az-Zubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah ibn Diʿamah and Ibn Jarir.

That exchange shows a heart so merciful it kept pressing at a door Allah had already described as shut. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the matter is settled explicitly a little later, at ayah 84 — "and never offer a prayer on anyone of them who dies" — where the detailed explanation belongs.

## Living it

- **Do not bargain with Allah for what you cannot carry.** The Prophet ﷺ discouraged Thaʿlabah's request before he ever granted it. A little that keeps you near the masjid is better than an abundance that moves you further out each year.
- **Watch the drift, not the collapse.** Thaʿlabah never announced an apostasy. Nobody falls in a single step.
- **Fulfil what you pledged**, especially a pledge made in need. Ayah 77 makes the broken covenant itself the doorway to the disease, and the hadith of the Two Ṣaḥīḥs names promise-breaking as a sign of the hypocrite.
- **Give your best, and let others give theirs in peace.** Ayah 79 defends both the large gift and the small one — and condemns the running commentary on other people's charity.
- **Judge no one's heart.** After the Prophet ﷺ, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, no one knows the hypocrisy hidden inside a person; whoever repents and professes Islam and īmān is treated as Muslims are treated. The passage is a mirror for your own giving, not a lens for inspecting someone else's.

passages.title: Rejoicing in staying behind; no prayer for their dead
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These four ayat follow the men who stayed home from Tabuk into their sitting rooms, and then all the way to the grave. They open on men pleased with themselves for having avoided a hard march, and close with the Prophet ﷺ forbidden ever to pray over one of their dead. What holds them together is a single movement: a small, cheap comfort taken now, and the permanent losses it buys. Comfort now, fire later (ayah 81); laughter now, weeping later (ayah 82); a seat at home now, permanent exclusion from the ranks of the strivers (ayah 83); and finally no prayer, no standing at the graveside, no forgiveness sought (ayah 84).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the conduct of the hypocrites who did not take part in the battle of Tabuk, despite the general call to jihad, has been the running theme for several passages already. These ayat give another example — and the two sentences it earns: punishment in the Hereafter, and, already in this world, the elimination of their names from the list of the mujahidin of Islam forever.

## The scene: the hottest march

Ibn Kathir sets the stage plainly: Tabuk occurred at a time when the heat was intense and, as he puts it, the fruits and the shade had become delightful.

So they said to one another — Ibn Kathir stresses that they said it *to each other* — **لَا تَنفِرُوا فِي الْحَرِّ**, "March not forth in the heat." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the sting: they prompted others too, telling them not to march in that hot weather. Discouragement passed around as friendly advice.

## The word that turns the tables: al-mukhallafūn

Ayah 81 does not call them "those who chose to stay behind." It calls them **الْمُخَلَّفُونَ** (*al-mukhallafūn*) — the plural of *mukhallaf*, which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means "abandoned" or "left out."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the reversal in that. These men are pleased with the idea that they kept themselves out of danger by not going. But the truth of the matter is that Allah did not consider them worthy of this supreme honour. So it is not they who abandoned the jihad; it is the jihad that abandoned them — because Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, at their discretion, considered it fit that they should be left out.

**بِمَقْعَدِهِمْ** (*bi-maqʿadihim*) — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "their sitting back," and explains that it appears here in the sense of *quʿūd*, "sitting," as a verbal noun.

**خِلَافَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ** (*khilāfa rasūli-llāh*) — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān translates this as "to the displeasure of the Messenger of Allah," and notes that the word *khilāf* can be taken in more than one sense:

- It could be taken to mean "behind" or "after" — and this is the meaning Abu ʿUbayd went by. On that reading, these people were rejoicing at staying at home *after* the departure of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — an occasion, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān remarks, not really worth the mirth.
- It is also possible to take *khilāf* in the sense of *mukhālafa* (contravention, opposition). On that reading, they sat at home in contravention of the command of the Prophet ﷺ.

Notice too what they disliked: **وَكَرِهُوا أَن يُجَاهِدُوا بِأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَنفُسِهِمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ** — they hated to strive and fight with *both* their properties and their lives in the cause of Allah.

## "The fire of Hell is more intense in heat"

The answer in ayah 81 is not an argument but a comparison, and it lands exactly on the excuse they gave. They measured one thing only — the temperature of a summer march. So Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ: **قُلْ نَارُ جَهَنَّمَ أَشَدُّ حَرًّا**. Ibn Kathir explains that this Fire will be their destination because of their disobedience, and that it is more intense in heat than the heat they sought to avoid.

Ibn Kathir cites two hadith on how far this is beyond ordinary fire.

**First**, Imam Malik narrated that Abu az-Zinad said that al-Aʿraj narrated that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The fire that the son of Adam kindles is but one part of seventy parts of the Fire of Jahannam."* They said, "O Allah's Messenger! This fire alone is enough." He said: *"(Hellfire) was favoured by sixty-nine parts."* Ibn Kathir says the Two Sahihs collected this hadith.

**Second**, al-Aʿmash narrated that Abu Ishaq said that an-Nuʿman bin Bashir said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"On the Day of Resurrection, the person who will receive the least punishment among the people of the Fire wears two slippers made from the Fire of Jahannam, causing his brain to boil just as a pot boils. He thinks that none in the Fire is receiving a more severe torment than he, when in fact he is receiving the least torment."* This too, Ibn Kathir says, the Two Sahihs collected.

He then gathers ayat on the same theme: that it takes away the scalp, burning it completely (70:15–16); that boiling water is poured down over the heads of its people, melting what is within their bellies as well as their skins, with hooked rods of iron for them, and every time they seek to get away from its anguish they are driven back (22:19–22); and that skins roasted through are changed for other skins so that the punishment may be tasted again (4:56).

Then: **لَّوْ كَانُوا يَفْقَهُونَ** — "if only they could understand." Ibn Kathir comments: if they have any comprehension or understanding, they would have marched with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ *during the heat*, so as to save themselves from the Fire of Jahannam, which is much more severe. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as a question: these people see the heat of a certain given time and try to beat it one way or another, without worrying about the fire their disobedience leads to — is the heat of our seasons really more intense than the heat of Hell?

## Ayah 82: laugh a little, weep a lot

**فَلْيَضْحَكُوا قَلِيلًا وَلْيَبْكُوا كَثِيرًا** — "So let them laugh a little, and weep a lot."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that although the imperative form is used, the commentators interpret it in the sense of a plain statement of fact. The wisdom they give for the imperative form is that it makes the outcome categorical and certain: this *is* going to happen. Such people may laugh for the days they have in this mortal world; in the Hereafter they must weep, and weep forever.

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān bring the same comment from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās — Ibn Kathir through the report of Ibn Abi Talhah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān through Ibn Abi Hatim: the world is short-lived, so let them laugh in it as much as they wish; but when the world comes to an end and they are returned to Allah, the Exalted and Most Honoured, they will start a weeping that never comes to an end.

Hold *qalīlan* (a little) against *kathīran* (much): that is the exchange rate the whole passage is built on. And the ayah closes with **جَزَاءً بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ**, "as a recompense of what they used to earn" — the weeping is not an arbitrary penalty but wages for work done.

## Ayah 83: shut out of the ranks

**فَإِن رَّجَعَكَ اللَّهُ إِلَىٰ طَائِفَةٍ مِّنْهُمْ** — "If Allah brings you back to a party of them." Ibn Kathir explains this as the return from this battle, and reports from Qatadah that "a party of them" is a reference to the twelve hypocrite men.

If they then ask permission to go out with him to another battle, the Prophet ﷺ is told to answer: **لَّن تَخْرُجُوا مَعِيَ أَبَدًا وَلَن تُقَاتِلُوا مَعِيَ عَدُوًّا** — "Never shall you go out with me nor fight an enemy with me." Ibn Kathir says this is an admonishment and a punishment for them; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that most of the commentators have said this injunction was enforced as their punishment in the present world — even if they themselves request to be allowed to take part, they should not be allowed.

The reason given is precise: **إِنَّكُمْ رَضِيتُم بِالْقُعُودِ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ** — "You were pleased to sit (inactive) on the first occasion." The very thing they chose is made permanent for them. Ibn Kathir draws out the principle behind this: *the recompense of an evil deed includes being directed to follow it with another evil deed, while the reward of a good deed includes being directed to another good deed after it.* He supports it with "And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe therein for the first time" (6:110), and notes that Allah used the same title, *al-mukhallafūn*, concerning the ʿUmrah of Hudaybiyyah: "Those who lagged behind will say, when you set forth to take the spoils" (48:15).

The closing words, **فَاقْعُدُوا مَعَ الْخَالِفِينَ** — "then you sit now with those who lag behind" — refer, Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, to the men who lagged behind from the battle.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an angle from Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi's summary in his *Bayān al-Qurʼān*: even if such men do intend to take part in a future jihad, they would get out of it when they want to, under one pretext or another; and since they do not have faith in their hearts, their intention too is not backed by sincerity. So the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to tell them the truth — that he does not trust their word or their deed.

## Ayah 84: the funeral of ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy

**وَلَا تُصَلِّ عَلَىٰ أَحَدٍ مِّنْهُم مَّاتَ أَبَدًا وَلَا تَقُمْ عَلَىٰ قَبْرِهِ** — "And never pray the funeral prayer for any of them who dies, nor stand at his grave."

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is commanding His Messenger ﷺ to disown the hypocrites: to abstain from praying the funeral prayer when any of them dies, and from standing next to his grave to seek Allah's forgiveness for him or to invoke Allah for his benefit — because the hypocrites disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and died as such. The ruling applies to all those who are known to be hypocrites, even though it was revealed about the specific case of ʿAbdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul, the chief hypocrite. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that this occasion of revelation stands established from Sahih Ahadith and is confirmed by a consensus of the Muslim Ummah.

The story, recorded by al-Bukhari from Ibn ʿUmar (and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, appearing in the Sahih of Muslim as well): when ʿAbdullah bin Ubayy died, his son ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbdullah — a sincere Muslim and a Companion — came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him for his shirt to shroud his father in, and the Messenger ﷺ did that. He then asked that the Prophet ﷺ offer his father's funeral prayer, and Allah's Messenger ﷺ stood up to offer it. ʿUmar took hold of the Prophet's ﷺ robe and said, "O Allah's Messenger! Are you going to offer his funeral prayer even though your Lord has forbidden you to do so?" Allah's Messenger ﷺ said, *"I have been given the choice, for Allah says: 'Whether you ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them — even though you ask for their forgiveness seventy times, Allah will not forgive them' (9:80). Verily, I will ask more than seventy times."* ʿUmar said, "He is a hypocrite!" So Allah's Messenger ﷺ offered the funeral prayer — and then this ayah was revealed.

ʿUmar bin al-Khattab narrated the event in similar terms, adding that the Prophet ﷺ offered the prayer, walked with the funeral procession and stood at his grave until he was buried; that ʿUmar was afterwards amazed at his own daring in talking that way to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have better knowledge; and that soon afterwards these two ayat were revealed. Ever since that revelation came, the Prophet ﷺ never offered the funeral prayer for any hypocrite nor stood at his grave, until Allah brought death to him. At-Tirmidhi collected this hadith in the tafsir section of his Sunan and said "Hasan Sahih"; al-Bukhari also recorded it.

## Making sense of the Prophet's ﷺ conduct

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the questions this incident raises, leaning on al-Qurtubi and on Thanavi's *Bayān al-Qurʼān*.

**Why give his shirt to the chief of the hypocrites?** Two reasons are offered. First, it was done at the request of his son, who was a sincere Companion, and the motive was simply to console him on his loss. Second, there could be another reason, reported in al-Bukhari on the authority of Jabir: when some Quraysh chiefs were taken captive at Badr, one of them was al-ʿAbbās, the uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, who had no shirt on him. Al-ʿAbbās was tall, and no shirt other than that of ʿAbdullah bin Ubayy would fit him — so the Prophet ﷺ took that shirt and had his uncle wear it. Giving his own shirt now was repaying that favour (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān citing al-Qurtubi).

**What was ʿUmar's basis for saying "your Lord has forbidden you"?** No ayah had ever expressly forbidden the Prophet ﷺ from offering the funeral prayer for a hypocrite. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that ʿUmar must have deduced that sense of prohibition from 9:80 itself: once it stands proved that a hypocrite will not be pardoned, he found no reason to offer a funeral prayer for him and pray that he be forgiven — it might be redundant, and, in ʿUmar's judgement, against the station of a prophet.

**Why then did the Prophet ﷺ say he had been given a choice?** Because the formal arrangement of words in 9:80 does carry the sense of giving a choice ("ask pardon for them or do not ask pardon for them"), and the mention of "seventy times" there is not prescribing a limit but expressing "many times." The plain outcome of the ayah is that a hypocrite will not be pardoned however many times forgiveness is sought for him — but he ﷺ was not expressly prohibited from praying for their forgiveness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a parallel: "And it is all the same for them whether or not you warn them — they are not going to believe" (36:10) did not categorically stop him ﷺ from warning people, since other ayat kept the mission of calling and warning standing — "O Messenger, convey all that has been sent down to you from your Lord" (5:67), and "you are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide" (13:7).

**And he had reasons of policy.** He knew that neither his shirt nor the funeral prayer would bring the man forgiveness. But al-Bukhari records on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Had I known that he will be pardoned by praying for his forgiveness more than seventy times, I would have done that too" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān citing al-Qurtubi). Another hadith, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes without naming its collection, has him ﷺ saying that his shirt cannot save the man from the punishment of Allah, but that he did it in the hope that thousands of his people would embrace Islam. And, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, the books of *maghāzī* (the works recording the Prophet's ﷺ expeditions) and some books of tafsir report that a thousand people of the tribe of Khazraj did embrace Islam after witnessing this.

**So why was the prohibition then revealed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that there was indeed a religiously expedient advantage visible to the Prophet ﷺ in offering the prayer, but the act also carried a disturbing factor in it, almost the reverse of what was expected — an element that somehow did not attract his ﷺ attention. The likelihood was strong that this would create dissatisfaction among sincere Muslims, who might have thought that sincere Muslims and wily hypocrites had been officially put on the same footing. To offset that danger, this explicit prohibition was revealed. Both men stand vindicated: ʿUmar reasoning from what had been revealed, the Prophet ﷺ acting on a latitude not yet withdrawn.

## Rulings drawn from ayah 84

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists two:

1. Offering the funeral prayer for a disbeliever, or making duʿā seeking forgiveness for him, is not permissible.
2. Standing before the grave of a disbeliever as a mark of respect for him, or going to visit it, is forbidden. This does not include standing there to learn a lesson from it, or because of some compulsion. As an example of the latter, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a case from the legal work *Hidāyah*: should a disbelieving relative of a Muslim die leaving no guardian or heir behind, the Muslim relative can put the deceased into hollowed ground as it is, without having to make it conform to the manner of burial prescribed by the Prophet ﷺ.

The ayah's own reason is its final clause: **إِنَّهُمْ كَفَرُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَمَاتُوا وَهُمْ فَاسِقُونَ** — "Certainly they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and died while they were Fasiqun." The prohibition is not cruelty toward the dead; it is a refusal to say over a grave what is not true.

## Living it

Nobody in ayah 81 announces that they have abandoned Allah. They notice that it is hot, choose the shade, find words that make the choice sound sensible — and pass those words to others. *Law kānū yafqahūn*: had they had any comprehension, they would have walked into the summer to escape a fire that is far worse.

The men of ayah 83 get more of exactly what they chose — the seat they were so pleased with, made permanent, and the door to anything better locked from outside.

passages.title: Content with the stragglers while the Prophet strives
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat continue the Qur'an's account of the men who found reasons not to march out to Tabuk, and they set two lives side by side. On one side are people whose wealth and children keep them comfortably at home; on the other is the Messenger ﷺ and those who believed with him, striving with both wealth and lives. Ayah 85 answers a question the Muslims might have asked about the prosperity of such men; ayat 86–87 show them asking to be excused, and their hearts sealed; ayat 88–89 turn the whole picture over with a single word — "But" — and name what the believers actually receive.

## The setting: the army has left, and some stayed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these verses once again carry the description of the hypocrites who had avoided participating in the battle of Tabuk under one or another pretext. Among them, it points out, there were some rich people as well. That detail is the thread running through all five ayat: what a person does with his means when the call comes.

## Ayah 85 — when someone else's prosperity catches your eye

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the difficulty honestly. The affluent life of these men could have made the Muslims ask: *when these people are so unacceptable with Allah, why did they have to get all those blessings in this world?* It is an old question and a live one. The answer given is that a little thinking unfolds the reality behind what they possess in the form of wealth and children. These things are no mercy and no blessing for them. They are their trial and their punishment in this world — quite apart from the additional punishment due in the Hereafter.

The Qur'an's own wording carries this: **لِيُعَذِّبَهُم بِهَا** — *to punish them with these*. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, Allah wills to punish them **by and through these very possessions**. The commentary then makes the reason plain, and it is worth sitting with. They love wealth, they guard it, and they keep worrying about how to go on increasing it. They are never at peace. They collect things of comfort around them, yet genuine peace and comfort never knock at their doors — for those are things of the heart. And since this engrossment in the pursuit of wealth makes them heedless towards the concerns of the Hereafter, they indulge in acts of disobedience to their Creator, and that disobedience in turn becomes the cause of their punishment. So whether you look at the wealth as a cause or at the punishment as its effect, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, it remains a punishment either way.

Ibn Kathir states the ayah's meaning in the same direction and adds its terrible end: Allah only wants to punish them with these things in this world, **and that their souls shall depart — that they die — while they are disbelievers**. That is the real reckoning behind an enviable life. He also notes that the explanation of a similar ayah was mentioned before.

Notice, too, whom the ayah addresses. The command is to the Prophet ﷺ himself: *let neither their wealth nor children impress you*. What is being taught is a discipline of the gaze — not to let the surface of a life dictate your judgement of it.

## Ayat 86–87 — "Leave us behind"

Ayah 86 describes the moment a sūrah comes down enjoining them to believe in Allah and to strive hard and fight along with His Messenger ﷺ. The response is not open refusal. It is a request for exemption.

**The capable ones.** The Qur'an calls those who ask **اُولُوا الطَّولِ** — rendered "the capable ones" by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, and "the wealthy among them" in the translation Ibn Kathir gives. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine point here: this expression is not for particularization; it serves a purpose. It tells us there were others too, the ones not so capable — and the incapable ones had at least some obvious excuse to stay behind. The blame falls precisely where ability was present.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah in the same way: Allah chastises and admonishes those who stayed away from Jihad and refrained from performing it, **even though they had the supplies, means and ability to join it**. They asked the Messenger ﷺ for permission to stay behind, saying **ذَرْنَا نَكُن مَّعَ الْقَاعِدِينَ** — *"Leave us behind, we would be with those who sit at home."* Ibn Kathir's comment on that sentence is devastating: in saying it, they accepted for themselves the shame of lagging behind with women, after the army had left.

**Content with it.** Ayah 87 does not say they *were left* behind. The translation renders it *they preferred to stay behind with the helpless*; Ibn Kathir's rendering is **"They are content to be with those who sit behind."** The word to weigh is *content*: what the ayah records is not merely the sitting but their contentment with it.

**Cowards, then loud.** Ibn Kathir sketches their character in one line: if war starts, such people are the most cowardly of men; when it is safe, they are the most boastful. He supports this from the Qur'an itself. Of such people Allah says: *"Then when fear comes, you will see them looking to you, their eyes revolving like one over whom hovers death; but when the fear departs, they will smite you with sharp tongues"* (33:19) — their tongues directing their harsh words against you, Ibn Kathir notes, when it is safe to do so; in battle, however, they are the most cowardly among men. And again: *"Those who believe say, 'Why is not a sūrah sent down?' But when a decisive sūrah is sent down and fighting is mentioned therein, you will see those in whose hearts is a disease looking at you with a look of one fainting to death… Obedience and good words were better for them. And when the matter is resolved on, then if they had been true to Allah, it would have been better for them"* (47:20–21).

**The seal.** Then comes the sentence that should stop every reader: **وَطُبِعَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ** — *their hearts are sealed up*. Ibn Kathir ties the seal directly to what they did: it was **because of** their staying away from Jihad and from accompanying the Messenger ﷺ in Allah's cause. And the consequence, **فَهُمْ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ** — *so they understand not* — is spelled out by him with precision: they neither understand what benefits them so that they perform it, nor what hurts them so that they avoid it.

That is the sober logic of the passage. What Ibn Kathir names as the outcome of turning away is not only a missed expedition; it is the loss of the ability to tell benefit from harm.

## Ayat 88–89 — "But the Messenger ﷺ…"

Ayah 88 opens with **لَٰكِنِ** — *but*. Ibn Kathir marks the turn plainly: after Allah mentioned the sins of the hypocrites, He praised the faithful believers and described their reward in the Hereafter. These two ayat, he says, describe the qualities of the faithful believers as well as their reward.

Read the two halves of the passage against each other and the structure becomes visible. In ayah 85 the wealth (**أَمْوَٰل**) of the hypocrites is the very thing through which they are punished — held, guarded, never enough. In ayah 88 the same word returns in the believers' hands: **جَٰهَدُوا بِأَمْوَٰلِهِمْ** — *they strove hard and fought with their wealth and their lives*. Identical possessions; opposite direction. One group's property anchors them; the other group's property is spent and their persons are put on the line. The passage is not against wealth. It is about which way wealth points.

Notice also the phrase **مَعَهُ** — *with him*. The hypocrites wanted to be *with those who sit*; the believers are those who believed *with* the Messenger ﷺ and strove *with* him. The passage sets the two companies against each other.

**Their portion.** *Such are they for whom are* **الْخَيْرَاتُ** — *the good things*.
