Ibn Kathir specifies: this is in the Hereafter, **in the gardens of al-Firdaws and the high grades** — al-Firdaws being the name he uses here for the gardens of Paradise. The answer to ayah 85's question is now complete: the goods that mattered were never the ones on display in this world. And *it is they who will be successful* — the successful ones are not those whose lives looked prosperous, but these.

Ayah 89 makes the reward concrete: **أَعَدَّ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ** — *Allah has prepared for them* Gardens under which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever. Note the wording: already prepared. And the passage ends with the verdict that overturns every worldly ledger: *that is the supreme success*. The hypocrites kept their wealth, their children and their comfort; the believers strove with theirs. The Qur'an tells you, without hedging, which of the two came out ahead.

## Living it

**Guard the gaze.** The command in ayah 85 was given to the Prophet ﷺ, which tells you no one is above needing it. When another person's prosperity impresses you, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's answer is the corrective: you are seeing only the surface of what they possess. Wealth accompanied by heedlessness towards the Hereafter is not a mercy being withheld from you.

**Peace is not purchasable.** Things of comfort can be collected; peace cannot, because — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — peace and comfort are things of the heart. Any plan for contentment that runs entirely through acquisition is a plan that has already failed for the people in ayah 85.

**Capability is the question.** From Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of *the capable ones*: those who genuinely could not go had at least some obvious excuse to stay behind, and the Qur'an does not chase them. The weight falls on those with the supplies, means and ability. Before excusing yourself from something the religion asks of you, ask honestly which group you are in.

**Watch the word "content."** What ayah 87 records, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, is that they were *content* to be with those who sit behind. It is worth asking about one's own ease with being absent.

**Take the seal seriously.** Ibn Kathir ties the sealing of the hearts to their staying away from Jihad and from accompanying the Messenger ﷺ, and he states plainly what follows: they understand neither what benefits them so that they might do it, nor what harms them so that they might avoid it. That is what is at stake — not only a missed act, but understanding itself.

**Spend and go.** Ayah 88 names the two things the believers put forward: their wealth and their lives. Ayah 89 answers that with Gardens already prepared, to dwell in forever — and calls it the supreme success.

passages.title: Who is excused from marching and who is not
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat sort out everyone who did not march with the army: who has a real excuse, who has none, and who was left behind with a broken heart. Read together, they draw a line — not between those who went and those who stayed, but between the truthful and the false, whichever side of the city gate they ended up on.

One Arabic word runs through the unit and holds it together: **سَبِيل (sabīl)**. In ayah 91 Allah says **مَا عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ** — "No means (of complaint) can there be against the doers of good." In ayah 93 He says **إِنَّمَا السَّبِيلُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ يَسْتَأْذِنُونَكَ وَهُمْ أَغْنِيَاءُ** — "The means (of complaint) is only against those who are rich, and yet ask exemption." It is the same word both times, rendered in our translation as "blame". The passage is, in effect, a verdict delivered in two halves: against these people there is no case; against those, there is. Everything in between — the excuses of ayah 90, the tears of ayah 92 — is the evidence on which that verdict turns.

## Two ways of staying behind (ayah 90)

Ayah 90 opens on the bedouins who lived around Al-Madinah. Ibn Kathir explains that they asked for permission to remain behind from the fighting, coming to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to explain to him their weakness and inability to join. Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that these were people who *had* valid excuses — and Ibn Kathir gives the reason for reading them that way: because of what Allah says immediately afterwards, **وَقَعَدَ الَّذِينَ كَذَبُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ**, "and those who had lied to Allah and His Messenger sat at home." The second clause is set against the first. Ibn Kathir notes the telling detail in it: those people did not even ask for permission.

There is a kind of person who at least keeps up the form of obedience by asking, and a kind who has dropped the form altogether. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same shape out of the ayah, saying that the details in it tell us there were two kinds of people among the bedouins of the desert. The first visited the Prophet ﷺ and requested to be excused and allowed to stay behind. The second — the arrogant and rebellious among them — did not even bother to take the trouble of excusing themselves. They just stayed behind.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah that when the Prophet ﷺ allowed Jadd ibn Qays not to go out, some hypocrites also came to him, offered their excuses and sought his permission to stay out. He let them have the permission — but he realised they were making false excuses, and so he turned away from them. This ayah was revealed then. It made clear that their excuse was unacceptable, and they were served with the warning of a painful punishment.

**A mercy hidden in a single word.** The threat at the end of the ayah is not aimed at everyone who stayed: **سَيُصِيبُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ** — "a painful torment will seize *those of them who disbelieve*." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that by saying "those of them who disbelieve", a hint was given that the excuse of some of them was not a matter of disbelief or hypocrisy at all, but of natural laziness — and that those people were not to be affected by the punishment falling on the disbelievers. Notice the precision of the Qur'an: it can rebuke a mixed group without flattening it, and it will not let a lazy believer be swept into the sentence passed on a hypocrite.

## "No way against them" — the genuine excuses (ayah 91)

Having just narrowed the threat, the passage now turns fully to the other side of the ledger. Ibn Kathir says that Allah mentions here the valid excuses that permit one to stay away from the fighting, and he draws attention to the order in which they come.

**First, the excuses that stay with a person.** Ibn Kathir says Allah first mentions the excuses that remain with a person — the weakness in the body that disallows one from going out, such as blindness, limping, and so forth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture: these were sincere Muslims deprived of taking part because they were genuinely incapable of it. Some were blind, or sick, or handicapped. Their excuse, it says, was all too evident.

**Then the excuses that are not permanent.** Ibn Kathir mentions two together here: an illness that would prevent one from fighting in the cause of Allah, or poverty that prevents preparing for the campaign. Both come and go; neither is written into the body for life. And what that poverty meant in practice is spelled out in the very next ayah — no animal to ride.

But the exemption is not automatic. Two conditions sit inside the ayah and inside Ibn Kathir's comment. The first is the clause "**if they are sincere and true (in duty) to Allah and His Messenger**." The excuse of the body is only accepted where the heart is loyal — the exemption is written for people whose absence is a matter of incapacity, not of wanting out.

The second condition Ibn Kathir spells out: there is no sin in these cases if they remain behind, **providing that** when they remain behind, they do not spread malice or try to discourage Muslims from fighting, but observe good behaviour all the while in that state. This is a searching test. The man who cannot go can still do enormous damage from home with his tongue — sowing doubt, magnifying the danger, running down those who went. Sit out with a genuine excuse and a loyal heart and you are among **الْمُحْسِنِين**, the doers of good; sit out and corrode the morale of those who marched, and the excuse has stopped covering you.

Hence the closing of the ayah, which Ibn Kathir quotes as the proof of exactly this point: **مَا عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ ۚ وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ** — "No means (of complaint) can there be against the doers of good. And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Notice that after clearing them completely, Allah still closes with forgiveness and mercy — as if to reassure the sincere man who cannot stop worrying that his absence counted against him.

**How the early Muslims used this ayah.** Ibn Kathir records that Al-Awzaʿi said: the people went out for the *Istisqāʾ*, the prayer for rain. Bilal bin Saʿd stood up, praised Allah and thanked Him, then said, "O those who are present! Do you concur that wrong has been done?" They said, "Yes, by Allah!" He said, "O Allah! We hear Your statement, *No means (of complaint) can there be against the doers of good.* O Allah! We admit our errors, so forgive us and give us mercy and rain." He then raised his hands, and the people raised theirs — and rain was sent down on them. A whole congregation stood under this ayah, said out loud that they had done wrong, and asked anyway.

## The ones who wept (ayah 92)

If ayah 91 states the rule, ayah 92 gives it a face. Mujahid said it was revealed about Bani Muqarrin, from the tribe of Muzaynah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them. These were men ready to take part — in its words, *dying* to go — who could not make the trip because they had no animal to ride. The journey was long and the weather was very hot. They told the Prophet ﷺ how eager they were and how unfortunate it was that they had nothing to ride on, and requested him to see if they could have some mounts. He had nothing to give: **قُلْتَ لَا أَجِدُ مَا أَحْمِلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ** — "I can find no mounts for you."

And then the ayah shows us their backs as they walk away: "they turned back, with their eyes **overflowing** with tears of grief that they could not find anything to spend." Look closely at what they are weeping over. Not danger, not hardship, not being shamed in front of others — grief **that they could not find anything to spend**. Their sorrow is at being shut out of a cost they wanted to pay.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that there are many events of this nature recorded in the books of exegesis and history, and that different things happened to different men. To some of those who came initially, the Prophet ﷺ had no choice but to say there was no arrangement to provide them mounts. But they returned from him weeping, and when they kept weeping in despair, Allah took care of them in His own way: six camels arrived before the Prophet ﷺ right at that time, and he let them have these (reported from Mazhari). Then ʿUthman arranged mounts for three of them, though he had already made similar arrangements for many more of them earlier.

**And for those who still could not go.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Al-Hasan said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Some people have remained behind you in Al-Madinah; and you never spent anything, crossed a valley, or afflicted hardship on an enemy, but they were sharing the reward with you."* He then recited this very ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has a basis in what he calls the Two Sahihs — the two collections of Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — from Anas, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Some people have remained behind in Al-Madinah and you never crossed a valley or marched forth, but they were with you."* They said, "While they are still at Al-Madinah?" He said: *"Yes, as they have been held back by a (legal) excuse."*

This is one of the most consoling teachings in the Sunnah. The men weeping at their doorsteps in Al-Madinah were credited with every valley the army crossed. And note the reason the Prophet ﷺ gives for it, in his own words: they were held back by an excuse. The excuse that shut them out of the march is the very thing that kept them in the reward.

## The seal on the heart (ayah 93)

Ayah 93 closes the file on the other group, and it does so by picking the word *sabīl* back up. In ayah 91 there was no *sabīl* against the doers of good; here, **إِنَّمَا السَّبِيلُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ يَسْتَأْذِنُونَكَ وَهُمْ أَغْنِيَاءُ** — "The means (of complaint) is only against those who are rich, and yet ask exemption." Set that beside ayah 92 and the contrast is almost unbearable: one group weeps because it has nothing to spend, the other has everything to spend and asks to be let off.

Ibn Kathir says that Allah then criticised those who seek permission to remain behind while they are rich, admonishing them for wanting to stay behind with the women who remained in their homes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point bluntly: at the end the warning is repeated, that particularly cursed are those who, despite their ability, elected to stay away from the fighting like women — and it says the phrase "those who ask your permission despite being rich" means exactly this.

Then the final line: **وَطَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ فَهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ** — "and Allah has sealed up their hearts, so that they know not." A sealed thing is a closed thing: nothing further gets in. And note how Ibn Kathir completes the sense of the ending: they know not *what they are losing*. That is the punishment described inside the ayah itself — not a blow that lands from outside, but a blindness to what has just slipped past. The comparison the passage leaves us with makes it vivid: a man of means talks his way out and does not even know what he has forfeited, while a poor man of Muzaynah, sitting in Al-Madinah with wet eyes and no camel, is held back only by his excuse — and is with the army all the way.

## What the passage asks of us

**Bring your inability, don't just disappear.** The difference in ayah 90 between the two kinds of bedouins is that one group came and presented itself and the other did not bother. Even in weakness, keep the relationship — the request, the honesty, the showing up.

**Test the excuse, not the outcome.** Ibn Kathir's list is instructive because it is concrete: bodily incapacity, illness, lack of means. The passage exempts people from what they genuinely cannot do; it exposes people who could and would not. Only you and Allah know which one your reason is.

**A genuine excuse still comes with duties.** Ibn Kathir's condition stands over anyone sitting out: no spreading of malice, no discouraging those who are doing the work, good conduct throughout. The exemption covers your absence; it does not license your tongue.

**Wealth is not a way out; it is what is being asked of you.** Ayah 93 falls precisely on those whose means made them more obligated, not less.

**Grieve when you cannot serve.** The tears of ayah 92 are not a footnote in the passage; they are the reason Allah cleared these men in His own Book, and they stand behind the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that people held back in Al-Madinah by an excuse were sharing the reward with those who marched. If your circumstances keep you from something good, let the wanting be real — and remember how ayah 91 ends, with Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Excuses offered when the army returns
passages.tafsir:
**Three ayat, one scene.** The army is coming home to Madinah, and the men who stayed behind are preparing their story. Ayah 94 shows them offering excuses; ayah 95 shows them swearing oaths so they will be left alone; ayah 96 shows them swearing oaths so they will be liked again. What binds the passage together is that each request receives its own answer — and the three answers are not the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the passage exactly this way: as **three instructions** given to the Prophet ﷺ, one in each ayah. Reading them against each other is the key to the passage.

## The scene these ayat describe

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the line back to what came just before. Those earlier verses dealt with hypocrites who produced false excuses *while the expedition was still being prepared*, and who succeeded in being allowed to stay behind. These three ayat deal with the second act: the same sort of men now visiting the Prophet ﷺ *after his return* from the campaign, offering false excuses for their absence from it.

And here is the detail that unlocks the whole passage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these verses were revealed **before** the Prophet ﷺ reached Madinah, and that they told him beforehand what was about to happen — that the hypocrites would come to him as soon as he arrived and would offer their excuses. "And so it happened."

Set those two facts side by side. The verses came down before he reached Madinah; the excuses were offered after he arrived. The answer, then, was already in hand before the excuse was spoken.

## Ayah 94 — "Offer no excuses"

The reply the Prophet ﷺ is told to give has four movements, and each one closes a door.

**"Present no excuses, we shall not believe you."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: *we shall not believe what you say*. The problem is not that the excuse is weak. The problem is the man giving it.

**"Allah has already informed us of the news concerning you."** Ibn Kathir explains: *Allah has exposed your news to us*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what that exposure covered — Allah had already told the Prophet ﷺ about the condition of their thinking and their doing, including the details of their wicked plans and their secret intentions. That alone was enough to prove them liars, and so, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, offering excuses makes no sense. There is nothing to negotiate with a man who has already read the file.

**"And Allah and His Messenger will observe your deeds."** Two commentators open this clause in two complementary directions.

Ibn Kathir reads it as exposure in this world: *your actions will be made public to people in this life*. What is hidden inside a man does not stay hidden; conduct leaks, and eventually the community sees.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the clause as **respite**. Because the wording stipulates that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ shall see what they do and how they do it, the sense is that action will be taken in consonance with their behaviour pattern. The door was still open: they could still make their tawbah (repentance), renounce nifāq (hypocrisy), and become true Muslims — and if they repented sincerely, their sins would stand forgiven. Otherwise, these false excuses were not going to do them any good.

That is a remarkable thing to find in the middle of so severe a passage. The words are not "you are finished." They are: *we will watch what you actually do.* Statements are refused; deeds are still being accepted.

**"Then you will be brought back to the All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will inform you of what you used to do."** Note how the ayah arranges its knowers. The Messenger ﷺ is joined to the seeing of deeds — which Ibn Kathir explains as actions becoming public among people in this life — while the title *ʿĀlim al-ghayb wa'l-shahādah*, the All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, is reserved for Allah alone. That is the final court. Ibn Kathir: Allah will inform you of your deeds, whether they were good or evil, and will recompense you for them. The hypocrite's whole strategy is managing what people can see. This clause tells him that the file he cannot reach will be opened and read back to him.

## Ayah 95 — the request that is granted

Now the excuses escalate into oaths sworn by the name of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the manoeuvre: these people will come to the Prophet ﷺ after his return to Madinah, impress him with their feigned oaths, and try to satisfy him. And the ayah tells us precisely what those oaths were meant to buy: **لِتُعْرِضُوا عَنْهُمْ** — "so that you may turn away from them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the aim: that the believers ignore their absence from Jihād and spare them the reproach that was due for it. They wanted the subject dropped.

Then comes the surprise. Allah says: **فَأَعْرِضُوا عَنْهُمْ** — *so turn away from them*. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he might as well grant their wish.

But read what the granting means. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the sense of the instruction: "neither reproach and admonish, nor deal with pleasantly." This is not forgiveness; it is withdrawal. Ibn Kathir says the same from the other side — the hypocrites swore in apology so that the believers would turn away from them *without admonishing them*, and therefore Allah ordered disgracing them by turning away from them. The very thing they asked for became the sentence passed on them. They wanted to be left alone. They were left alone.

Why withhold even the reproach? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reasoning is sober: reproach usually brings no good — when they have no faith in their heart, and they do not want to have it either, what would come out of reproach? "So, why waste good time!" Admonition is a gift given to someone who might receive it. Where the sources tell us that willingness is absent, correction becomes noise.

**"Surely they are rijs."** Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *impure inwardly and in their creed*. The impurity named here is not on the clothes or the body; Ibn Kathir locates it inside — in the man's inward state and in what he believes. That is why this ayah's remedy is separation rather than argument: an apology does not reach the place where the problem is.

**"And Hell is their dwelling place, a recompense for that which they used to earn."** Ibn Kathir: their destination in the end will be Jahannam, a recompense for what they earned *of sins and evil deeds*. The end named here is presented as a recompense — the matching return on what was done.

## Ayah 96 — the request that is refused

Ayah 96 looks at first like a repetition of ayah 95. It is not. The oath is the same; the goal has grown. In 95 they swore so that the believers would *turn away*. In 96 they swear **لِتَرْضَوْا عَنْهُمْ** — so that you may be *pleased* with them. Not merely to be left alone, but to be approved of.

And here the answer flips. On this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: the order of Allah is that their wish was **not** to be granted, and the Prophet ﷺ was not to be pleased with them. Distance could be given. Approval could not.

Then the ayah closes off even that hope from behind: "and even if you are pleased with them, Allah is certainly not pleased with the rebellious people." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of it — even if the believers were to be pleased with them, it was not going to work for them in any manner, because Allah is not pleased with them; and how could Allah be pleased with them when they are still adamant about their denial and hypocrisy? Ibn Kathir makes the same point about the believers forgiving them when they swear: the community's forgiveness does not move the verdict stated at the end of the ayah.

This is the deepest lesson in the passage. The hypocrite's entire craft is the management of human opinion — the right excuse, the right oath, the right face at the right moment. Ayah 96 informs him that human opinion, even the opinion of the very best of people, is not what decides the matter. And the sources give a stated reason for the refusal: they remain adamant about their denial and hypocrisy — the very thing they are swearing about.

**"Fāsiqīn."** Ibn Kathir defines them as those who rebel against the obedience of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and glosses *fisq* as **"deviation."** Note that they are not called liars here, though their excuses were false, nor cowards, though they stayed behind. They are named by their relationship to obedience, because that is what the whole episode was really about.

## What the passage asks of us

**Track the two audiences.** These men were working hard on their record with people. Ayah 94 shows which record is permanent: the deeds go back to the All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, and are read out there.

**Do not let an oath end a conversation.** Both ayah 95 and ayah 96 show the name of Allah being used as a tool — sworn, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, as feigned oaths meant to buy silence or to buy goodwill. The passage teaches the believer to notice when a solemn word is being used as a lever rather than a testimony.

**Understand what "turn away" is and what it is not.** The withdrawal ordered in ayah 95 rests on a condition that the sources state plainly — no faith in the heart, and no desire for it. And ayah 94, in the same breath, holds the door of repentance open and says that deeds will still be watched. Where the door of tawbah is still open, this passage keeps it open.

**Bring deeds, not explanations.** The one sentence in this passage that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads as respite is "And Allah and His Messenger will observe your deeds." Excuses were refused outright; oaths bought only distance; the community's pleasure was declared useless. What was left open was action — repenting sincerely, renouncing hypocrisy, and becoming true Muslims, upon which, the source says, their sins would stand forgiven.

passages.title: Bedouins in disbelief, bedouins in faith, the foremost
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat climb from the very bottom of the scale to the very top. Ayat 97–98 describe the desert Arabs sunk in disbelief and hypocrisy; ayah 99 shows that the same desert produced sincere believers; ayah 100 lifts our eyes to the whole body of sincere believers and their degrees of excellence. Running through the passage is a single test applied to two kinds of people: **what does a person think of the wealth he parts with for Allah?** A fine, or a nearness? The answer exposes the heart.

## Where the passage stands: from the city's hypocrites to the desert's

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene plainly: the previous verses described the hypocrites *of Madinah*; these verses mention the hypocrites who lived on the desert around the outskirts of Madinah.

### The word *al-aʿrāb*: a class, not a race

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. **الأعراب (al-aʿrāb) is not the plural of العرب (al-ʿarab), "the Arabs."** It is an *ism al-jamʿ* — a collective noun — and it is used for the **Bedouins of the desert**. Its singular is *al-aʿrābiyy*, formed the way *al-Ansāriyy* is the singular of *al-Ansār*.

So the passage is not a verdict on Arabs as a people but a description of a way of life. The reason the sources give for the verdict is entirely about **distance from knowledge**, not about ancestry.

## "Harder in disbelief, further from the limits" (97)

Ibn Kathir opens by noting what the passage as a whole establishes: among the Bedouins there are **disbelievers, hypocrites and believers** — all three. Then Allah states that the disbelief and hypocrisy found among them is *worse and deeper* than that of others, and that they are the most likely to be ignorant of the commandments Allah has revealed to His Messenger ﷺ.

The ayah gives its own reason: **وَأَجْدَرُ أَلَّا يَعْلَمُوا حُدُودَ مَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِ** — "and more likely not to know the *ḥudūd*, the limits, of what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the mechanism plainly: these people generally remained ignorant and hard-hearted because **they lived far away from knowledge and from the knowledgeable**. The Qur'an did not come before them, nor did they have access to its meanings, explanations and injunctions.

### The man who did not know which hand

Ibn Kathir reports that al-Aʿmash narrated from Ibrahim an incident that makes the ayah vivid. A Bedouin man sat down next to Zayd bin Sawhan while Zayd was speaking to his friends. Zayd had lost his hand during the battle of Nahawand. The Bedouin said, "By Allah, I like your speech — however, your hand causes me suspicion." Zayd said, "Why are you suspicious because of my hand? It is the left hand that is cut." The Bedouin replied, "By Allah, I do not know which hand they cut off for committing theft — is it the right or the left?"

Zayd's response was to recite this very ayah: *"Allah has said the truth: the bedouins are the worst in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely to not know the limits which Allah has revealed to His Messenger."* Here was a man confident enough to suspect a Companion of theft, yet ignorant of the most basic detail of the ruling he had invoked — exactly the combination the ayah names.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites a narration of **Imam Ahmad** from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "He who lives in the desert becomes hard-hearted, he who follows the game becomes heedless, and he who associates with the rulers falls into fitnah."

Ibn Kathir adds that **Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i** collected this hadith, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "*Hasan Gharib*." Three settings, three injuries: isolation coarsens, chasing the hunt distracts, nearness to power tempts.

Ibn Kathir also relates that the Prophet ﷺ once had to give a Bedouin man many gifts in return for what the man had given him as a gift — after which the Prophet ﷺ said that he had almost decided not to accept a gift except from someone of Quraysh, Thaqafi, the Ansar or Daws. Ibn Kathir explains why: these people lived in cities — Makkah, at-Ta'if, al-Madinah and Yemen — and therefore their conduct and manners were nicer than those of the hard-hearted Bedouins.

### "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"

The ayah closes with **وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ**. On this Ibn Kathir writes: Allah knows those who deserve to be taught faith and knowledge, and He wisely distributes knowledge or ignorance, faith or disbelief and hypocrisy, between His servants. **He is never questioned as to what He does**, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

The upshot is humbling. That revelation reached *you*, and its meanings were opened to *you*, is not an achievement of yours. It is a distribution, made by the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

## The same wealth, two hearts (98 and 99)

### The first man: giving felt as a fine

**مَن يَتَّخِذُ مَا يُنفِقُ مَغْرَمًا** — "one who takes what he spends as a *maghram*." Ibn Kathir glosses this: what they spend in the cause of Allah they look upon **as a fine — as a loss and a burden**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the word as **a penalty**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then opens up the inner life behind that word: such people hardly have any faith in their heart. When it comes to Salah they will perform it — but just to camouflage their disbelief. They will even fulfil the obligation of Zakah — while their hearts keep worrying as to why they had to put good money down the drain. And so they **always look forward to the time when the Muslims are hit by some calamity or defeat** that might possibly deliver them from having to pay this penalty.

That is exactly what the next clause says: **وَيَتَرَبَّصُ بِكُمُ الدَّوَائِرَ** — "and he watches for calamities for you." Ibn Kathir: **awaiting afflictions and disasters to strike you**.

**The key word.** *Ad-dawā'ir* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders as "the cycles of time" — is the plural of *dā'irah*. According to the Arabic lexicon, a *dā'irah* is **the changed state that shifts away from the good state into a bad one**.

The Qur'an's answer: **عَلَيْهِمْ دَائِرَةُ السَّوْءِ** — "upon *them* is the evil cycle." Ibn Kathir: evil will touch them instead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: the evil state of affairs they wish would strike the Muslims is going to descend upon them all right — and because their words and deeds are such, they will find themselves far more disgraced.

Then: **وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ**. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah **hears the invocation of His servants and knows who deserves victory and who deserves failure**. These calculations are made quietly, out in the tents, at a safe distance from Madinah — and they are heard.

### The second man: giving felt as a nearness

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the turn: it was considered appropriate that the true and staunch Muslims **from among the same stock of Bedouins** should also be mentioned — very much in line with the typical style of the Qur'an — so that it stands established that **the Bedouins too are not all alike**. Among them there are many sincere Muslims, and people of sense and discernment as well. Their style of life is different.

Both men part with wealth. The first "takes what he spends" as *maghram*, a fine. The second "takes what he spends" as **قُرُبَاتٍ عِندَ اللَّهِ** — *qurubāt*, means of nearness to Allah — **وَصَلَوَاتِ الرَّسُولِ**, and as a cause of receiving the Messenger's ﷺ invocations. Identical outward deed; opposite inward reality. Ibn Kathir calls this **the praiseworthy type of Bedouin**: they give charity in Allah's cause as a way of achieving nearness to Allah, and seeking the Messenger's ﷺ invocation for their benefit.

**Why hope for the Prophet's ﷺ prayer?** That charity brings one near to Allah is obvious, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān; but the hope of prayers from the Prophet ﷺ rests on a different basis. Wherever the Qur'an asked the Prophet ﷺ to collect the Zakah, it also directed him to pray for those who pay it. The forthcoming ayah 103 is a good example: *"Take out of their wealth a ṣadaqah through which you may cleanse and purify them, and pray for them"* — **وَصَلِّ عَلَيْهِمْ**, where the instruction to pray is expressed with the word *ṣalāh*. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is precisely why the sense of the Prophet's ﷺ prayers is carried in our ayah by the same word: **ṣalawāt ar-rasūl**.

Then comes the divine confirmation: **أَلَا إِنَّهَا قُرْبَةٌ لَّهُمْ** — "Indeed these are a means of nearness for them." Ibn Kathir's comment is one line, and it lands: **they will attain what they sought.** And the ending is pure generosity: **سَيُدْخِلُهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ** — Allah will admit them to His mercy; certainly Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful. Not merely paid a reward — brought *inside* the mercy.

## The foremost (100)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes the movement: this verse mentions **all** sincere and true Muslims, along with their relative degrees of excellence.

**وَالسَّابِقُونَ الْأَوَّلُونَ مِنَ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنصَارِ وَالَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُم بِإِحْسَانٍ** — "And the foremost, the first, of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them with excellence."

### Who are "the first and foremost"?

The commentators name different milestones:

- **Those who prayed towards both qiblahs** — that is, who embraced Islam before the change of the qiblah. Ibn Kathir reports this from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, Saʿid bin al-Musayyib, Muhammad bin Sirin, al-Hasan and Qatadah, describing them as those who performed the prayer towards the two qiblahs with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — first towards Jerusalem and later towards the Kaʿbah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah for this view.
- **Those who took part in the battle of Badr** — the view of ʿAṭā' ibn Abi Rabāḥ, per Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.
- **Those who were party to the Bayʿat ar-Riḍwān**, the pledge taken at the time of the expedition of Hudaybiyyah — the view of ash-Shaʿbi, reported by both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.

And according to each of these views, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the rest of the Companions — Muhajir or Ansari — fall into a second category.

### One small word, two readings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that all of the above rests on taking **مِن (min)** in *min al-muhājirīn wal-anṣār* for *tabʿīḍ* — the *min* that denotes a part of something, translated "**out of** the Emigrants and the Helpers," which sets up two categories of the noble Companions. This is how most commentators took it.

But Tafsir Mazhari, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, records another interpretation: that this *min* is not for *tabʿīḍ* but for *bayān* — the *min* that explains the preceding words and stands for "**that is**." On that reading the ayah says: "As for the first and the foremost people, that is, all the Emigrants and all the Helpers…" — meaning that all the Muhajirin and the Ansar are the first and foremost as compared with the rest of the Muslim Ummah.

**And "those who followed them with iḥsān"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the phrase as the Muslims who followed the footsteps of the first and foremost precisely and perfectly in all fields of deeds and morals. On the first reading, all Muslims after the Companions fall into this second category, right through to the Day of Qiyamah. On the other reading, the expression takes in the great people who came after the Companions — the **Tābiʿīn**, the Successors, in Islamic terminology — and after them all Muslims who will keep appearing right through to Qiyamah and who follow the Companions precisely and perfectly in purity of faith and goodness of deeds.

### "Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him"

Ibn Kathir states it directly: Allah mentions that He is pleased foremost with the Muhajirin, the Ansar and those who followed them in faith, and that they are well-pleased with Him, for He has prepared for them the gardens of delight and eternal joy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a beautiful piece of reasoning. Someone asked Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓi what he said about the noble Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. He answered: **"The Sahabah, all of them, are in Jannah"** — irrespective of whether mistakes and sins may have been committed by some of them. Asked on what basis he said that, he replied: read this ayah. What is said of the Companions carries no condition — *Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Allah*. But a **condition** is placed in the case of the Tābiʿīn: *following with goodness*. The presence of a condition in the one clause and its absence in the other is the argument.

The author of Tafsir Mazhari, after reporting that statement, says that in his view another verse carries an even more solid proof: *"Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest… they are greater in degree than those who spent and fought afterwards — yet to all Allah has promised al-ḥusnā, the best."* First or last, all were promised al-ḥusnā.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in Hadith the Prophet ﷺ has been reported to have said that the fire of Jahannam cannot touch the Muslim who has seen him, or who has seen those who have seen him — reported from **Tirmidhi**, from Sayyidnā Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him).

### A note of warning

Both commentaries close on the same warning. Ibn Kathir writes that woe is to those who dislike or curse the Companions, or any one of them — especially their master after the Messenger ﷺ, the best and most righteous among them, the Ṣiddīq and grand Khalifah, Abu Bakr bin Abi Quḥafah, may Allah be pleased with him. He names **the Rafidah (a sect of Shiites)** as the enemies of the best Companions, who hate and curse them — we seek refuge with Allah from such evil — and he asks where such minds stand in relation to believing in the Qur'an: **they curse those whom Allah stated He is pleased with.** As for the followers of the Sunnah, Ibn Kathir says, they are pleased with those whom Allah is pleased with; they are followers, not innovators.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution aimed at a subtler danger: people who criticise some of the revered Companions on the basis of what transpired during their mutual controversies, with the aim of sowing seeds of suspicion and discord in the hearts of those who hold them in esteem, are really treading a dangerous course. We seek the protection of Allah against it.

## Living it

**Check which ayah your giving belongs to.** The Zakah is the same amount either way; the whole distance between ayah 98 and ayah 99 lies in what happens in your chest as the money leaves. Rename it in your own heart before you transfer it.

**Do not let your surroundings do your thinking.** Both commentaries locate the problem in the setting: far from knowledge and the knowledgeable, with the Qur'an never placed before them. Whatever desert a person lives in, the remedy points the same way — get close to the Qur'an's meanings, and close to people who know them.

**Watch what you find yourself hoping for.** Looking forward to the day the Muslims are struck by calamity is presented here as what a heart with hardly any faith in it does — and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Private hopes are not private.

**Guard your tongue about the Companions.** The passage ends with Allah announcing His pleasure with them. The safest place a Muslim can stand is beside that declaration, never in argument with it.

passages.title: Hidden hypocrites and those who confessed their sins
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat sort out the people who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. Ayah 101 deals with hypocrites so skilled at concealment that even the Prophet ﷺ did not know who they were; ayat 102–106 turn to believers who failed and then owned their failure. What happens to a person whose record is not clean? Concealment ends in a punishment repeated twice over, while confession opens onto forgiveness, purification through charity, and a mercy worth waiting for.

## The map: who stayed behind from Tabuk

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background. The call to Tabuk came in extreme heat, over a long journey, against the trained army of a great state — the first such episode in Islamic history. People split into five groups: those who prepared at the first call; those who hesitated and then joined (ayah 117); the genuinely handicapped (ayah 91, "There is no blame on the weak"); sincere believers with no excuse who stayed back out of laziness; and the hypocrites. Ayah 101 closes the file on that fifth group; ayat 102 and 106 open the file on the fourth.

## Ayah 101: the hypocrites no one could see

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the distinction. The hypocrites named in earlier verses had exposed themselves through their words and deeds, and the Prophet ﷺ did realise what they were. Ayah 101 speaks of a different set — bedouins in the settlements ringing Madinah, and residents of the city — whose camouflage was so perfect it stayed hidden from him until then.

Of these Allah says **maradū ʿalā al-nifāq**. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase: they insisted on hypocrisy and continued in it. Not a slip or a wavering — settled practice, hypocrisy worn smooth by repetition.

**"You know them not; We know them."** Ibn Kathir anticipates the objection: does this contradict "Had We willed, We could have shown them to you… but surely, you will know them by the tone of their speech" (47:30)? No — that ayah describes them by their *characteristics*, not that the Messenger ﷺ knew every individual carrying doubt and hypocrisy. He knew some of those who kept his company were hypocrites, and saw them day and night, without knowing exactly who they were. Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet ﷺ did inform Hudhayfah of the names of fourteen or fifteen hypocrites — but that knowledge was specific to that case, not a disclosure of all their names, and Allah knows best.

Qatadah drew a lesson from this that still stings. What is the matter, he asked, with people who claim knowledge about others, saying "So-and-so is in Paradise and so-and-so is in the Fire" — when if you asked such a man about *himself* he would say, "I do not know"? You have more knowledge of yourself than of other people, and you have assumed a job the Prophets before you refrained from assuming: Nuh said, "And what knowledge have I of what they used to do" (26:112); Shuʿayb said, "And I am not a guardian over you" (11:86).

**"We shall punish them twice."** The scholars read the two punishments differently; the readings complement rather than compete. Mujahid said: by killing and capture; in another narration from him, by hunger and the torment of the grave. ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said the torment in this life strikes their wealth and offspring, reciting ayah 55: "let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; Allah only wants to punish them with these things in the life of this world." The same afflictions, Ibn Kathir notes, torment them but bring reward for the believers. And as for the torment of the Hereafter, "thereafter they shall be brought back to a great torment" — Ibn Kathir says plainly that this is in the Fire.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds punishments that need no external event. In this world, such a man is consumed by the concern to hide his hypocrisy and the fear that it may be exposed; and it is no small punishment to be under compulsion to respect and follow Islam and Muslims outwardly, despite extreme malice and hostility toward them. Then there is the punishment of the grave and the punishment of Barzakh — the state between death and resurrection — which will reach them well before Qiyamah (doomsday) and the Hereafter.

## Ayah 102: the men tied to the pillars

Ibn Kathir marks the transition: having described the hypocrites who avoided the battle out of denial and doubt, Allah turns to the *disobedient* — men who stayed away out of laziness and a preference for comfort, while truly believing. They admitted their error to themselves and to their Lord. They had performed good deeds before, as well as this evil deed — and for such people there was forgiveness and pardon.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the incident from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ten believers missed Tabuk with no valid excuse. Afterwards they were sorry, and seven of them — all narrations agree Abu Lubabah was among them, though the other names differ — tied themselves to the pillars of the Prophet's Mosque, resolved to stay bound like prisoners until the Prophet ﷺ accepted their repentance and untied them.

When the Prophet ﷺ saw them tied up and was told what they had resolved, he said: "By Allah, I too shall not untie them until Allah orders me to do that. The crime is serious." Then this ayah came down, and he ordered that they be untied.

From Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab: when people came to untie Abu Lubabah, he refused — he would stay tied until the Prophet ﷺ himself, with his pleasure, untied him with his own blessed hands. So when the Prophet ﷺ came out for Fajr, he untied him personally.

**What were the "mixed" deeds?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists them. On the good side: faith, prayer, fasting, participation in earlier battles alongside the Prophet ﷺ — and then, after Tabuk, their admission of misconduct, their shame, their repentance. On the bad side: they had not gone out to Tabuk, and in that one respect had acted in a manner resembling the approach of the hypocrites.

**This verse belongs to everyone.** Ibn Kathir states it directly: the ayah is general, covering all sinners who combine good and evil and so become partly impure, though it was revealed about some people in specific. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Tafsir al-Qurtubi — its ruling valid until the Day of Qiyamah; whoever repents from his sins may hope to be pardoned and forgiven. Abu ʿUthman said of it: this verse of the Qurʼan brings great hope for this ummah.

## From the Sunnah: the half-beautiful men

Al-Bukhari records from Samurah bin Jundub that the Prophet ﷺ described a vision: two angels came to him and took him to a city built with bricks of gold and silver, where they met men, one part of whose bodies was as handsome as anything you ever saw and another part as ugly as anything you ever saw. The angels ordered them to go to a river and submerge themselves in it; they did, and came back, the ugliness gone from them, having become the most beautiful of forms. The angels said, "This is the garden of Eden, and this is your residence in it." And of those men: "they have mixed a deed that was righteous with another that was evil. Allah has pardoned them." Al-Bukhari records this hadith in short form in his commentary on this very ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same hadith within the account of the Ascension, where Jibril explains that the bright faces were those who believed and then kept clean of sins — "those who have believed and have not mixed their faith with injustice" (6:82) — while those with spots and stains had done what was a mixture of good and evil, then repented, and Allah accepted their repentance. The sin is real, it shows on you, and it washes off.

## Ayat 103–104: charity as the finishing of repentance

Once their repentance was accepted and they were released from their self-imprisonment, these men presented their **entire wealth** to the Prophet ﷺ as a token of gratitude, so it could be given out as sadaqah. He refused, saying he did not have the authority to take it. Then came the command of ayah 103: "Take out of their wealth a sadaqah" — and he accepted one third of it.

He did not take the whole, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows why in the Arabic itself: *khudh **min** amwālihim*, "take **out of** their wealth." The preposition **min** is partitive — a portion, not the whole. Zeal offered everything; revelation set a limit.

**Why charity when the sin was already forgiven?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question: purification was accomplished through the very act of repentance, so what sense is there in saying that taking a portion of their wealth purifies them? The answer: the sin has been forgiven by virtue of the repentance, but it is quite possible that it left behind residual effects, and those traces could become a cause of falling into sin. Sadaqah removes the residue and makes the purification perfect.

**Zakah is worship, not a government tax.** The sadaqah is taken "through which you may cleanse and purify them" — a clear hint, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that zakah and sadaqat are not like taxes governments collect to run the system. Their purpose is to cleanse the men of wealth themselves from sins and from the germs of moral disease generated by greed for wealth. Collecting zakah yields two benefits — the owner's own purification, and support for the weaker members of society: orphans, widows, the handicapped, the poor and needy — but this passage names only the first, indicating that the giver's purification is the real objective and relief of the needy a corollary. Hence even where no orphan, widow or needy person is present, the obligation on the wealthy does not lapse. Zakah is a financial act of worship, very similar to prayer and fasting.

**The command outlives the man it was addressed to.** Ibn Kathir records that some bedouins later argued from this very ayah that paying zakah to the leader was legislated only to the Messenger ﷺ himself. Abu Bakr As-Siddiq and other Companions refuted that comprehension and fought them until they paid zakah to the Khalifah, just as they used to pay it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the debate: ʿUmar at first hesitated over waging jihad against such people — Muslims who did not deny that zakah was a religious obligation but took cover behind a verse — thinking they should not be treated as ordinary apostates are. Abu Bakr was immovable: "we shall wage Jihad against anyone who will differentiate between Salah and Zakah." The same logic would gut the prayer, since ayah 17:78 ("Establish prayer at the decline of the sun") also addresses the Prophet ﷺ yet binds the entire ummah. ʿUmar was satisfied, and the campaign went out by the consensus of the Companions. The principle, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from Tafsir al-Qurtubi, Ahkam al-Qurʼan of al-Jassas and Tafsir Mazhari: most Qurʼanic rulings came down against some particular background, yet nobody has ever confined them to it — absent certain proof of restriction, a ruling is universally applicable. So ayah 103 binds every Amir who succeeds the Prophet ﷺ, whose duty it is to administer the collection of zakah and ensure it is disbursed on authorised heads.

**"And pray for them."** *Wa ṣalli ʿalayhim* means, Ibn Kathir says, supplicate for them and ask Allah to forgive them. In the Sahih, Muslim records from ʿAbdullah bin Abi Awfa that whenever charity was brought to the Prophet ﷺ he would invoke Allah for the one who brought it; when his own father brought his, the Prophet ﷺ said, "O Allah, I invoke You for the family of Abu Awfa." Ibn ʿAbbas glossed "your ṣalāt are a **sakan** for them" as: a mercy for them. And "Allah is All-Hearer" of your invocation, "All-Knower" — Ibn Kathir adds — of those worthy of it.

Two points of adab (proper manners) from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. First, the word *salah* here means praying for Allah's mercy, and the Prophet ﷺ did use it for others, as in the supplication for the family of Abu Awfa; but later the word became special to the Prophets, peace be upon them, so the jurists say one should not now use it for anyone else on its own, to avoid ambiguity — though it is permissible alongside a Prophet ("O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon his family and his Companions"). Second, since the Prophet ﷺ was told here to pray for those who give sadaqah, some jurists rule this obligatory (wajib) on the Muslim head of state, while others take the command as recommendatory (mustahabb) — Qurtubi reports both.

**Ayah 104** turns this into a question aimed at the heart: "Know they not that Allah accepts repentance from His servants and accepts the Sadaqat?" Ibn Kathir reads it as encouragement toward both repentance and charity, because each of them erases, deletes and eradicates sins. He cites a narration from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah accepts charity, receives it in His Right Hand, and develops it for its giver just as one of you raises his pony, until the bite of food becomes as large as Uhud — and notes that the Book of Allah testifies to this hadith, here and in "Allah will destroy Riba and will give increase for Sadaqat" (2:276). ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud caught the same sense: "Charity falls in Allah's Hand before it falls in the needy's hand," and he then recited this ayah.

## Ayah 105: "Do deeds" — and know you are seen

Mujahid said this ayah carries a warning from Allah to those who defy His orders: their deeds will be shown to Allah, to the Messenger ﷺ and to the believers. Ibn Kathir says this will certainly occur on the Day of Resurrection — "That Day shall you be brought to Judgement, not a secret of you will be hidden" (69:18) — and that Allah might also expose some deeds to people in this life.

Al-Bukhari relates that ʿAishah said: if the good deeds of a Muslim person please you, then say, "Do deeds! Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers."

Read beside the hidden hypocrites of ayah 101, this answers the problem of concealment: you cannot audit another man's heart, and are not asked to. Do the work; the disclosure is Allah's business.

Ibn Kathir pairs this with a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Anas — and notes that only Imam Ahmad collected it — in which the Prophet ﷺ warned against being pleased with anyone's deeds until you see what he ends on: one might work with good deeds such that if he died then he would enter Paradise, then change and commit evil; and one might commit evil deeds such that if he died then he would enter the Fire, then change and perform good deeds. When Allah wants good for a servant He "employs" him before he dies — meaning, as the Prophet ﷺ explained when asked, that He directs him to perform good deeds and takes his life in that condition.

## Ayah 106: the three left waiting

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Ad-Dahhak and several others said this ayah refers to three men made to wait to know whether their repentance was accepted: Mararah bin Ar-Rabiʿ, Kaʿb bin Malik and Hilal bin Umayyah.

The distinction from ayah 102 is exact. Both groups stayed behind out of laziness and a preference for comfort, ease, ripe fruits and shade — not out of hypocrisy or doubt. But some of them tied themselves to the pillars, as Abu Lubabah and several of his friends did, and those men received their pardon first. These three did not, and so had not openly admitted their misconduct. The Prophet ﷺ therefore ordered the Companions to boycott them, so no Muslim would speak to them. When things reached those limits they learnt their lesson, confessed to their misconduct and repented sincerely, and orders were given for their pardon (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Their release comes later in the sūrah: "And the three who stayed behind, until for them the earth, vast as it is, was straitened."

Meanwhile ayah 106 leaves them suspended: "whether He will punish them or will forgive them." Ibn Kathir explains: they are at Allah's mercy — if He wills, He pardons them or punishes them. And the sentence to read slowly: **Allah's mercy comes before His anger.** The ayah closes, "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise" — knowing who deserves the punishment and who the pardon, All-Wise in His actions and His statements; there is no deity worthy of worship nor Lord besides Him.

## Living it

**Stop reading hearts.** Qatadah's rebuke is the practical yield of ayah 101. If the Prophet ﷺ was told "you know them not," no one after him is licensed to assign people to Paradise or the Fire. Turn that scrutiny on yourself.

**Confess plainly, and early.** The men at the pillars did not explain themselves or minimise; they named the fault as a fault. That is what ayah 102 honours — not the rope, but the acknowledgement. And the three of ayah 106, who did not openly admit their misconduct, also waited longer for their relief.

**Let charity finish what repentance starts** — with the restraint of "take **out of** their wealth."

**Do not despair over a mixed record.** This is the ayah Abu ʿUthman called great hope for this ummah: men half-beautiful and half-ugly walked into the river and came out whole. But hold that hope beside ayah 105 — no one's file is closed while he still breathes. Keep working, and ask Allah to direct you to a righteous deed at the end and take your soul while you are doing it.
